Plant species removal caused slight increases in bacterial alpha-diversity, paralleled by less diverse but more even plant communities. We show that soil acidification by urea fertilization outweighs plant species loss in its negative effect on bacterial soil biodiversity in Tibetan grasslands.
authors: Wu D, Quzong C, Jia Z, Schwalb A, Guggenberger G, Wang S, Dorji T, Pester M.

title: Iron limitation reduces diatom carbon flow to bacteria through shifts in exometabolite consumption.
abstract: Iron is required for photosynthesis and thus affects carbon fixation rates in widespread aquatic regions where availability is limited. Turnover of aquatic photosynthetically derived fixed carbon is largely constrained by bacterial activity, but it is unknown how algal iron limitation alters dissolved organic matter composition and subsequent processing through the microbial loop. We examined a bacterial community dependent on carbon from the diatom Phaeodactylum tricornutum to investigate how iron limitation alters bacterial carbon processing. By quantifying activity at single-cell-resolution with nanoSIMS, we found that iron limitation led to a 43% reduction in carbon-fixation but an 80% reduction in carbon transfer into bacterial biomass. Ultra-high-resolution exometabolomics revealed that iron limitation led to bacterial consumption of less labile compounds including aromatics, specific lipids, and nucleobases. A population of bacteria specific to the iron-deplete condition exhibited high anabolic activity yet low incorporation of newly fixed carbon, supporting a shift to consumption of compounds with longer residence times. From metagenome assembled genomes we identified candidate taxa and gene pathways responsible for this carbon processing shift. These results provide a mechanistic link between decreased carbon flow to bacteria under iron limitation and consumption of less labile exometabolites responsible for this decreased flow. This has implications for predicting organic matter composition and turnover in iron deplete surface oceans and manipulating algal-bacterial interactions in engineered systems.
authors: Gilbert NE, Coffey NR, McCall N, Kimbrel JA, Carlson CA, Halewood E, Ramon CE, Diep P, Weber PK, Mayali X, Boiteau RM, Stuart RK.

title: RNA viruses as drivers of rapid diatom succession within a single bloom event.
abstract: Diatoms frequently dominate seasonal phytoplankton blooms and contribute ~40% of marine primary production. Viruses drive phytoplankton mortality and bloom collapse, yet how viruses regulate diatom bloom dynamics is not well resolved. Here, using quantitative metatranscriptomics, we tracked temporal patterns of diatoms and associated viruses at near-daily resolution during the spring bloom in the Gulf of Aqaba, Red Sea. We captured distinct phases and rapid restructuring within both the diatom community and cell-associated virosphere. Diatom transcriptional profiling indicated activation of stress and death pathways prior to taxon-specific demise. RNA viruses emerged as dominant players within the bloom, with fluctuations of putative diatom-infecting RNA viruses across intracellular and extracellular fractions revealing sequential waves of active virus infection that were consistent with virus-mediated diatom mortality. Correlation and codon usage analyses further implicated specific diatom taxa as putative hosts for the identified RNA viruses. Rather than a uniform 'boom and bust', the spring diatom bloom comprised a mosaic of overlapping successional waves of diatom and viral taxa unfolding on daily timescales. These findings support RNA viruses as drivers of diatom turnover, advancing our understanding of how viruses temporally structure diverse diatom assemblages and the biogeochemical trajectory of diatom blooms in marine systems.
authors: Mellijor JL, Tennenbuam-Azulai Y, Spungin D, Avrahami Y, Vardi A, Frada MJ, Kranzler CF.

title: A microfluidic platform reveals the role of liquid movement on the dispersal of Pseudomonas putida via Pythium ultimum hyphal highways.
abstract: Hyphal networks contribute to the connectivity between discrete soil microbial populations by providing a physical network through unsaturated soil matrixes. This network serves as a scaffold for bacteria to disperse and access previously isolated spaces via the 'fungal highway'. As bacteria require a liquid film for flagellar swimming, liquid saturation is a significant limiting factor for their dispersal in soil. The current working hypothesis is that bacteria can utilize thin liquid films associated with fungal or fungal-like hyphae to cross air gaps in soil environments. Studying these interactions at the microbial scale, however, is challenging due to the complex and stochastic 'black box' nature of soil environments. Hence, the microfluidic Hyphal Highways Device was developed to accomplish long-term quantification of bacterial dispersal along hyphal networks at single-cell level. Key findings highlight that Pythium ultimum is essential for Pseudomonas putida movement across an unsaturated environment, with mycelial biomass and liquid transport being key factors influencing bacterial dispersal. Additionally, P. putida actively modified the distribution of the transported liquid, increasing liquid patch connectivity. The Hyphal Highways Device provided quantitative insights into hyphal-mediated bacterial dispersal, opening new opportunities to study microscale interactions that shape microbial dynamics in natural and agricultural soils.
authors: Moratto E, Masters-Clark E, Clark AJ, Pachmann A, Murphy CWM, Bindschedler S, Junier P, Stanley CE.

title: Characterization of syntons across bacterial genomes using non-redundant genomic contexts.
abstract: Bacterial genomes are dynamic, shaped by gene gain, loss, and horizontal transfer; yet selection preserves the colocalization of functionally coupled genes into recurrent modules known as syntons. Many large-scale approaches do not explicitly account for phylogenetic relatedness between genomes which can inflate support for associations that are simply shared by close relatives. To address this, we introduce a scalable framework that clusters gene-family occurrences by genomic neighborhood and counts co-occurrences across distinct genomic contexts, reducing redundancy from vertical inheritance and uneven database sampling without explicit phylogenetic reconstruction. Applied to 32 791 RefSeq genomes comprising 123 million genes, this approach identifies 15 million syntons across 779 000 synton families, characterizing their diversity and revealing structured associations among antiphage defense systems. Leveraging this context-aware framework, we also introduce context residual entropy to quantify gene families neighborhood variability. By prioritizing independent evolutionary events over redundant genome-level counts, our approach provides a scalable, phylogenetic tree-free view of modular organization across bacterial genomes.
authors: Hervé A, Cury J, Bernheim A.

title: Data-Driven Virus Discovery with Virushunter and Virusgatherer
UniProt data pruning and the growing invisibility of the dark proteome
Pan-cancer multi-omics analysis reveals upregulation of the POLE2 subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon and its associations with patient survival and cellular pathways beyond DNA replication
Representation and detection of inversions in pangenome graphs
Representation and detection of inversions in pangenome graphs.
abstract: Pangenome graphs are increasingly used in genetic diversity analyses because they reduce reference bias in read mapping and enhance variant discovery and genotyping from SNPs to structural variants. In pangenome graphs, variants appear as bubbles, which can be detected by dedicated bubble calling tools. Although these tools report essential information on the variant bubbles, such as their position and allele walks in the graph, they do not annotate the type of the detected variants. While simple SNPs, insertions, and deletions are easily distinguishable by allele size, large balanced variants like inversions are harder to differentiate among the large number of unannotated bubbles and remain underexplored in pangenome graph benchmarks and analyses. In this work, we focused on inversions, which have been drawing renewed attention in evolutionary genomics studies in the past years, and aimed to assess how this type of variant is handled by state of the art pangenome graph pipelines. We identified two distinct topological motifs for inversion bubbles: one path-explicit and one alignment-rescued, and developed a tool to annotate them from bubble-caller outputs. We constructed pangenome graphs with both simulated data and real data using four state of the art pipelines, and assessed the impact of inversion size, genome divergence, and variant density on inversion representation and accuracy. Our results reveal substantial differences between pipelines in simulated graphs, with some inversions either misrepresented or lost. In addition, recovery rates are strikingly low in real human datasets, highlighting major challenges in analyzing inversions through pangenomic approaches.
authors: Romain S, Dubois S, Legeai F, Lemaitre C.

title: UniProt data pruning and the growing invisibility of the dark proteome.
abstract: The protein resource UniProtKB has undergone a major, multi-stage reorganization of its protein space, implemented from release 2025_04 through release 2026_02. Analysis of UniProtKB and UniParc records accessed on 20 January 2026 showed that 125.9 million entries were last present in UniProtKB in 2025 and are now represented in UniParc, while ~200.0 million entries remained in UniProtKB at the access date. Of these, 58.9 million were designated for removal in release 2026_02, whereas 141.2 million were classified as retained. The reorganization retains all reviewed UniProtKB/Swiss-Prot entries (the expert-curated subset of UniProtKB), along with proteins from selected reference proteomes and unreviewed entries with additional biologically important data, including experimentally determined three-dimensional structures. The expected benefits include reduced redundancy, easier navigation, and a protein set that is more tractable for annotation and routine searches. However, the reorganization may reduce the visibility of protein sequences from uncultured microorganisms and metagenomic surveys, phylogenetically underrepresented lineages, particularly many archaeal groups, proteins belonging to the so-called "dark proteome," and strain-level variants of well-studied species such as Escherichia coli. We argue that the main consequence is not the loss of the sequences themselves, because affected proteins remain recoverable through UniParc and related resources, but a reduction in their discoverability, annotation context, and accessibility within routine workflows. These effects are likely to be most important for biodiversity-oriented analyses, retrospective reuse of older datasets, studies of specialized protein families, and downstream pipelines that rely on UniProtKB as an annotation hub. As UniProt shifts toward a more explicitly reference-proteome-centered model, a critical question arises: What are the implications of UniProtKB contraction for the representation of evolutionary diversity across the tree of life, particularly in under-sampled and uncultured lineages?
authors: Al-Fatlawi A, Schroeder M.

title: Pan-cancer multi-omics analysis reveals upregulation of the POLE2 subunit of DNA polymerase epsilon and its associations with patient survival and cellular pathways beyond DNA replication.
abstract: DNA polymerase epsilon (Polε) is essential for high-fidelity leading-strand synthesis. It comprises a catalytic subunit, POLE, and three accessory subunits, including POLE2. In contrast to POLE, the biological functions and clinical significance of POLE2 remain unexplored. POLE2 is vital for the assembly of Polε and for interactions with the CMG helicase. Yeast studies show that dysfunction of its ortholog, Dpb2, causes genomic instability and impaired cell cycle progression. To investigate the significance of POLE2, this study provides a comprehensive multi-omics analysis across tumor types. We show that POLE2 upregulation is associated with decreased overall survival in a cancer-type-specific manner. Its expression levels, rather than copy number variation (CNV), emerge as a more reliable prognostic marker. POLE2 expression regulatory mechanisms include promoter methylation, isoform usage, and epigenetic regulators. Elevated POLE2 messenger RNA levels rarely translate into increased protein levels, possibly because of abundant non-coding isoforms. Co-expression and pathway enrichment analyses reveal an association between POLE2 and transcriptional regulation involving E2F, EZH2, and RB. Our findings highlight POLE2 as a contributor to genome stability, a candidate cancer biomarker, and a possible therapeutic target.
authors: Krasilia A, Chaudhry D, Fijalkowska IJ, Dmowski M.

title: Data-Driven Virus Discovery with Virushunter and Virusgatherer.
abstract: We present Virushunter and Virusgatherer, a bipartite computational workflow for discovering viral genomes from unprocessed next-generation sequencing data. Virushunter conducts a profile Hidden Markov Model-based sequence homology search for viral hallmark protein-coding sequence reads to construct microcontigs, which are used as seeds for targeted viral genome assembly by Virusgatherer. We showcase the application of Virushunter and Virusgatherer through an RNA virus-wide screen in 3348 bat transcriptome sequencing experiments from the Sequence Read Archive. Many of the discovered viruses are likely prototypes of new putative virus species, including a novel alphacoronavirus identified in a South American velvety free-tailed bat and a novel rhabdovirus in a European barbastelle bat. The tools are implemented as a reproducible Snakemake pipeline, which is available at https://github.com/lauberlab/VirusHunterGatherer.
authors: Chuprikova L, Chong LC, Ruff S, Seitz S, Lauber C.

title: Nanopore sequencing combined with adaptive sampling and NanoExpansion enables accurate characterization of repeat expansion disorders.
abstract: Expansion repeat disorders are caused by abnormal expansions of short tandem repeats (STRs). We evaluated targeted long-read nanopore sequencing for comprehensive characterization of STR expansions in 132 participants, including patients with myotonic dystrophy type 1 (DM1, n = 51) and DM2 (n = 3) already characterized by Southern blot, C9orf72-associated amyotrophic lateral sclerosis (ALS n = 11) evaluated by repeat primed polymerase chain reaction (RP-PCR; validation group), suspected spinocerebellar ataxia (SCA, n = 46), cerebellar ataxia with neuropathy and vestibular areflexia syndrome (CANVAS; n = 13), Huntington's disease (1), Kennedy disease (1), Friedreich ataxia (FRDA, 2), and 4 healthy controls (test group). Native DNA was sequenced using adaptive sampling (AS) on Oxford Nanopore GridION or PromethION-2Solo platforms. Long-PCR sequencing was performed for comparison. We also developed NanoExpansion, a Python-based tool for sizing expanded alleles and detecting sequence interruptions. We correctly characterized all DM1, DM2, ALS, FRDA, Huntington's disease, and Kennedy disease cases, and identified eight SCA27B, two SCA37, three SCA31, one SCA3, and nine CANVAS cases. Compared with the AS approach, long-PCR underestimated alleles exceeding 800 repeats. Repeat interruptions were detected in 27/51 (52.9%) DM1 cases and 1/10 (10%) ALS, but not in CANVAS, FRDA, Huntington's disease, Kennedy disease, or SCA cases. This integrated sequencing analysis pipeline provides accurate, comprehensive characterization of repeat expansion disorders and has the potential to improve routine genetic diagnosis.

title: CIT8, a machine learning-optimized antimicrobial peptide, exhibits potent activity against carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter baumannii.
abstract: As the burden of antimicrobial resistance continues to rise worldwide, the need for novel antimicrobial therapeutics has become increasingly urgent. Machine learning (ML) has emerged as a promising strategy for accelerating antimicrobial peptide discovery; however, experimental characterization remains essential to define the biological properties and broader applicability of ML-optimized peptides. CIT8 is a 13-residue, citropin-based peptide previously developed through ML-optimization with potent antimicrobial activity against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA). Here, we demonstrate that its activity extends to multidrug-resistant Gram-negative pathogens. Among these, CIT8 displayed the most potent activity against Acinetobacter baumannii, maintaining an MIC of 4 μg/mL against 15 of 16 A. baumannii strains tested, including multiple carbapenem-resistant (CRAB) clinical isolates. At 20 μg/mL (5 × MIC), CIT8 reduced an initial population of approximately 5 × 107 CFU/mL of exponential-phase A. baumannii to below the limit of detection within 15 min. Consistent with its rapid bactericidal activity, CIT8 induced rapid, dose-dependent membrane depolarization and permeabilization, accompanied by leakage of intracellular ATP. In addition, CIT8 and, even more notably, its D-enantiomer CIT8-D exhibited strong antibiofilm activity while maintaining relatively low mammalian cytotoxicity, with therapeutic indices of >32 for CIT8 in both cell lines and 16.2 and 18.5 for CIT8-D in HaCaT and HKC-8 cells, respectively. Moreover, CIT8 potentiated the bactericidal activity of meropenem against CRAB, with the combination exhibiting bactericidal synergy by time-kill assay. These findings highlight CIT8 as a promising scaffold for further optimization and preclinical evaluation against multidrug-resistant A. baumannii.

title: CjejuniTyper: integrated in silico typing of Campylobacter jejuni capsule and lipooligosaccharide loci with GBS-associated genomic profiling.
abstract: Campylobacter jejuni (C. jejuni) is the leading bacterial cause of gastroenteritis worldwide and the most common antecedent pathogen linked with Guillain-Barré syndrome (GBS), an acute autoimmune neuropathy. The risk of GBS development is associated with the structure of the bacterial lipooligosaccharide (LOS), especially sialylated LOS classes that mimic human peripheral nerve gangliosides, as well as with the Penner heat-stable (HS) capsular polysaccharide (CPS) serotype. Accurate simultaneous determination of LOS class and CPS type is important for surveillance of GBS-associated C. jejuni lineages but currently requires culture-based serology or separate molecular assays. CjejuniTyper is an automated bioinformatic workflow that performs Penner CPS complex prediction, LOS class assignment, Cst-II allele calling, putative ganglioside-mimic prediction, virulence-factor detection, and antimicrobial-resistance profiling from genome assemblies. Penner prediction uses marker-gene searches, full-locus alignment, and subtype-resolution rules, whereas LOS classes are assigned using a BLAST-based scoring and confidence system. The workflow was evaluated using 617 assemblies with previously assigned LOS classes, 96 C. jejuni assemblies with Penner reference labels, and 113 retained genomes comprising 89 isolates previously reported from GBS patients and 24 enteritis controls. LOS typing correctly classified 595 of 617 assemblies, corresponding to 96.4% accuracy, Cohen's kappa of 0.958 and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.958. Penner typing correctly classified 93 of 96 assemblies, corresponding to 96.9% accuracy, Cohen's kappa of 0.961, and a Matthews correlation coefficient of 0.962. Most incorrect classifications involved closely related or structurally overlapping loci in fragmented draft assemblies. Among 84 GBS-associated genomes with published LOS-class assignments, CjejuniTyper produced 83 concordant calls, corresponding to 98.8% concordance. In the Bangladesh case-control cohort, HIGH or MODERATE genomic profiles were identified in 34 of 38 GBS-associated isolates and 10 of 24 enteritis controls, corresponding to 89.5% sensitivity, 58.3% specificity, and 73.9% balanced accuracy. Across all 89 retained GBS-associated genomes, 81 (91.0%) received HIGH or MODERATE profiles. These profiles were enriched among GBS-associated isolates but were also present in some controls, indicating genomic mimicry-associated potential rather than patient-level clinical prediction. CjejuniTyper provides a reproducible workflow for integrated C. jejuni capsule and LOS typing with ganglioside-mimic, virulence, and antimicrobial-resistance annotations in a single output.
authors: Jurić D, Ferenčak I, Grginić AG, Žmak L, Tabain I.

title: Potential contribution of enveloped virions to long-distance movement of plant rhabdoviruses.
abstract: Current models of plant virus movement are based largely on extensive studies of nonenveloped viruses, particularly those possessing positive-sense RNA genomes. In contrast, how enveloped, negative-sense RNA plant viruses access and transit through vascular tissues remains largely unexplored. Here, we aim to address this question using two rhabdovirus-host pathosystems: rice stripe mosaic virus (RSMV) infection of rice and tomato yellow mottle-associated virus (TYMaV) infection of Nicotiana benthamiana. Immunofluorescence staining of RSMV-infected rice tissues revealed that viral antigens were predominantly localized to vascular tissues, including both xylem and phloem. Transmission electron microscopy revealed that mature enveloped virions accumulated abundantly within xylem parenchyma cells. RSMV particles were also observed in two vascular conduits: xylem vessel lumens and sieve elements. Moreover, major viral structural proteins and morphologically intact virions were detected in xylem sap. Similarly, enveloped TYMaV virions were detected in both xylem vessel elements and phloem sieve elements of infected N. benthamiana plants. Furthermore, reverse genetics analyses demonstrated that a TYMaV matrix gene deletion mutant deficient in virion morphogenesis retained wild-type levels of cell-to-cell movement but was completely defective in long-distance movement. Together, these results indicate that intact rhabdovirus virions constitute an important mobile entity for vascular long-distance trafficking, with both phloem and xylem potentially contributing to systemic movement.

title: Enhanced antifungal efficacy of azole drugs through combination with usnic acid.
abstract: IntroductionDrug-resistant fungal infections remain a major clinical challenge, and antifungal adjuvants offer a promising strategy to restore azole efficacy. This study investigated whether usnic acid (UA), which lacks intrinsic antifungal activity, enhances the activity of itraconazole (ITR), voriconazole (VOR), posaconazole (POS), isavuconazole (ISA), and fluconazole (FLU) against clinically relevant fungal pathogens.MethodsThe synergistic effects of UA combined with each azole were evaluated against clinical isolates of Aspergillus spp. (n = 64), Candida spp. (n = 24), Exophiala dermatitidis (n = 14), and Cryptococcus neoformans (n = 8) using CLSI-standardized broth microdilution and checkerboard assays. According to their clinical use, ISA was tested against molds, whereas FLU was tested against Candida spp. and C. neoformans. Interactions were classified by the fractional inhibitory concentration index as synergy (FICI ≤ 0.5), indifference (0.5  4.0). Rates were reported with 95% Wilson confidence intervals and compared using Fisher-Freeman-Halton and pairwise Fisher exact tests with Benjamini-Hochberg correction.ResultsUA alone showed no antifungal activity. The overall synergy rates were 67.27% (74/110; 95% CI 58.05-75.33%) for UA+POS, 11.82% (13/110; 95% CI 7.04-19.18%) for UA+ITR, 9.09% (2/22; 95% CI 2.53-27.81%) for UA+FLU, 5.45% (6/110; 95% CI 2.52-11.39%) for UA+VOR, and 0% (0/78; 95% CI 0-4.62%) for UA+ISA. UA+POS showed a significantly higher synergy rate than each other combination after multiple-comparison correction (P C. neoformans (100%, 8/8 and 87.5%, 7/8, respectively). UA+POS produced broad synergy against A. terreus and E. dermatitidis regardless of susceptibility, whereas activity against A. fumigatus was mainly restricted to susceptible isolates. Mechanistic assays showed increased reactive oxygen species levels in five of seven synergistic strains and efflux pump inhibition in four, with strains 382 and PY1b exhibiting both mechanisms.DiscussionThese findings identify UA+POS as the most promising adjuvant combination, while the species- and resistance-dependent effects suggest that its activity requires careful contextual interpretation. The dual involvement of reactive oxygen species accumulation and efflux pump inhibition supports a mechanistically diverse mode of synergy. However, these results are limited to in vitro testing, and further mechanistic and in vivo studies are required to evaluate the therapeutic potential and safety of UA+POS.

title: Host receptor networking and molecular mechanisms of innate immune evasion in hepatitis E virus pathogenesis.
abstract: Hepatitis E virus (HEV), the causative agent of hepatitis E, is a major global health concern, with seroprevalence estimates suggesting that approximately 939 million people worldwide have been exposed to the virus. Although historically regarded as a predominantly self-limiting cause of acute hepatitis, HEV is now recognized as a clinically diverse pathogen capable of causing acute liver failure, chronic hepatitis in immunocompromised individuals, and neurological, renal, hematological, and other extrahepatic manifestations. This review integrates current understanding of HEV cell entry, tissue and host tropism, innate immune recognition, and viral immune evasion. HEV exists in two particle forms: non-enveloped (nHEV) and quasi-enveloped (eHEV). Both use distinct but partially convergent entry pathways involving attachment factors, entry cofactors, endosomal trafficking machinery, and lysosomal processing rather than a single canonical receptor. We evaluate the evidence supporting established and candidate host factors and propose a dual-module heuristic to organize current receptor evidence while emphasizing that this framework remains provisional and requires validation in physiologically relevant models. We further examine how viral genetic determinants, receptor engagement, post-entry replication compatibility, and host antiviral responses collectively shape tissue tropism and cross-species transmission. Innate recognition involves RIG-I and MDA5 signaling through MAVS-TBK1-IRF3, alongside TLR pathways converging on IRF3 and NF-κB, driving type I and III interferon responses. HEV, however, counteracts these defenses at multiple levels. Functional regions within ORF1 interfere with pathogen sensing and interferon signaling; ORF2 contributes to immune evasion through a secreted glycosylated decoy isoform and modulation of NF-κB signaling; and ORF3 exerts context-dependent immunomodulatory effects while facilitating quasi-enveloped virion egress through the ESCRT pathway. Together, these mechanisms support a model in which HEV induces a sustained but incompletely effective antiviral response that may permit viral persistence, particularly under immunosuppression. Integrating entry biology with tropism, zoonotic determinants, and innate immune evasion highlights key unresolved mechanisms and provides a framework for developing improved experimental models, antiviral strategies, and diagnostic approaches for hepatitis E.
authors: Zohaib A, Yamin M, Butt MU, Ge XY, Aljedani SS, Abdulal RH.

title: Inflammatory and immunologic analysis of bronchoalveolar lavage from patients with post-COVID-19 lung disease.
abstract: RationaleInfection with SARS-CoV-2 frequently leads to persistent pulmonary symptoms and radiographic abnormalities, of which several clinical phenotypes have been described. The etiology and inflammatory milieu of these processes is unknown.ObjectivesTo study the alveolar milieu in subjects with suspected post-COVID-19 lung disease up to 2 years after acute infection.MethodsClinical bronchoalveolar lavage (BAL) samples were processed for analysis of cell differential, presence of spike protein, and SARS-CoV-2 antibody responses. Findings were linked to chest CT findings and clinical outcome.ResultsClinical BAL fluid samples from patients with suspected post-COVID-19 lung disease can be separated into three inflammatory phenotypes: a lymphocytic predominant pattern, a neutrophilic predominant pattern, and a normal cellular differential. Spike protein is found in BAL many subjects at the time of study. Robust antibody responses to SARS-CoV-2 are seen in many subjects. No clear association was observed between chest CT scan patterns and the type of inflammatory milieu in the lung. BAL inflammatory pattern was unable to predict long term outcome, though early bad outcomes were not seen in subjects with a normal BAL differential.ConclusionSuspected post-COVID-19 lung disease exists in several forms, each with characteristic inflammatory milieus. Persistent viral protein may contribute to these responses. These findings highlight the potential difficulty of performing studies of post-COVID-19 lung disease predicated solely on clinical presentation due to patient variability.

title: HIV-1 Vpr: a multifunctional accessory protein with potential contributions to AIDS pathogenesis and persistence.
abstract: Human immunodeficiency virus type 1 (HIV-1) infection can progress to acquired immune deficiency syndrome (AIDS), which is characterized by a rapid decline in CD4+ T lymphocyte counts, severe impairment of host immune competence, and recurrent opportunistic infections. Over the past four decades, HIV infection has remained one of the major threats to global public health. Viral protein R (Vpr) is one of nine proteins encoded by HIV RNA genome. Despite consisting of merely 96 amino acids, Vpr exerts multiple functions throughout viral infection and replication and is potentially associated with the progression of AIDS. In this review, we summarize the structural features and biological functions of Vpr, and focus on its multifaceted roles, including the induction of G2/M cell-cycle arrest and apoptotic cell death, facilitation of HIV-1 infection and replication via Env enhancement, modulation of cellular signaling cascades and host gene expression, and participation in AIDS progression. We also include Vpr-mediated regulation of human endogenous retroelement activity and its potential impacts on cellular innate immune responses. This work aims to provide novel analytical perspectives and research directions for in-depth elucidation of Vpr functions and their contributions to AIDS pathogenesis.
authors: Du J, Li Q, Wang SH, Zhao Y, Zhao K.

title: Comparative genomics identifies a cyl-like region in Streptococcus sinensis isolates from a patient with infective endocarditis.
abstract: Streptococcus sinensis is an uncommon member of the viridans group streptococci reported in infective endocarditis (IE), but its genomic characteristics remain incompletely defined. We performed whole-genome sequencing of three S. sinensis isolates recovered from blood culture and valvular tissue from a single patient with IE and compared them with 199 public Streptococcus genomes. Orthology analysis, phylogenetic reconstruction, SNP analysis, VFDB and CARD screening, gene-specific BLAST, Pfam/HMMER analysis, read mapping, synteny comparison, in silico structural modeling, and erythrocyte hemolysis assays were integrated. The three isolates differed by only 0-1 SNPs and formed a near-clonal group. Core single-copy ortholog phylogeny placed S. sinensis closest to S. cristatus, followed by S. sanguinis and S. gordonii. The three isolates retained the host-interaction-associated genes eno, pavA, and plr/gapA and carried an identical 11,341-bp, 12-gene cyl-like block comprising 11 cyl-like genes and acpC. Core-gene phylogeny analysis indicated that the distribution of the complete block was lineage-associated. Gene-specific BLAST and read mapping confirmed full-length sequence conservation and complete mapped-base coverage of the block, while Pfam/HMMER supported enzyme- and transporter-associated domain assignments for several encoded proteins. Structural modeling predicted soluble enzyme-like folds for CylG-like and CylZ-like proteins and a membrane-permease-like architecture with transmembrane helices for CylB-like. On Columbia sheep-blood agar, all three clinical isolates showed visible hemolytic zones and exhibited detectable hemolytic activity in a sheep erythrocyte hemolysis assay. All three S. sinensis isolates shared a type 1 CARD-derived resistance-marker profile containing only Spne_parC_FLO. These findings clarify the phylogenomic position of the near-clonal clinical isolates and identify a shared cyl-like genomic region accompanied by measurable hemolytic activity, providing a basis for further investigation of their host-interaction and pathogenic potential.

title: Characterization of KPC-287 conferring high-level ceftazidime-avibactam resistance in an ST11-KL64 Klebsiella pneumoniae isolate.
abstract: BackgroundKlebsiella pneumoniae is a major global public health threat because of its increasing antimicrobial resistance and capacity for dissemination. Ceftazidime-avibactam (CAZ/AVI) is a key therapeutic option for infections caused by KPC-producing Enterobacterales, but emerging KPC variants compromises its efficacy. Here, we characterized multidrug-resistant K. pneumoniae isolate KP22-83 and investigated the contribution of KPC-287 to antimicrobial resistance, bacterial fitness, and virulence.MethodsKP22-83 was characterized by antimicrobial susceptibility testing, whole-genome sequencing, resistance and virulence gene annotation, KPC phylogenetic analysis, and structural analysis. The bla KPC-287 gene was cloned into pUC19 and introduced into Escherichia coli DH5α and K. pneumoniae ATCC 13883 for functional validation. Growth, motility, in vitro competition, and biofilm formation assays were performed to evaluate fitness-associated phenotypes associated with KPC-287 carriage. The transferability and retention of bla KPC-287 were examined by conjugation assay and serial passage with or without CAZ/AVI. Virulence was evaluated using a Galleria mellonella infection model.ResultsKP22-83 belonged to ST11-KL64 and exhibited multidrug-resistance. Whole-genome sequencing identified bla KPC-287 together with 11 additional antimicrobial resistance-associated genes and 34 virulence-associated genes. KPC-287 clustered close to KPC-155 and differed by P168Q and A242del while retaining a highly conserved predicted global fold. Introduction of pUC19-KPC-287 increased the CAZ/AVI MIC to 64/4 mg/L in both E. coli DH5α and K. pneumoniae ATCC 13883, demonstrating that bla KPC-287 conferred high-level CAZ/AVI resistance. In contrast, meropenem MICs were not substantially altered. KPC-287 carriage caused modest reductions in growth, motility, and competitive fitness, together with greater crystal violet-stained biofilm biomass than the corresponding empty-vector controls. The bla KPC-287 was detected in transconjugants together with IncFII and IncR replicon markers and remained detectable after 30 passages with or without CAZ/AVI. Furthermore, KP22-83 caused substantial larval mortality, whereas KPC-287 acquisition did not markedly affect virulence in K. pneumoniae ATCC 13883.ConclusionThis study provides a systematic functional characterization of KPC-287 in an ST11-KL64 K. pneumoniae clinical isolate in China. KPC-287 confers high-level CAZ/AVI resistance with limited fitness cost and bla KPC-287 is transferable in an IncFII/IncR plasmid background and remains detectable during serial passage. These findings highlight the need for continuous genomic surveillance and functional characterization of emerging KPC variants.

title: Microclimate characteristics, temporal dynamics of soil bacterial communities, and potential co-occurrence network differences between greenhouse and open-field cultivation environments.
abstract: IntroductionGreenhouse cultivation modifies agricultural microclimates and may be associated with temporal changes in soil microbial communities. We investigated a representative vegetable greenhouse and an adjacent open-field site in the subtropical red-soil region of Jiangxi Province, China.MethodsAir temperature and relative humidity were monitored continuously for one year in both environments, while soil temperature and volumetric water content were monitored within the greenhouse. Monthly soil samples were analyzed using 16S rRNA gene amplicon sequencing.ResultsThe greenhouse exhibited pronounced daytime warming, nighttime heat retention, and generally higher relative humidity. Soil bacterial community composition differed significantly between greenhouse and open-field soils, while alpha-diversity differences varied among seasons. Month-resolved analyses revealed significant temporal dynamics. Air temperature and relative humidity jointly explained 15.59% of the variation in bacterial community structure. Potential co-occurrence networks also differed between the two environments in topology and in the proportions of positive and negative correlations.DiscussionThe results document year-round differences in microclimate and soil bacterial community dynamics between greenhouse and open-field cultivation environments. The measured atmospheric microclimate variables showed statistically detectable but limited associations with bacterial community composition, providing a basis for soil microbiome monitoring and environmental management in subtropical protected agriculture.
authors: Xue L, Chen Y, Zhong Y, Wan C.

title: Integrating preclinical and clinical evidence: a meta-analysis of probiotic/synbiotic interventions on metabolic syndrome.
abstract: BackgroundPublished meta-analyses present inconsistent findings regarding the effects of probiotics on metabolic syndrome (MetS), with most lacking in-depth mechanistic exploration.ObjectiveTo systematically assess the efficacy of probiotic/synbiotic interventions for MetS across preclinical and clinical settings, and to explore underlying mechanisms by quantifying inflammatory and metabolic biomarkers.MethodsWe systematically searched PubMed, Embase, the Cochrane Central Register of Controlled Trials, CNKI, and Wanfang Data from inception to June 10, 2025. Both animal and clinical studies were included. For outcomes reported in different units, all values were standardized to a single common unit prior to pooling. Meta-analyses were performed using Stata 15.0 to calculate pooled mean differences (MD) and 95% confidence intervals (CIs). Sensitivity and subgroup analyses were used to assess result stability and heterogeneity.ResultsThis meta-analysis of 35 studies (12 clinical trials with 696 MetS patients and 23 animal studies) demonstrated significant metabolic improvements with probiotic/synbiotic interventions. In animal models, these interventions can significantly improve body weight (BW) (MD = -13.27 g, 95%CI: -18.66,-7.88), glucose metabolism (fasting plasma glucose (FPG), MD = -41.05 mg/dL, 95%CI: -46.50, -35.60; HbA1c, MD = -1.17%, 95%CI: -1.50, -0.84), lipid metabolism (TG, MD = -51.38 mg/dL, 95%CI: -71.46, -31.30; TC, MD = -36.66 mg/dL, 95%CI: -50.10, -23.22), inflammatory and metabolic targets (IL-6, MD = -15.07 pg./mL, 95%CI: -18.23, -11.91; Leptin, MD = -20.95 ng/mL, 95%CI: -39.79, -2.11; FFA, MD = -130.36 μmol/L, 95%CI: -191.52, -69.21), as well as liver function indicators in animal models of MetS. In patients, changes in FPG were non-significant (MD = -8.76 mg/dL, 95%CI:-18.29,0.77), whereas significant improvements were observed for BW (MD = -1.06 kg, 95%CI:-1.70,-0.42), waist circumference (MD = -2.12 cm, 95%CI:-3.70,-0.55), and lipid profiles: TG (MD = -20.51 mg/dL, 95%CI:-27.69,-13.34), TC (MD = -12.09 mg/dL, 95%CI:-16.15,-8.04), LDL-C (MD = -10.56 mg/dL, 95%CI:-14.96,-6.17), and HDL-C (MD = 1.97 mg/dL, 95%CI:0.55,3.39). Sensitivity analyses confirmed result stability, with low risk of publication bias.ConclusionProbiotic and synbiotic supplementation effectively improves body composition and lipid metabolism in MetS patients and animal models, and improves glucose metabolism in animals. In MetS patients, supplementation reduces HbA1c without altering FPG. These interventions produce favorable changes in adipokines, inflammatory cytokines and metabolic stress markers. Further high-quality, long-term RCTs are required to validate these effects and optimize intervention strategies.Systematic review registrationhttps://www.crd.york.ac.uk/PROSPERO/, identifiers CRD420261373917 and CRD420261374049.
authors: Li C, Li X, Li J, Shi Y, Sun L, Yang Q, Ren Z.

title: Gut-liver axis in liver pre-metastatic niche formation: immune networks, microbial, and metabolic and emerging therapeutic opportunities.
abstract: The liver is a leading target for distant metastasis across multiple cancer types, and liver metastasis invariably portends poor prognosis. The formation of pre-metastatic niches (PMNs) within the hepatic microenvironment creates a permissive "soil" for disseminated tumor cells. However, how the gut-liver axis integrates microbial and metabolic signals to remodel the hepatic PMN remains incompletely understood. In this review, we delineate the six hallmark features of PMN assembly, with an emphasis on the complex crosstalk among gut microbiota, their bioactive metabolites, and resident liver cells-including hepatocytes and hepatic immune populations. Notably, these elements engage in a dynamic, reciprocally regulated network characterized by bidirectional feedback loops, rather than a linear signaling cascade. We further survey the emerging landscape of diagnostic biomarkers, including exosomal microRNAs and neutrophil extracellular traps, alongside microbiota-targeted therapeutic interventions. This framework provides testable hypotheses for early interception of liver metastasis and highlights precision medicine opportunities targeting the gut-liver-immune axis.
authors: Zhao L, Lin Q, Zhang D, Liu Y, Zong M, Xi L, Xie F, Song S, Xue P, Zhu S, Chu X.

title: Genomics and metabolomics analyses reveal the endophytic fungus Neocucurbitaria sp. VM-36 as a potential source of bioactive metabolites against methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus.
abstract: Endophytic fungi associated with medicinal plants represent valuable sources of specialized metabolites with potential biological activities.MethodsHere, we investigated Neocucurbitaria sp. VM-36, an understudied endophyte isolated from the medicinal plant Vinca minor, using an integrated genomic, metabolomic, and antibacterial approach.ResultsWhole genome analysis suggests substantial biosynthetic potential for a range of secondary metabolites based on the presence of various biosynthetic gene clusters. Metabolomic profiling revealed a broad chemical repertoire, including metabolites putatively assigned as decalin-containing tetramic acids (DTAs). Among the compounds examined experimentally, compound 1 was structurally identified and exhibited potent antibacterial activity against Gram-positive pathogens, particularly methicillin-resistant Staphylococcus aureus (MRSA), with MIC and MBC values of 0.5-1 and 2-4 μg/mL, respectively. Compound 1 displayed rapid bactericidal activity and showed an additive effect in combination with daptomycin against a clinical MRSA isolate (FICI = 0.625). These findings provide evidence for the occurrence of DTA-related metabolites in Neocucurbitaria and experimentally demonstrate the antibacterial activity of compound 1.DiscussionCollectively, this study provides integrated genomic and metabolomic insights into an endophytic Neocucurbitaria strain, expands the known occurrence of DTA-related metabolites in fungi, and supports the potential of Neocucurbitaria as a source of antibacterial hit compounds.

title: Enhanced detection of polymicrobial bloodstream infections with 16S rDNA PCR library amplicons and clinical relevance.
abstract: IntroductionPolymicrobial bloodstream infections (BSIs) are clinically challenging because conventional blood culture may fail to recover all causative microorganisms, particularly in patients with low microbial burden, prior antimicrobial exposure, or infections caused by fastidious organisms. This study evaluated a 16S rDNA PCR library construction strategy based on cloning and Sanger sequencing as a complementary approach to conventional blood culture and compared its microbial detection profile with that of direct 16S rDNA amplicon high-throughput sequencing.MethodsWe retrospectively analyzed 16,970 blood culture specimens collected at a hospital in northwestern China to characterize the clinical distribution and epidemiological features of BSIs. In a retrospective cohort of 295 patients with culture-confirmed BSI, clinical predictors associated with blood culture-defined polymicrobial BSI were evaluated using multivariable logistic regression and receiver operating characteristic (ROC) curve analyses, with particular emphasis on white blood cell (WBC) count and procalcitonin (PCT) levels. In a separate molecular comparison cohort of 20 patients, cell-free DNA (cfDNA) was analyzed using two 16S rDNA-based workflows: a clone-based approach involving PCR amplification, gel purification, cloning, amplified ribosomal DNA restriction analysis (ARDRA), and Sanger sequencing, and a direct 16S rDNA amplicon high-throughput sequencing approach.ResultsAmong the 16,970 blood culture specimens, 1,321 were positive, including 45 polymicrobial BSI cases. Escherichia coli was the most frequently identified pathogen, followed by coagulase-negative staphylococci and Brucella spp. Compared with monomicrobial BSI, polymicrobial BSI was associated with higher WBC counts and PCT levels. In multivariable analysis, both WBC count and PCT were independently associated with polymicrobial BSI, and their combination showed good discriminatory performance (AUC = 0.927). In the separate molecular comparison cohort of 20 patients, the three methods showed distinct detection ranges. Blood culture detected 0-1 microbial taxon per patient, with one pathogen identified in 17 patients and negative results in 3 patients. The clone-based method detected a broader microbial spectrum, identifying 0-5 taxa per patient, whereas direct 16S rDNA amplicon sequencing showed the broadest detection range, with more than five taxa detected in 9 patients. In contrast, 16S rDNA high-throughput sequencing generated broader taxonomic profiles but showed lower agreement with blood culture. Compared with conventional blood culture, the 16S rDNA PCR library method showed an overall percent agreement of 80.0%.ConclusionWBC and PCT may help identify patients at increased risk of polymicrobial BSI and may support the selection of patients for additional molecular testing. The cloning-based 16S rDNA PCR library strategy provides a complementary approach to conventional blood culture and may offer a balance between broader microbial detection and more focused sequence-level interpretation compared with direct amplicon high-throughput sequencing. Its potential utility may be particularly relevant in selected patients with culture-negative or clinically suspected polymicrobial BSI.
authors: Li G, Wu G, Yin H, McGraw KA, Hou J, Zhao Z.

title: Oral microbiota-immune crosstalk in the pathogenesis and progression of periodontitis: mechanisms and therapeutic potential.
abstract: Periodontitis is a common oral inflammatory disease characterized by chronic inflammation and progressive destruction of the tooth-supporting tissues. Its initiation and progression are not driven solely by infection with specific periodontal pathogens, but rather arise from complex interactions among oral microbial dysbiosis, dysregulated host immune responses, and tissue remodeling. In recent years, oral microbiota-immune crosstalk has emerged as a central mechanistic link between microbial dysbiosis and periodontal tissue damage. Accumulating evidence indicates that oral microorganisms can modulate both innate and adaptive immune responses through microbial structural components, biofilm-associated factors, and metabolites. Conversely, persistent immune-inflammatory responses may reshape the composition and function of the oral microbiota by disrupting barrier integrity, altering the local metabolic milieu, and remodeling ecological niches, thereby establishing a potential self-reinforcing feedback loop. This review focuses on oral microbiota-immune crosstalk in periodontitis, summarizing the molecular mechanisms through which the microbiota regulates host immunity and, reciprocally, immune responses reshape the microbial ecosystem. Particular emphasis is placed on the dynamic changes in these interactions across disease-associated states, including inflammatory initiation, maintenance of chronic inflammation, periodontal tissue destruction, and establishment of a disease-associated microbial ecosystem. We further review the therapeutic and translational advances targeting the microbiota-immune network, including conventional periodontal therapy, biofilm modulation, probiotics, prebiotics and dietary interventions, adjunctive antimicrobial therapy, bacteriophage-based approaches, and engineered bacteria. Finally, we discuss future directions involving multi-omics integration, precision microbiota modulation, and individualized therapeutic strategies, with the aim of providing a conceptual framework and new avenues for the precision prevention and treatment of periodontitis and for the development of microbiota-immune-targeted therapies.
authors: Jin Y, Xu H.

title: Endangered plant growth was influenced by soil microbial life-history strategies across elevations.
abstract: Elevations can influence belowground microbial diversity, network complexity, life history strategy, and the growth of endangered plants. However, how elevation affects endangered plant growth by modulating soil microbial network complexity and life-history strategies remains poorly understood. This study focused on Abies yuanbaoshanensis and systematically examined tree height, diameter at breast height (DBH), soil physicochemical properties, enzyme activity, and microbial communities at different elevations (1,750 m, 1,850 m, 1,950 m, and 2,050 m). The results showed that tree height and DBH were highest at 1,750 m and lowest at 1,850 m compared to other elevations. At an elevation of 1,850 m, soil total phosphorus (TP), total potassium content, and fungal and bacterial diversity were the lowest, while soil water content and fungal oligotrophs/copiotrophs ratios were the highest. The complexity of bacterial-fungal networks increased with elevation. Structural equation modeling suggests a potential chained correlative pathway, wherein elevation was associated with shifts in soil water content, which in turn correlated with alterations in TP content, subsequently showing associative relationships with the abundance of oligotrophic fungi and microbial network complexity, and finally exhibiting links to changes in plant growth. These findings underscore that soil physicochemical properties and microbial communities jointly determine the growth of endangered mountain plants along altitudinal gradients. Although bacterial and fungal diversity exert distinct effects on the growth of endangered plants, their life history strategies should be considered a critical factor in the management of these species. This research provides a new perspective for the ex situ conservation and in situ management of endangered plants.
authors: Teng Q, Wang Y, Lyu S, Wei J, Xu G, Ding T.

title: Engineering the FK228 biosynthetic gene clusters for high-yield production.
abstract: FK228 (romidepsin) is a potent HDAC inhibitor; however, its clinical application is severely constrained by low natural yields and the genetic intractability of its native producer. Here, we leveraged the established Burkholderia chassis KOGC1 to develop a high-performance platform for FK228 production. Through systematic fermentation optimization, we addressed major production constraints including potential end-product toxicity and precursor supply. Specifically, the integration of XAD-16 resin adsorption together with the combined feeding of key amino acids (cysteine, valine, and threonine) elevated the titer to 743.5 mg/L. Subsequent refactoring of the biosynthetic gene cluster and promoter engineering further increased the titer to 1109.4 mg/L. Furthermore, the engineered strain exhibited remarkable genetic stability over five generations without antibiotic selection, which may help address a key barrier to future scale-up. Overall, this study establishes a highly productive laboratory-scale FK228 biosynthetic platform, providing a foundation for future process development of this important therapeutic agent.
