To characterize the mechanisms of MeV spread, we generated a replication-deficient adenoviral vector expressing the MeV M, F, and H proteins in a doxycycline-inducible manner. This viral vector formed infectious centers that preserved epithelial function like those from MeV infection. To further dissect this process, we generated Ad vectors expressing individual MeV proteins, termed Ad-M, Ad-F, and Ad-H. Transduction of HAE with single, double, and triple Ad vector combinations revealed that Ad-F and Ad-H are necessary and sufficient to form MeV-like infectious centers. MeV enters and spreads within airway epithelia via H protein binding to adherens junction protein, nectin-4. To disrupt spread, we introduced the point mutation HY543A, a mutation previously described to inhibit nectin-4 binding, in the Ad-H vector. Co-transduction of Ad-F and Ad-HY543A did not result in MeV-like infectious center formation. Finally, we assessed whether the MeV-related paramyxovirus Nipah (NiV) attachment and fusion proteins (G and F, respectively) support cell-to-cell spread. Co-transduction of HAE with Ad-NiV-G and Ad-NiV-F did not result in infectious center formation, suggesting that decoupling of the membrane fusion apparatus function from replication is a unique feature of the MeV envelope glycoproteins.IMPORTANCEMeasles virus is a highly contagious pathogen. We characterized a mechanism by which measles virus spreads rapidly through the cells that line the human airway in an ex vivo model. We show that the proteins of the viral membrane fusion apparatus, hemagglutinin (H) and fusion (F), move independently from and reach newly infected cells before the proteins of the replicative complex. Thus, viral protein spread is assembled and arranged in order (i.e., marshaled). Using adenovirus-based vectors, we show that co-expression of H and F proteins promotes rapid sequential spread to multiple cells and the formation of infectious centers. Further elucidation of the mechanism of measles virus amplification and cell-to-cell spread within the lung may help explain its highly contagious nature.
authors: Clark SE, Kaufman JW, Yadav K, Cattaneo R, Singh BK, Sinn PL.

title: Operational integration of FT-IR spectroscopy into a genomics-based surveillance algorithm for Listeria monocytogenes.
abstract: Rapid and cost-effective tools are needed to complement whole-genome sequencing (WGS) in Listeria monocytogenes surveillance, particularly in settings with limited sequencing capacity. We evaluated the operational integration of Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR) spectroscopy as a first-line screening method within a genomics-based surveillance algorithm. A total of 24 L. monocytogenes isolates, including two epidemiologically confirmed outbreaks (n = 15) and unrelated sporadic isolates (n = 9), were analyzed. Species identification was performed by matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and genomic characterization was conducted using WGS, including multilocus sequence typing and single-nucleotide polymorphism (SNP) analysis. FT-IR spectra were acquired using the IR Biotyper system, and serogroup prediction and clustering were assessed using artificial neural network-based classification and multivariate analysis. FT-IR achieved 100% concordance with WGS for serogroup assignment, with consistently high confidence scores. Clustering analysis generated FT-IR groupings broadly concordant with WGS-defined outbreak clusters, correctly grouping isolates differing by ≤9 SNPs within the same outbreak-associated clusters while differentiating most genetically unrelated strains. FT-IR excluded seven of nine unrelated isolates from outbreak-associated clustering, although partial overlap was observed among highly clonal CC1 isolates. Operationally, FT-IR enabled preliminary results within 48-72 h after isolation, significantly reducing turnaround time compared to WGS. This tiered approach improves cost-efficiency by optimizing sequencing resource allocation, which is particularly relevant for low- and middle-income settings. These findings demonstrate that FT-IR spectroscopy provides rapid and reliable preliminary typing and can be effectively integrated into routine workflows, enhancing early outbreak detection and supporting more efficient measures. To our knowledge, this is among the first studies describing the structured integration of FT-IR into a genomics-based national surveillance workflow for L. monocytogenes, including its use as a real-time triage tool to optimize WGS allocation and accelerate epidemiological response in a public health reference laboratory setting.IMPORTANCEUsing a well-characterized data set, including two epidemiologically confirmed outbreaks and sporadic isolates, we demonstrate complete concordance (100%) between Fourier-transform infrared (FT-IR)-based serogroup prediction and whole-genome sequencing, along with the capacity of FT-IR to support rapid preliminary clustering. Notably, this study was conducted following the implementation of the first FT-IR system installed in Argentina, representing a major step forward in the incorporation of innovative technologies into national surveillance programs. To our knowledge, this is the first manuscript reporting the combined use of FT-IR spectroscopy, matrix-assisted laser desorption ionization-time-of-flight mass spectrometry, and genomics within an integrated surveillance framework for Listeria monocytogenes. This approach provides a novel and pragmatic model for strengthening microbiological surveillance in resource-constrained settings. Beyond analytical performance, this work provides a real-world, operational framework for integrating rapid phenotypic screening with genomic confirmation, enabling earlier outbreak detection, optimized use of sequencing resources, and the potential to accelerate source-tracking investigations.
authors: Rocca MF, Gianecini A, Cipolla L, Etcheverry P, Cisterna D, Prieto M.

title: Pentosan polysulfate sodium limits pulmonary inflammation in a SARS-CoV-2 mouse model.
abstract: Severe acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) infection remains prevalent globally, causing severe pulmonary inflammation and mortality in up to 10% of patients. While the introduction of effective vaccines has substantially reduced the number of severe coronavirus disease 2019 (COVID-19) cases, there are currently few available therapeutics that have been developed. Pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) has been shown to possess potent anti-inflammatory activity in influenza infection and allergen-induced rhinitis models and was recently demonstrated to inhibit SARS-CoV-2 infection in vitro. As such, we hypothesized that PPS may represent an attractive therapeutic that could be utilized for SARS-CoV-2 infection and COVID-19. Using the K18-hACE2 mouse model of SARS-CoV-2 infection, we administered PPS (6 mg/kg) from either 1 (early) or 3 (late) days post-infection via intranasal instillation and then examined the efficacy in mitigating viral-induced inflammation and severe disease outcomes. We found that the early administration of PPS was accompanied by significant improvements in weight loss, clinical disease presentation, and neutrophilic airway inflammation. Early PPS administration also significantly reduced pro-inflammatory cytokine production at both the mRNA and protein levels while having no impact on viral titers or interferon and antiviral gene expression. Histologically, early treatment significantly prevented severe pulmonary inflammation and tissue remodeling. Comparatively, late administration of PPS worsened weight loss and clinical disease presentation following SARS-CoV-2 infection. Moreover, late administration was unable to prevent significant increases in pro-inflammatory cytokines and was further associated with significantly downregulated antiviral-associated genes. Histological examination also showed no protection in the late PPS administered groups. Taken together, these findings underscore the significance of time-dependent administration and demonstrate the therapeutic potential of PPS for treatment of SARS-CoV-2-induced inflammation.ImportanceSevere acute respiratory syndrome coronavirus 2 (SARS-CoV-2) continues to cause infections globally, with most cases resulting in mild to moderate disease outcomes. However, approximately 10% of patients experience virally induced hyperinflammation leading to poor outcomes. As such, new or repurposed therapeutics need to be rapidly implemented to address this urgent medical need. Here, we show that pentosan polysulfate sodium (PPS) is a leading Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-approved therapeutic that significantly mitigates SARS-CoV-2-induced pulmonary inflammation. Critically, timing of PPS during the infection establishment and progression is critical for PPS efficacy, highlighting time-dependent responses that must be considered for further human clinical implementation. The findings from this study demonstrate that PPS holds significant promise as a repurposed anti-inflammatory agent for SARS-CoV-2 infection.
authors: Johansen MD, Miemczyk S, Nguyen DH, Zhao G, Stapledon CJM, Krishnan R, Hansbro PM.

title: Genomic diversity of human-associated Mycobacterium bovis in Canada.
abstract: Human infections caused by Mycobacterium bovis in Canada are not well documented. The following study analyzed M. bovis (excluding BCG) isolates identified in public health laboratories across Canadian provinces between 2000 and 2025. Whole-genome sequencing was used to catalog mutations linked to antimicrobial resistance and evaluate the genomic relatedness of isolates. The majority of samples in this study were non-respiratory (60%). Of 74 study isolates, 69 (93%) were phenotypically sensitive to first-line drugs isoniazid, rifampin, and ethambutol. The most frequently encountered M. bovis clusters belonged to M. tuberculosis complex lineages La 1.7 and La 1.8. Although some isolates showed phylogenetic clustering, their lack of spatial and temporal relatedness suggested sporadic cases rather than local M. bovis transmission. Of all first-line drugs evaluated, isoniazid showed the lowest concordance (94.4%) between phenotypic and genotypic methods. The isolates in this study harbor some mutations that are not currently documented in the WHO mutation catalog, indicating that these variants may be rare. The findings suggest that the prevalence of M. bovis infection in Canada is low with cases unlikely to be acquired through human-to-human transmission.IMPORTANCEIncidence of human infections due to Mycobacterium bovis in Canada is largely unknown as these data are not collected or annually published. This research is a first effort to identify historical M. bovis isolates that were available for culture, had drug susceptibility testing data, and were analyzed through whole-genome sequencing. The annual reporting of these data in Canada holds value.
authors: Sharma MK, Andrievskaia O, Tyrrell GJ, Akochy P-M, Sekirov I, Richard-Greenblatt M, Ma A, Adam H, Alawa M, Simms E, Islam MR, Rabb M, Soualhine H.

title: A multiplex real-time PCR subtyping assay combining chromosomal (pmpH) and plasmid (pgp3) markers for differentiation of LGV and non-LGV Chlamydia trachomatis.
abstract: Lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV), caused by invasive Chlamydia trachomatis genovars L1-L4, requires timely differentiation from non-LGV strains to guide appropriate treatment and to strengthen case-based surveillance. We aimed to develop and validate a multiplex real-time PCR assay for simultaneous detection and differentiation of LGV and non-LGV C. trachomatis, targeting an LGV-associated chromosomal pmpH deletion, an LGV-associated single-nucleotide polymorphism in the plasmid pgp3 gene, and the human RNaseP gene as an internal control. Primers and probes were adapted from published assays and optimized for multiplex performance. Analytical validation was performed using synthetic gBlocks, cultured LGV and non-LGV strains, and Quality Control for Molecular Diagnostics (QCMD) proficiency panels. Clinical evaluation was conducted using 239 C. trachomatis NAAT-positive specimens submitted to the National Microbiology Laboratory for LGV detection and previously characterized using a pmpH-based assay. All targets demonstrated efficient amplification (PCR efficiency ~100%) with no cross-reactivity. The limit of detection was 5-50 copies/reaction, and analytical specificity for LGV/non-LGV differentiation was 100%; results were fully concordant with QCMD panels. Clinical testing showed complete agreement with the original pmpH assay for LGV-positive, non-LGV, and dual-positive specimens, while improving classification of indeterminate and previously pmpH-negative samples. This assay enables improved, single-reaction LGV detection to support routine public health laboratory workflows and surveillance.IMPORTANCEAccurate differentiation of lymphogranuloma venereum (LGV) from non-LGV Chlamydia trachomatis is essential for appropriate treatment and effective surveillance. Current typing methods have reduced sensitivity in low-bacterial-load specimens, resulting in missed cases and reduced surveillance accuracy. We developed a multiplex real-time PCR assay that simultaneously detects and differentiates LGV and non-LGV C. trachomatis using chromosomal and plasmid targets. This assay provides a streamlined and reliable approach for LGV detection. Implementation of the assay will improve turnaround time for actionable results, support appropriate treatment decisions, and reduce non-typeable results.
authors: Shaikh S, Beirnes J, Deng H, Roy F, Klenke C, Ta K, Schulz V, Abrenica B, Murdock Q, Sivro A.

title: Deletion of ppe27 in Mycobacterium bovis BCG augments macrophage immune responses during infection.
abstract: Mycobacterial infection induces dynamic transcriptional changes in both the host and pathogen. In slow-growing mycobacteria, the ESX-5 secretion system plays a crucial role in virulence by exporting Pro-Glu (PE) and Pro-Pro-Glu (PPE) proteins, which modulate host immune responses and contribute to pathogenesis. Previous studies demonstrated that ppe27 overexpression in Mycobacterium smegmatis enhances bacterial survival and promotes host cell death, suggesting that PPE27 plays an important role in resistance to macrophage-induced cytotoxicity. However, its function during host-pathogen interactions remains poorly defined. To elucidate the function of PPE27, we generated a ppe27 deletion mutant of Mycobacterium bovis Bacillus Calmette-Guérin (BCG∆ppe27) and performed RNA-seq to simultaneously profile host and bacterial transcriptional responses during macrophage infection. Host transcriptome analysis revealed that ppe27 deletion led to upregulated pro-inflammatory responses, including enhancement of the TNF-α, IFN-α, and IL-6 signaling pathways. In parallel, bacterial transcriptome analysis identified downregulation of JTY_3006 in BCG∆ppe27 during infection compared with its expression in wild-type BCG. Amino acid sequence analysis indicated that JTY_3006 shares 100% identity to a S-adenosylmethionine (SAM)-dependent methyltransferase conserved among mycobacterial species. Taken together, these findings suggest that PPE27 may contribute to the negative modulation of host inflammatory responses and suggest that manipulation of PPE27 might reshape pathogenicity and inform future vaccine strategies.IMPORTANCETuberculosis remains the leading cause of death from a single infectious agent worldwide. Understanding the mechanisms that allow Mycobacterium tuberculosis to evade host defenses is essential for developing better vaccines, therapeutics, and prevention strategies. This study focuses on PPE27, a member of the PE/PPE protein family secreted through the ESX-5 secretion system. Although PE/PPE proteins are known to trigger strong immune responses, their precise role in pathogenesis has been unclear. Our study reveals that ppe27 deletion is associated with enhanced macrophage inflammatory responses. Understanding this mechanism provides valuable insight into host-pathogen interactions and offers new directions for tuberculosis vaccine and therapeutic development.
authors: Guo T-C, Seto S, Hijikata M, Keicho N.

title: The preprotein translocase YajC mediates biofilm formation and symbiotic nitrogen-fixation in Mesorhizobium huakuii.
abstract: In bacteria, the auxiliary complex SecDF-YajC participates in the Sec system, facilitating post-translational translocation of preproteins across the membrane through the SecYEG channel. Although YajC homologs are strongly conserved in rhizobial strains and may play important roles in many processes, the functions and mechanisms by which they are involved in the interaction between rhizobia and host legumes are unknown. By constructing Mesorhizobium huakuii yajC mutant, we observed an increase in the strain growth rate, but a reduction in both the biomass and average thickness of the biofilm in the yajC gene mutant compared to the wild type. Deletion of yajC gene results in severe suppression of competitive ability in the plant rhizosphere, alongside a substantial reduction in root hair curling and infection thread initiation during the early infection stages. The yajC-deficient mutant formed more numerous but smaller root nodules, with a 77% decrease in nitrogen-fixing capacity. Scanning electron microscopy analysis revealed that yajC mutant bacteroids displayed, alongside clear hallmarks of cellular deformation, dissociation, and premature senescence. From nodule bacteroid proteomic analysis, we further identified 210 differentially expressed proteins, including 32 transport-related proteins, and 10 associated with nitrogen fixation. Altogether, our findings reveal the importance of YajC-mediated transport and biofilm formation in rhizobial infection and nodule development during M. huakuii-Astragalus sinicus symbiosis.ImportanceIn Mesorhizobium huakuii-Astragalus sinicus symbiosis, deletion of the conserved Sec subunit YajC delays early biofilm formation by impairing flagellar-driven attachment. However, the yajC mutant restores wild-type biofilm biomass later, via upregulation of EPS synthesis genes (exoA/exoY), the PTS(Ntr) regulator ptsN, and polysaccharide deacetylase. This recovery contrasts with permanent biofilm defects in other bacteria, underscoring the need for longer-term assessment. YajC loss also disrupts nitrogenase activity by impairing iron-sulfur cluster biogenesis, Nif complex assembly, and electron transfer. As a compensatory response, plants form more nodules, offsetting reduced nitrogenase activity per nodule. Thus, multipath processes like biofilm formation show adaptability to secretion defects, whereas essential, linear pathways (e.g., nitrogenase maturation) remain highly sensitive. Our work redefines YajC: beyond its canonical role in Sec-mediated secretion, it is a rhizobium-specific factor critical for symbiosis, advancing understanding of secretion system roles in host-microbe interactions.
authors: Ren Q, Zou Q, Yang S, Xie J, Cheng G.

title: Mallard super-shedders of avian influenza exhibit distinct cloacal microbial abundance profiles.
abstract: In many infectious disease systems, a small fraction of hosts accounts for a disproportionate share of transmission, but the biological basis of this heterogeneity remains poorly resolved. In avian influenza, mallards show substantial variation in viral shedding, raising the possibility that only a subset of individuals contributes strongly to environmental contamination and onward spread. To examine whether host microbiome structure is associated with this variation, we experimentally infected wild, captive mallards with low-pathogenic avian influenza virus. We characterized cloacal microbiomes across control, low-shedding, and high-shedding birds using shotgun metagenomic sequencing combined with read-based taxonomic profiling and co-assembled metagenome-assembled genome (MAG) reconstruction. Although infected and uninfected birds were highly similar in species presence-absence, abundance-based analyses showed clear differences in shared taxa, particularly in high-shedding birds relative to controls. Differentially abundant taxa were dominated by taxa that belonged to groups that include host-associated opportunists, consistent with compositional imbalance rather than complete community restructuring. The phylum Pseudomonadota, especially the families Enterobacteriaceae and Moraxellaceae, is well represented. Together, these findings suggest that avian influenza infection is associated with shifts in the abundance of cloacal bacterial taxa rather than broad changes in species membership and that microbiome structure is associated with heterogeneity in shedding in a key wildlife reservoir.IMPORTANCEA small fraction of infected hosts often accounts for a disproportionate share of pathogen shedding, but the biological factors underlying this variation remain poorly understood. In experimentally infected mallards, a key wildlife reservoir for avian influenza A viruses, we found that high viral shedding was associated with shifts in the abundance of cloacal bacterial taxa rather than broad changes in microbial species membership. These results suggest that host-associated microbiome structure may be linked to shedding heterogeneity and could help explain why some individuals contribute more strongly to environmental contamination and onward transmission.
authors: Ruth N, Shakya M, Lewis CD, Erickson CE, Dolinski A, Jankowski M, Fair JM, Owen JC, Bartlow AW.

title: Interaction mechanisms of core dominant fungi during fermentation of Massa Medicata Fermentata: volatile compounds of Saccharomycopsis fibuligera inhibit the growth of Rhizopus oryzae.
abstract: Massa Medicata Fermentata (MMF) is a traditional fermented medicine whose quality is governed by complex microbial interactions. This study investigated the antagonistic effect of the core yeast Saccharomycopsis fibuligera against the filamentous fungus Rhizopus oryzae and its underlying mechanisms. In vitro co-culture assays demonstrated that S. fibuligera suppressed R. oryzae growth and amylase activity in a cell-density-dependent manner, with significant inhibition observed at cell densities of ≥1 × 10⁷ cells·mL⁻¹. The antagonism was driven by two putative pathways: direct spatial/nutritional competition and indirect suppression mediated by yeast-secreted volatile organic compounds (VOCs). HS-SPME-GC-MS analysis identified six major VOCs, primarily fatty acid ethyl esters and 2-phenylethanol, with the latter being the most abundant (0.5664 ± 0.0422 µg·g⁻¹ medium). Single-compound antifungal assays confirmed that isoamyl acetate, ethyl hexanoate, and 2-phenylethanol completely inhibited the growth of R. oryzae at elevated doses. Mechanistic investigations via SEM, PI staining, and biochemical assays revealed that these VOCs induce cell death by disrupting mycelial morphology, compromising membrane integrity, inhibiting ergosterol biosynthesis, and triggering lipid peroxidation. These findings elucidate a key antagonistic interaction between core functional fungi during MMF fermentation, providing a theoretical basis for targeted fermentation regulation and industrial standardization of this traditional herbal medicine.IMPORTANCEBy revealing the cell-density-dependent dual-mode antagonism between S. fibuligera and R. oryzae, this study deepens our understanding of microbial interactions in traditional fermentation. The discovery of specific inhibitory VOCs and their membrane-disrupting mechanisms provides a theoretical basis for targeted process regulation. These insights are crucial for achieving precise fermentation control, which is essential for improving product consistency, reducing batch-to-batch variability, and advancing the traditional fermentation standardization of herbal medicines.
authors: Chang R, Liu J, Lian Y, Zhao J, Cao Q, Zhan X.

title: Putative conjugative transfer and persistence of carbapenem resistance gene blaOXA-72 from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii.
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRA) has been associated with increased morbidity and mortality in clinical settings. In this study, we explored the transfer potential of a mobilizable plasmid-harboring blaOXA-72 gene between Acinetobacter species originating from patients, municipal wastewater, and pig farm wastewater. PCR-based evidence suggested putative transfer of blaOXA-72 from Acinetobacter pittii to Acinetobacter baumannii. In this pair, the apparent frequency of PCR-marker-positive putative transconjugants varied depending on temperature and meropenem supplementation, with a higher frequency observed at 27°C than at 17°C and 37°C. Likewise, the presence of antibiotic pressure yielded a higher apparent conjugation frequency; however, this observation was limited to a single donor-recipient pair. Further, we revealed a phenotypic conversion in terms of meropenem susceptibility and a fitness cost in the putative transconjugants. While whole-genome sequencing did not conclusively verify the presence of blaOXA-72 or a fully resolved plasmid configuration, Oxford Nanopore read mapping consistently detected the chromosomal strA gene in all isolates. In contrast, only a limited number of reads aligned with the blaOXA-72 gene, traC, or the complete plasmid sequences. Comparative analyses further revealed variations in the composition of surface-associated factors and defense systems of the recipient strains, which could be considered as barriers to conjugation. Lastly, the persistence of PCR-detectable marker genes in putative transconjugants was variable and generally unstable over a 30-day period. Overall, these findings provide preliminary insights into the factors that may influence horizontal gene transfer and short-term maintenance of blaOXA-72.IMPORTANCECarbapenem-resistant Acinetobacter (CRA) is a serious clinical concern linked to elevated morbidity and mortality. This study shed light on how the carbapenemase gene blaOXA-72 spreads in the environment via horizontal gene transfer. Using isolates of Acinetobacter pittii and Acinetobacter baumannii from municipal wastewater treatment plants, we show that PCR-based evidence of putative conjugative transfer of the blaOXA-72 gene depends on temperature and antibiotic exposure. The process also incurs fitness costs, and the transferred gene persists only briefly in recipient cells. These results emphasize the importance of environmental sources as reservoirs for antimicrobial resistance gene exchange. Additionally, variations in surface structures and defense systems may act as potential barriers to conjugation. Overall, the work improves our understanding of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) movement and supports the need for better integrated surveillance under a One Health approach.
authors: Bongulto K, Tauchi H, Suzuki S, Watanabe K.

title: Ligilactobacillus salivarius inhibits GII.4[P16] human norovirus replication in zebrafish larvae.
abstract: Human gut bacteria can modulate human norovirus (HuNoV) infection, underscoring the need to characterize virus-bacterium interactions. This study evaluated the effect of Ligilactobacillus salivarius on HuNoV GII.4[P16] replication using a zebrafish larva model. A GII.4[P16]-positive stool specimen was resuspended in phosphate-buffered saline (PBS), centrifuged, and the supernatant stored at -80°C. L. salivarius was grown overnight in de Man, Rogosa, and Sharpe broth, from which bacterial cells and cell-free supernatant (CFS) were collected. The overnight broth (OB), cells, and CFS were each mixed with virus suspension at a 1:1 ratio, and 3 nL were microinjected into 3-day post-fertilization larvae; controls received PBS with virus. Daily until 4 days post-infection (dpi), 2 samples of 10 pooled larvae were collected, and RNA was extracted and quantified by droplet digital PCR. Two-way analysis of variance showed that treatment and time significantly influenced viral RNA levels (P P = 0.051) indicating consistent inhibitory trends across the study period. CFS-injected larvae showed replication comparable to controls (P > 0.05), peaking at 5.31 log RNA copies/larva at 1 dpi, whereas cell-containing treatments (cells and OB) significantly reduced replication (P in vitro binding assay showed that 67% of the virus inoculum physically bound to L. salivarius. In a further comparison, both live and heat-killed bacteria reduced replication initially; live L. salivarius significantly inhibited replication at 3 dpi (P L. salivarius physically binds to HuNoV GII.4[P16] and inhibits viral replication, highlighting its potential as a probiotic intervention for HuNoV infection.IMPORTANCENorovirus remains the leading cause of acute gastroenteritis worldwide, responsible for nearly 700 million cases and substantial economic burden annually, yet no vaccine or antiviral therapy currently exists. This study's findings are significant because they identify a specific probiotic strain, Ligilactobacillus salivarius, capable of directly binding to and inhibiting replication of a clinically relevant norovirus genotype (GII.4[P16]), which is responsible for many recent outbreaks globally. By demonstrating that live bacterial cells-not just secreted metabolites-drive this antiviral effect, the study points toward a mechanistic, cell-mediated mode of action that could inform targeted probiotic formulations. The use of a zebrafish larva model also offers a valuable, scalable in vivo system for studying norovirus-microbiome interactions, addressing a major bottleneck in norovirus research caused by the lack of robust cell culture systems. Together, these findings advance understanding of bacterium-virus interactions and support further development of probiotic-based strategies for preventing or reducing norovirus infection severity.
authors: Chandran S, Gibson KE.

title: A putative GtrB-like glycosyltransferase modulates cation-dependent BCP8-2 phage infection and cell surface structure in Bacillus cereus.
abstract: Bacillus cereus is a foodborne pathogen of growing concern due to its persistence and antimicrobial resistance. To identify host determinants influencing susceptibility to phage BCP8-2, a mini-Tn10 transposon mutant library of B. cereus ATCC 14579 was constructed and screened for altered phage susceptibility. A mutant (BC2012) showing partial resistance carried an insertion in BC_RS27090 (previously BC_5432), encoding a putative GtrB-like bactoprenol glycosyltransferase. Complementation restored phage sensitivity, confirming its functional involvement. The mutant showed a slight reduction in efficiency of plating, whereas, adsorption assay revealed significantly reduced phage binding and infectivity, particularly under cation-rich conditions. Furthermore, adsorption kinetics and one-step growth curve in mutant supported that gtrB mutation affects initial adsorption. Microscopy showed altered surface morphology with thinner, smoother cell walls. These data indicate that gtrB affects surface properties essential for cation-dependent phage adsorption and infection and provide a foundation for future studies on the role of surface glycosylation and ionic interactions in Gram-positive phage biology.IMPORTANCEPathogenic Bacillus cereus is resilient across diverse environments and produces diverse toxins linked to foodborne outbreaks. Bacteriophages provide an effective strategy to control B. cereus; however, molecular targets of phage-host interaction are poorly understood, limiting the effective phage-based control. The current study addresses this gap by identifying a putative bactoprenol glycosyltransferase (GtrB), a viral factor in phage BCP8-2 susceptibility. Data obtained highlight a partial reduction of phage infection in the gtrB mutant, demonstrating that GtrB-like glycosyltransferase significantly contributes to BCP8-2 phage infection and adsorption. Our findings provide significant insights into advancing phage therapy, antibiotic resistance, and B. cereus biocontrol in food and clinical settings.
authors: Asare PT, Manasa G, Kwon Y-H, Ji SH, Cha MS, Wen Y-P, Bhunia AK, Klumpp J, Kim K.

title: Oxidation of Fe(II) by nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizers enriched from Fe(III)-rich microbial mats of an extreme acidic river (Río Tinto, Spain).
abstract: Nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizing (NRFeOx) microorganisms have been detected in the subsurface of the Iberian Pyrite Belt (Spain), where the Río Tinto originates. However, it is not known whether NRFeOx microorganisms are present in the Fe(III)-rich microbial mats that developed within the surface waters where the river originates, and the geochemical conditions progressively shift from circumneutral to highly acidic. Moreover, it is not known what the main (microbial) Fe(II) oxidation pathway is under in situ pH conditions. To answer these questions, we (i) analyzed the in situ bacterial community and Fe mineralogy of the Fe(III)-rich microbial mats, (ii) set up NRFeOx enrichment cultures (either with NO3-/Fe2+aq or acetate/NO3-/Fe2+aq), and (iii) evaluated denitrification and Fe(II) oxidation capabilities of the NRFeOx enrichments under in situ pH conditions. We found that the microbial mat was composed mainly of poorly crystalline minerals, such as ferrihydrite and schwertmannite, with the microaerophilic Fe(II)-oxidizing genus Gallionella (18.3% ± 4.9% DNA-based and 10.8% ± 1.9% RNA-based relative 16S rRNA [gene] abundances) being the main bacteria present and active. NRFeOx was only observed in the enrichment culture amended with acetate/NO3-/Fe2+aq, where Rhodoblastus (between 73.1% and 91.0% DNA-based) was the main enriched genus. The production of nitrite in the Rhodoblastus-dominated culture suggested that chemodenitrification, i.e., the abiotic oxidation of Fe(II) by nitrite, was the main Fe(II) oxidation pathway at pH between 6.2 and 7. However, under more acidic conditions (pH 5.8), nitrate reduction still occurred without Fe(II) oxidation. Overall, this study suggests that NRFeOx microorganisms present in the Río Tinto microbial mats may couple NO3- reduction to Fe(II) oxidation in anoxic circumneutral microniches where nitrate and organic carbon are also available.IMPORTANCEThe potential role of nitrate-reducing Fe(II)-oxidizing (NRFeOx) microorganisms in subsurface pyrite weathering and the formation of acid mine drainage environments, such as the Río Tinto river, is still poorly understood. By focusing on Fe(III)-rich microbial mats formed at the interface between anoxic Fe(II)-rich groundwater and oxic conditions, this study addresses how NRFeOx microorganisms contribute to nitrogen, iron, and carbon cycling in this acidic environment. Moreover, identifying and enriching NRFeOx microorganisms adapted to low pH can deepen our understanding of their metabolic versatility and resilience. These insights extend beyond characterizing the origin of Río Tinto by informing models of acidic rock drainage generation, guiding bioremediation strategies for the simultaneous removal of nitrate and heavy metals from contaminated waters, and providing analogs for potential microbial life in iron-rich, anoxic extraterrestrial environments such as early Mars.
authors: Bottaro M, Abramov S, Amils R, Straub D, ThomasArrigo L, Kleindienst S, Shuster J, Obst M, Kappler A.

title: Acetate scavenging and aromatic funneling of lignocellulose-derived carbon in the denitrifier Pseudomonas veronii.
abstract: Lignocellulose degradation and denitrification frequently co-occur in soils and sediments with fluctuating or limited O2 availability, yet the ability of facultative denitrifiers to couple aromatic carbon turnover to nitrate respiration remains poorly understood. Here, we characterized a novel isolate, Pseudomonas veronii strain B19, for its genetic potential and physiological performance during growth on hemicellulose- and lignin-derived substrates under oxic and denitrifying conditions. Genome analysis revealed extensive aromatic catabolic pathways, including a complete β-ketoadipate route funneling lignin-derived compounds to central metabolism. Despite lacking classical endo-xylanases, the strain grew on acetylated xylan, with faster denitrification kinetics than on glucose. Proteomic and electron flow analyses indicate that xylan utilization proceeds via deacetylation and acetate assimilation through acetyl-CoA. Notably, the carbon source governed the denitrification regulatory phenotype: glucose elicited bet hedging and transient nitrite accumulation at the oxic-anoxic transition, whereas xylan-derived acetate supported a seamless transition to denitrification. On alkali-solubilized lignin, the strain utilized soluble monoaromatic compounds under both oxic and denitrifying conditions. Oxic metabolism proceeded through strong induction of O2-dependent mono- and dioxygenases, enabling extensive aromatic catabolism, whereas under denitrifying conditions, conversion was only partial, with vanillate accumulation and electron-limited but stoichiometrically efficient nitrate reduction at minimal N2O formation. Together, these findings demonstrate that B19 links lignocellulose-derived carbon turnover to denitrification under limited O2, prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Its preference for soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin fractions and converging catabolic pathways indicate a role in downstream turnover of already-depolymerized lignin-derived aromatics, consistent with biological funneling and relevant to lignin valorization.IMPORTANCEDenitrification and the breakdown of plant-derived carbon are central to nitrogen and carbon cycling in soils and sediments, yet how these processes intersect when oxygen is scarce is poorly understood. Most denitrifiers are thought to rely on simple carbon sources, while the breakdown of polymeric lignin is considered oxygen-dependent. Here, we show that the facultative anaerobe Pseudomonas veronii B19 couples the turnover of acetylated hemicellulose and soluble, low-molecular-weight lignin-derived aromatics to denitrification, sustaining respiration under oxygen limitation by prioritizing electron flux over carbon yield. Notably, the carbon source itself dictated the organism's denitrification behavior, switching it between distinct regulatory strategies. By resolving these mechanisms in a single isolate, this work clarifies how facultative denitrifiers may process depolymerized plant carbon and shape nitrogen gas emissions in oxygen-limited environments, and identifies traits relevant to the downstream microbial valorization of lignin-derived aromatics.
authors: Røsdal K, Rese M, Østby M, Junghare M, Bakken LR, Tuveng TR, Arntzen MØ.

title: A cryptic lactate cycle in CO fermentation by Clostridium ljungdahlii.
abstract: The valorization of C1 gases presents a route toward the utilization of industrial waste gases as resources. Acetogens such as Clostridium ljungdahlii serve as promising microbial cell factories for light-independent carbon fixation and high-value compound production, yet their efficiency is often limited by energy constraints and poorly understood metabolic pathways. Here, we investigated lactate metabolism in C. ljungdahlii during carbon monoxide (CO) fermentation via growth and product profiling, 13C-labeling, gene knockouts, and transcriptomics. Although lactate cannot serve as the sole source of carbon and energy for C. ljungdahlii's growth, we found that lactate can be co-fermented with CO into acetate. 13C-tracing further revealed concurrent lactate production and oxidation during CO fermentation, with the unlabeled lactate fraction increasing from 1.0% (day 2) to 5.0% (day 6), indicating the existence of an active lactate cycle. Genetic and transcriptional analyses showed that lactate production and oxidation were catalyzed by two distinct lactate dehydrogenases: LdhA (CLJU_RS15865) and the electron-bifurcating Ldh/EtfAB_1 complex (CLJU_RS10590-CLJU_RS10600), respectively. Disruption of the lactate cycle, particularly in the Ldh/EtfAB_1 mutant, improved energy metabolism and triggered intracellular metabolic rearrangements. This mutant produced approximately 10-fold more lactate and shifted the acetate/ethanol ratio from 3.7:1 to 2.1:1, accompanied by upregulation of the AOR (aldehyde:ferredoxin oxidoreductase)-mediated ethanol production pathway. Subsequent ldhA overexpression further elevated lactate titer to ~2.5 mM, confirming the potential for lactate production from CO. The results imply that the cryptic lactate cycle dissipates energy but aids in intracellular redox balancing during CO fermentation. These findings provide new insights into the metabolic engineering of acetogens to produce target compounds, such as lactate and ethanol.ImportanceAcetogens possess a natural carbon fixation pathway, the Wood-Ljungdahl pathway, enabling them to fix CO or CO2 to produce acetate. Among various acetogens, Clostridium ljungdahlii exhibits strong tolerance to CO and thus holds great application potential for the resource utilization of syngas. However, the physiological and metabolic mechanisms underlying its autotrophic fermentation remain incompletely understood, which imposes limitations on metabolic engineering efforts. In this study, we systematically investigated lactate metabolism in C. ljungdahlii and revealed the existence of a cryptic lactate cycle during CO fermentation. By characterizing this cycle's operation and its impacts on energy metabolism and carbon distribution, we elucidated its potential physiological functions. These findings not only expand our understanding of the physiological and metabolic behaviors of acetogens during autotrophic fermentation but also provide theoretical guidance for the future metabolic engineering of lactate, ethanol, and other compounds.
authors: Sun H, Yi J, Huang H, Wang S.

title: Combined application of Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains and zinc suppresses Alternaria alternata leaf spot in chili pepper.
abstract: Chili pepper (Capsicum annuum L.) is a vital vegetable crop susceptible to yield loss from Alternaria alternata (Fr.), Keissl., which causes leaf spot/blight and fruit rot. Harnessing beneficial rhizobacteria offers an eco-friendly strategy to enhance plant resilience to biotic stressors. In vitro screening identified Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains viz., P. chlororaphis subsp. aurantiaca (ARS-38) and P. chlororaphis subsp. chlororaphis (RP-4) as potent antifungal strains, inhibiting A. alternata growth by 62% and 64%, respectively. In a zinc (Zn)-amended medium, their antifungal activity increased further, reducing fungal growth by 70% with individual strains and 93% when combined. Microscopy revealed fungal growth inhibition linked to conidia and conidiophore disintegration. In planta under open-field pot conditions, A. alternata infection resulted in 100% disease incidence (DI) and altered histochemical, photosynthetic, and enzyme responses. Treatment with ARS-38 + RP-4 in Zn-amended soil enhanced plant resistance by increasing lignin and phenolic accumulation and reducing enzyme activities, resulting in a 96% reduction in DI. Zinc supplementation improved plant health and enhanced disease suppression when combined with the bacterial strains. Combining rhizobacteria with Zn (2 mg/kg) emerges as a promising strategy to mitigate Alternaria leaf spot disease and enhance biostress tolerance in chili plants.ImportanceBiological control offers a sustainable approach for reducing fungal diseases while limiting reliance on chemical fungicides. This study shows that two Pseudomonas chlororaphis strains, ARS-38 and RP-4, combined with low-level zinc supplementation, strongly suppress Alternaria alternata, an important chili pepper pathogen. The combined treatment reduced fungal growth in vitro and substantially decreased disease development in plants while improving structural, physiological, and biochemical responses associated with plant health. The findings demonstrate the potential value of integrating beneficial rhizobacteria with micronutrient supplementation for sustainable disease management and provide a basis for further development of microbial-micronutrient strategies for crop protection.
authors: Shoaib A, Sohail M, Perveen S, Javed S, Rafiq M.

title: Mechanistic insights into atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP)-induced genomic alterations and phenotypic evolution in Saccharomyces cerevisiae.
abstract: Atmospheric and room-temperature plasma (ARTP) is a potent tool for microbial strain engineering; however, the mechanistic basis of its genome-wide mutagenic effects remains poorly understood. Utilizing Saccharomyces cerevisiae as a model, we performed a comprehensive characterization of the mutational landscape and DNA repair pathways elicited by ARTP. Under high-lethality conditions (~99% mortality), ARTP treatment induced a substantial mutational burden, with SNVs and InDels rates increasing 25.2- and 36.7-fold relative to untreated controls, respectively. These mutations exhibited a pronounced bias toward C-T/G-A and A-T/T-A substitutions and InDels within AT-rich regions. Remarkably, the frequency of loss of heterozygosity (LOH) surged 57.4-fold, suggesting a potent capacity for inducing DNA breaks. Through sectored colony assays, we demonstrate that ARTP primarily inflicts pre-replicative double-strand breaks (DSBs), with reciprocal crossovers serving as the predominant driver of terminal LOH. The distribution and pattern of LOH were also altered in ARTP-treated cells. Mechanistically, our study establishes that the translesion synthesis polymerases Rev1 and Pol ζ are indispensable for converting ARTP-induced lesions-likely pyrimidine dimers-into fixed point mutations. In contrast, Rad30 facilitates high-fidelity bypass across these dimers. The base excision repair pathway appears largely dispensable for the processing of these lesions. In contrast, the nucleotide excision repair pathway plays a predominant role in mitigating ARTP-induced mutations. Finally, the strategic application of iterative ARTP mutagenesis facilitated the rapid evolution of acetate-tolerant strains. Our findings provide fundamental insights into the molecular signatures of ARTP mutagenesis, offering a framework for its optimized application in directed evolution.ImportanceWhile ARTP is a cornerstone of non-thermal mutagenesis in industrial biotechnology, its genetic impact has long been treated as a "black box." This study provides a high-resolution molecular dissection of ARTP-induced genomic alterations using a diploid yeast model. We demonstrate that ARTP is not merely a source of point mutations but a potent catalyst for pre-replicative double-strand breaks and extensive mitotic recombination. By elucidating the pivotal roles of specific DNA repair pathways in mutation fixation, we transition ARTP from a purely empirical screening tool to a mechanistically grounded platform for directed evolution. Furthermore, we demonstrate the practical utility of this platform by evolving acetate-tolerant strains and identifying the underlying genetic drivers of their resilience.
authors: Sheng H, Yao J, Liu Y, Li K-J, Zhang J-Z, Zheng D-Q, Zhang K.

title: Rapid detection of the oak wilt pathogen (Bretziella fagacearum) using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP).
abstract: Oak wilt, caused by Bretziella fagacearum, is a destructive disease of Quercus species. Symptoms consist of leaf scorch, dieback, defoliation, vascular discoloration, and eventual death. Prompt diagnosis is crucial for timely management that involves laborious and expensive practices such as sanitation, cutting of infected trees, and proactive tree removal to create a buffer zone, root trenching, and/or fungicide injections. Due to these resource-intensive management tactics, laboratory test accuracy and speed are paramount. Diagnoses of oak wilt currently rely on culturing, nested PCR, or qPCR, but all these methods have limitations, ranging from ambiguous results to high barriers to application. We developed a rapid, robust, and sensitive loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) diagnostic test using primers and probes that target a section of the internal transcribed spacer region of the rDNA of the oak wilt pathogen, B. fagacearum. This assay can detect B. fagacearum from pure isolates and environmental samples, including branch sapwood, leaf petioles, nitidulid sap beetle vectors, and degraded fungal mats. The LAMP assay developed here is sensitive to a detection limit as low as 1 pg/μL and can detect the pathogen in under 20 min. This real-time LAMP-based diagnostic test is thoroughly validated to specifically detect the oak wilt pathogen, B. fagacearum, and is demonstrated to detect the fungus from a variety of routinely collected sample types. Our rapid molecular detection protocol can provide a useful tool for diagnostic labs, forest health practitioners, and researchers studying oak wilt.IMPORTANCEOak wilt is a deadly disease of oaks that represents a growing threat to natural and planted forests throughout eastern North America. To enhance the speed and accuracy of molecular diagnostics for this disease, we designed a molecular test using loop-mediated isothermal amplification (LAMP) to reliably and rapidly detect the oak wilt pathogen, Bretziella fagacearum. To optimize the practicality of this assay in real-world conditions, we developed a rigorous validation process that incorporated the known breadth of genetic diversity of the oak wilt pathogen, sample tissue range, and a panel of non-target fungi to assess the potential for false positives. The novel assay is demonstrated to be highly specific and can detect B. fagacearum from host sapwood, leaf petioles, and nitidulid sap beetles, serving as a versatile new tool for forest health surveillance. Our approach also represents a thorough framework for researchers interested in the development of rapid molecular methods for the detection of forest microbes more broadly.
authors: Meinecke CD, Loyd AL, Chahal K, Eshleman R, Ony MA, Pietsch GM, Hadziabdic D, Klingeman W, Sakalidis ML, Gomez DF, Villari C.

title: Development of improved host-vector system for enhanced production of santalene isoforms in Azospirillum brasilense.
abstract: Azospirillum brasilense is a non-photosynthetic bacterium that possesses the ability to produce carotenoids, in which squalene is a critical intermediate of the carotenoid biosynthetic pathway. Farnesyl pyrophosphate (FPP) serves as a precursor for the production of sesquiterpenoids; hence, its availability is a major bottleneck in the microbial biosynthesis of several major plant sesquiterpenes. We improved the utility of A. brasilense Cd for the heterologous production of sesquiterpenes by enhancing intracellular availability of FPP and disrupted the chromosomal hpnC gene to block the squalene biosynthetic pathway to decrease a competing sink for FPP, along with the introduction of the heterologous Escherichia coli ispA gene, together with additional copies of the native A. brasilense dxps and crtE genes. These genetic manipulations, along with the expression of codon-harmonized santalene synthase from Santalum album, enabled an increase in the production of α-santalene by 50-fold, α-exo-bergamotene by 20-fold, and β-santalene by 10-fold in A. brasilense Cd. Additionally, we developed a fructose-inducible santalene synthase expression system, which may be more efficient and economical than the isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside-inducible system. Finally, by cloning and expressing genes encoding cytochrome P450 monooxygenase and its cognate NADPH-cytochrome P450 reductase, we have shown the potential of A. brasilense to produce santalols, the most desired ingredient of sandalwood oil.IMPORTANCESandalwood oil is among the most valuable natural fragrances and is also known for its diverse biological activities. The biosynthesis of santalene, a major constituent of sandalwood oil, originates from the universal precursors isopentenyl diphosphate (IPP) and dimethylallyl diphosphate (DMAPP) via the MEP pathway. This pathway is naturally present in Azospirillum brasilense, a plant growth-promoting rhizobacterium, making it a suitable host for the heterologous production of sesquiterpenes. This study has shown the possibility of using A. brasilense as a promising host-vector system for enhancing the production of santalene isomers by several fold. It has also shown the superiority of a fructose-inducible system over the isopropyl β-D-1-thiogalactopyranoside-inducible system for the industrial production of high-value secondary metabolites in this bacterium.
authors: Tiwari N, Narayanan AK, Mishra S, Rai S, Nagegowda DA, Tripathi AK.

title: AspA activity orchestrates a growth-stress survival trade-off in Yersinia pestis via metabolic reprogramming.
abstract: The aspA gene of Yersinia pestis exhibits a pronounced polymorphism at codon 363, with the dominant TTG allele encoding an inactive aspartate ammonia-lyase (AspA) while the GTG allele encoding an active enzyme. We previously demonstrated that this polymorphism drives an environment-dependent fitness trade-off, yet the underlying mechanism remains unclear. To address this, we first characterized the phenotypic differences between the two strains and revealed a clear growth-stress survival trade-off: the GTG (AspA-active) strain grew faster and produced more ATP, whereas the TTG (AspA-inactive) strain, despite slower growth, exhibited superior survival under nutrient limitation with oxidative, anaerobic, or hyperosmotic stress. Exogenous aspartate reversed the GTG strain's disadvantages under anaerobic or cold stress. To dissect the metabolic basis, we performed 13C-labeled metabolic flux analysis on these two strains. The GTG strain rapidly converted aspartate to fumarate via AspA, fueling the TCA cycle and boosting ATP production. In contrast, the TTG strain displayed stalled aspartate utilization and accumulated amino acids and lipids. Supplementation with TCA cycle intermediates (fumarate, succinate, or malate) partially rescued TTG growth, confirming that reduced TCA flux limits its proliferation. Collectively, AspA activity orchestrates a growth-stress survival trade-off through metabolic reprogramming, underlying the antagonistic pleiotropy of Y. pestis in aspartate-available or stressful environments. The "metabolic congestion" strategy of the TTG strain enhances survival under multiple stresses relevant to the flea gut, and it is plausible that this metabolic reprogramming may contribute to transmission and provide a selective advantage under flea-borne conditions.IMPORTANCEThe plague bacterium Yersinia pestis encounters oxidative, anaerobic, and hyperosmotic stresses-conditions relevant to its flea gut environment during transmission. This study reveals that a single, naturally occurring polymorphism in the aspA gene shifts the bacterium's metabolism from a growth-focused mode to a "metabolic congestion" state that enhances survival under these stresses in vitro. Our work provides a mechanistic framework for understanding how metabolic reprogramming could influence adaptation to vector-like conditions, offering a plausible basis for the environment-dependent fitness trade-offs that may shape transmission dynamics.
authors: Li J, Song K, Shi J, Wei Y, Wei M, Tan Y, Bi Y, Han Y, Du Z, Yang R, Song Y.

title: Anaerobic microorganisms alter heavy oil chemistry by oxygenation and sulfurization.
abstract: Microbial transformation of heavy oil under anoxic conditions involves complex changes in hydrocarbon and heteroatom-containing molecular compositions. However, the molecular-level evolution of sulfur-containing compounds and their relationship to hydrocarbon transformation remain insufficiently resolved. In this study, long-term anaerobic microcosms containing heavy oil from Pitch Lake, Trinidad and Tobago, were analyzed using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) and microbial community profiling to evaluate temporal changes in molecular compositions and microbiota structure over 945 days of incubation. FT-ICR MS detected 4,499 molecular formulas dominated by CHO-, CHNO-, CHOS-, and CHNOS-class formulas. Pronounced compositional shifts occurred during incubation, with sulfur-containing molecular formulas becoming increasingly abundant and resulting in a marked increase in CHOS-class formulas over time. Intensity-weighted elemental formulas showed increasing oxygen and sulfur abundances, while the average m/z increased from 344 at day 93 to 366 at day 945, corresponding to an approximately 6.4% increase in the intensity-weighted average molecular mass. Multivariate analyses revealed distinct temporal clustering of samples and parallel shifts in microbial community composition, depicting a greater contribution of anaerobic and sulfur-associated taxa. Correlation analyses further showed associations between microbial community shifts and increasing abundances of oxidized sulfur-containing compounds, particularly CHSO3- and CHSO4-class formulas. These findings indicate substantial reorganization of the heteroatom-containing molecular pool during anoxic incubation and highlight the potential roles of microbial and sulfur-related processes in the transformation of heavy oil under anoxic conditions.IMPORTANCEHeavy oil reservoirs contain complex mixtures of hydrocarbons and heteroatom-containing compounds that undergo transformation under anoxic conditions. Characterizing the molecular-level changes occurring during these transformations is important for understanding hydrocarbon biodegradation, the persistence of recalcitrant compounds, and the formation and fate of organic sulfur species in oil reservoirs. Using Fourier transform ion cyclotron resonance mass spectrometry (FT-ICR MS) and microbial community analyses, this study reveals that long-term anaerobic incubation drives enrichment of CHOS-class formulas, reduced microbial diversity, and shifts toward anaerobic, sulfur-associated taxa. These findings demonstrate that microbial and sulfur-driven processes play a key role in reorganizing oil chemistry and suggest that co-metabolic activity contributes to the accumulation of partially transformed sulfur-containing compounds. By directly linking changes in microbial community composition with ultrahigh-resolution molecular characterization, this work provides important new insights into the microbial and chemical mechanisms controlling heavy oil transformation and sulfur metabolism in subsurface oil reservoirs.
authors: Harir M, Pannekens M, Voskuhl L, Brauer V, Schmitt-Kopplin P, Meckenstock RU.

title: Nest ecology-associated impacts of wastewater on wild bee microbiomes.
abstract: Anthropogenic pollution affects environments differently depending on proximity to the pollution source, exposure route, and species ecology. Thus, understanding an organism's ecological role and exposure route to contaminants is central to assessing pollution impact. Treated municipal wastewater releases contaminants into waterways and alters microbial communities. Plants absorb contaminants and expose animals through foraging and nest-building activities. Nesting ecology differences of ground and wood cavity-nesting bees offer insight into niche-specific susceptibility to pollution. We compared gut microbiomes of directly exposed soil-nesting Halictus ligatus and indirectly exposed wood-nesting Ceratina spp. upstream and downstream of wastewater. We collected bees, flowers, and soil and analyzed their bacterial microbiomes using 16S rRNA sequencing. The effect from wastewater explained a much larger proportion of the variance in the ground-nesting H. ligatus microbiome than wood cavity-nesting Ceratina adults, Ceratina larvae, and pollen provisions. Conversely, soil and flower microbiomes remained stable, indicating higher stability. These findings suggest that wastewater exposure leads to strong host-associated microbiome disruption, with ground-nesting bees most affected.IMPORTANCEBecause contaminants bind strongly to soil, ground-nesting bees near wastewater are likely most impacted, while wood cavity-nesting bees are likely less impacted since plant uptake of contaminants is species dependent. These results suggest that exposure routes drive contaminant susceptibility, with bee-associated microbes most vulnerable. Because bees are important pollinators and biodiversity contributors, these disruptions point to broader ecological risks in increasingly contaminated landscapes.
authors: Ngor L, Palmer-Young E, Vo H, Alkhunder A, Verma V, McFrederick QS.

title: Assembly mechanisms and successional patterns of sediment bacterial communities along a riverine wetland restoration chronosequence.
abstract: Understanding the assembly mechanisms of bacterial communities in sediment is vital for assessing ecological outcomes of wetland restoration. This study examined these processes within sediment bacterial communities along a restoration chronosequence (2, 4, and 8 years) in riverine wetlands. Employing multi-seasonal sampling combined with 16S rRNA gene sequencing, null model frameworks, and co-occurrence network analyses, we observed distinct stage-dependent differences in community assembly. The 2-year wetland was characterized by a relatively high contribution of stochastic processes (notably dispersal limitation), although deterministic processes already dominated assembly. With increasing restoration age, the influence of deterministic processes, especially homogeneous selection, strengthened and remained dominant through the late stage (8 years). Community assembly exhibited significant spatiotemporal variation, with seasonal fluctuations strongly associated with this variation. Concurrently, bacterial co-occurrence networks demonstrated increased modularity, indicative of increasingly modular, functionally compartmentalized community structures. Network topology differed consistently along the restoration gradient, from simple and loosely connected to highly complex and modular configurations, reflecting ecosystem maturation. These findings reveal a pattern of increasing deterministic selection and network modularity with restoration age, thereby advancing understanding of microbial processes during wetland restoration and providing a scientific foundation for ecosystem recovery assessment.IMPORTANCEWetland restoration is widely regarded as a nature-based solution, yet the microbial recovery trajectories following restoration remain poorly characterized. Our study reveals a consistent pattern across restoration ages in sediment bacterial communities across 2-, 4-, and 8-year restored wetlands: from relatively high stochasticity alongside dominant deterministic selection, to strengthened deterministic dominance, and finally to modular, functionally compartmentalized networks. This pattern is associated with restoration duration itself, not with measured environmental factors, and occurs despite strong seasonal variation. Importantly, we show that co-occurrence network modularity and robustness can serve as quantitative, sensitive indicators of ecosystem maturation-more informative than traditional diversity indices. These findings provide a scientific basis for evaluating restoration success and suggest that allowing at least 8 years is necessary for functional stabilization. Our work offers microbial ecological criteria to guide adaptive management and engineering decisions in nature-based wetland restoration.
authors: Chen Y, Li C, Xie S, Zhu L, Liu M, Li H, Zhang W.

title: Nitrate potentiates kanamycin activity in bacteria through metabolic reprogramming and CpxR-associated respiratory activation.
abstract: Antibiotic resistance in foodborne bacteria profoundly compromises the effectiveness of antimicrobial therapies and represents a persistent global threat to public health and livestock production. There is therefore an urgent need to develop adjuvant strategies that can improve the activity of existing antibiotics against drug-resistant pathogens. In this study, comparative proteomic profiling of kanamycin-susceptible and laboratory-passaged kanamycin-resistant Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis (S. Enteritidis) revealed coordinated differences in the tricarboxylic acid (TCA) cycle, nitrogen metabolism, and the respiratory electron transport chain. The resistant strain displayed reduced NADH production, proton motive force (PMF), and intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Because these proteomic analyses were performed under antibiotic-free conditions and whole-genome sequencing was not conducted, these differences are interpreted as physiological features associated with the resistant phenotype rather than as evidence of the specific genetic mechanism responsible for the increased kanamycin MIC. Mechanistically, nitrate acted as a potent kanamycin adjuvant by increasing cellular bioenergetic activity through the nitrate-glutamine-glutamate-associated pathway. Nitrate increased NADH production, enhanced TCA cycle activity, and elevated PMF, thereby increasing intracellular kanamycin accumulation. Nitrate also altered CpxR-associated regulation of respiratory genes, providing an additional route by which respiratory activity could be enhanced. Genetic disruption of nitrate transport or selected metabolic and regulatory components attenuated nitrate-mediated potentiation, supporting contributions from both metabolic flux and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation. Importantly, nitrate enhanced kanamycin-mediated killing not only in the laboratory-derived Kana-R strain but also in kanamycin-susceptible Kana-S, indicating a general kanamycin-potentiating effect rather than specific reversal of an acquired resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved treatment outcomes against clinically resistant S. Enteritidis isolates, including increased survival in murine and chicken infection models. Collectively, these findings identify nitrate as a metabolic adjuvant that can potentiate kanamycin activity by increasing bacterial bioenergetics and drug accumulation. They further illustrate how bacterial physiological state can modulate aminoglycoside efficacy without establishing that nitrate reverses the underlying genetic mechanism of kanamycin resistance.IMPORTANCEAntibiotic efficacy is influenced not only by inherited resistance determinants but also by the physiological and metabolic state of bacterial cells. Our study shows that nitrate can potentiate kanamycin activity in Salmonella enterica serovar Enteritidis by enhancing central metabolism, respiratory activity, proton motive force, and intracellular drug accumulation. This potentiation was observed in both a kanamycin-resistant laboratory-passaged strain and a kanamycin-susceptible strain, supporting a general adjuvant effect rather than specific reversal of a defined resistance mechanism. The nitrate-kanamycin combination also improved outcomes in animal infection models using resistant strains. These findings identify inorganic nitrogen metabolism and CpxR-associated respiratory regulation as potential leverage points for developing aminoglycoside adjuvant strategies.
authors: Li X, Li L-M, Lu J-H, Wu Y-L, Jiang M.

title: Integrated genomics and metabolomics survey of steroids from myxobacteria.
abstract: Steroids from myxobacteria remain largely underexplored compared to other natural product classes, leaving a significant gap in our understanding of their biosynthetic diversity, evolutionary trajectories, and pharmacological potential. To address this, we conducted a systematic genomic survey of myxobacterial genomes to delineate the distribution and phylogenetic context of sterol biosynthetic genes, which we found to be organized in a dispersed manner across the chromosome rather than clustered into canonical biosynthetic gene clusters. While the sterol biosynthetic machinery is broadly distributed across Myxococcota, its occurrence is strikingly uneven among lineages, with Nannocystaceae exhibiting the highest biosynthetic potential. Sequence similarity network mining of the oxidosqualene cyclases (OSCs) essential for sterol biosynthesis revealed extensive sequence divergence and unexplored space for discovering novel catalytic functions. Motivated by these bioinformatics predictions, we further demonstrated that integrated chromatographic pre-fractionation with NMR-based metabolic profiling streamlines the targeted isolation of steroids. This approach yielded 12 (seco-)steroids from 2 in-house myxobacterial strains, including 4 previously undescribed structures featuring diverse oxidative decorations, skeletal rearrangements, and ring degradation. Bioactivity assays uncovered that a co-produced metabolite alkylglycoside synergistically potentiates the antimicrobial activity of select secosteroids. Collectively, this study establishes an integrated genomics-metabolomics pipeline that not only expands the structural repertoire of myxobacterial steroids but also provides a blueprint for future discovery of cryptic sterol metabolites and their hidden biological functions.IMPORTANCEThis study presents a systematic phylogenomic survey of sterol biosynthetic genes across the phylum Myxococcota, revealing a dispersed genomic architecture that diverges from canonical bacterial secondary metabolite gene clusters. Beyond this conceptual advance, we demonstrate, for the first time, that NMR-based metabolomics coupled with chromatographic pre-fractionation can accelerate steroid discovery from myxobacteria, leading to the discovery of previously undescribed (seco-)steroids that expand the known chemical space. This integrated pipeline not only enables efficient discovery of cryptic sterol metabolites but also establishes a foundation for understanding the ecological roles of steroids in myxobacteria.
authors: Fan B-J, Niu L, Liu T, Zhao X-Y, Zhang W-J, Wang D-G, Feng J, Hu J-Q, Zhuo L, Wang C-Y, Wu C.

title: E8^E2 controls the formation of E2-positive replication centers that precede E4 expression during productive HPV16 infection.
abstract: Human papillomaviruses (HPVs) couple their replication cycle to keratinocyte differentiation. Viral genomes are maintained at low copy numbers in undifferentiated cells and undergo amplification within nuclear replication foci in differentiated suprabasal cells. The viral proteins E2 and E8^E2 function as activators and repressors of viral replication, respectively. Using a novel polyclonal antiserum together with the monoclonal antibody 22E2-B9, which recognize both E2 and E8^E2, we identified distinct nuclear E2 foci in keratinocytes harboring episomal HPV16 wild-type (wt) or E8^E2 mutant genomes. These foci colocalized with viral genomes and the cellular proteins RPA32, RAD51, γH2AX, and BRD4, consistent with viral replication centers. Cell-cycle analysis showed that E2 foci formed during the S phase and persisted into the G2 phase. Loss of E8^E2 expression or repression activity increased the number of replication foci and induced diffuse nuclear E2 staining. Only a subset of E2 focus-positive cells expressed the late viral protein E4, indicating that replication centers arise before robust late gene expression. In organotypic cultures, E2 focus-positive/E4-negative cells were detected in suprabasal layers before E2 focus-positive/E4-positive cells, whereas E2-negative/E4-positive cells suggested dynamic regulation of E2 during productive infection. Moreover, many wt cells displayed E2 focus phenotypes resembling E8^E2 mutant cells, suggesting that E8^E2 activity declines during keratinocyte differentiation. These findings demonstrate that E2-positive viral replication centers are tightly regulated by E8^E2, emerge early during productive HPV16 infection, and are accompanied by dynamic modulation of E2 and E8^E2 during the productive phase of the viral life cycle.ImportanceHuman papillomaviruses (HPVs) couple their replication cycle to keratinocyte differentiation, but the mechanisms controlling productive viral genome amplification remain incompletely understood. Here, we identify distinct E2-positive nuclear replication centers in HPV16-infected keratinocytes and show that they contain viral genomes and cellular factors involved in DNA replication and repair. We demonstrate that these structures form during the S phase, persist into the G2 phase, and arise before robust expression of the late viral E4 protein, indicating that viral genome amplification is initiated earlier in the productive cycle than previously appreciated. We further show that the viral repressor E8^E2 regulates the organization of E2-positive replication centers and that E8^E2 activity appears to decline during keratinocyte differentiation. Together, our findings reveal dynamic regulation of E2 and E8^E2 during productive HPV16 infection and provide new insights into how viral genome amplification and late gene expression are coordinated in differentiating epithelial cells.
authors: Kuehner F, Hirn F, Beyer M, Straub E, Rehm TM, Renner J, Roos N, Iftner T, Wieland A, Stubenrauch F.

title: Deep-sea siliceous sponges harbor distinct and functionally diverse microbiomes.
abstract: Sponges, phylum Porifera, are long-lived and basal-branching metazoans that play important roles in ocean biogeochemistry and host diverse microbial communities. Siliceous sponges form a major clade of the Porifera; however, their microbiome is not well characterized, particularly in the deep ocean. Here, we used shotgun metagenomics to investigate the composition of the microbial communities of 13 siliceous sponges collected from four sites near Puerto Rico from depths ranging from 400 to 1,900 meters. Nine of the sponges in this study are from five sponge families that have not previously been sequenced using shotgun metagenomics. We assembled a total of 176 metagenome-assembled genomes from 20 bacterial phyla and 1 archaeal phylum. Ammonia-oxidizing archaea (AOA) Nitrosopumilaceae dominated most siliceous sponge microbial communities and was strikingly the sole symbiont associated with one sponge (Farrea). Overall, microbiome diversity was relatively low across siliceous sponges, except for a Phloeodictyidae, which is likely a high microbial abundance (HMA) sponge. Our results suggest that host sponge phylogeny may shape microbial community structure, with limited evidence for an environmental role. The sponge-associated microbial communities contained genetic capabilities for diverse metabolic functions, particularly contributing to the carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycles. In addition to the AOA, evidence of potential for microbial autotrophy was found through the presence of genes for RuBisCO, methanotrophy, and ATP citrate lyase. These results reveal both conserved relationships and metabolic flexibility across siliceous sponge lineages, suggesting unique evolutionary dynamics and demonstrating the importance of microbial metabolism to sponge host health and nutrient cycling in the oligotrophic deep ocean.IMPORTANCEMarine sponges, emerging ~600 million years ago, have close relationships with microorganisms, but the microbiome of deep-sea siliceous sponges is not well understood. Siliceous sponges play essential roles in deep-sea ecosystems by providing habitats for other metazoans and mediating carbon, nitrogen, and sulfur cycling; however, they remain some of the least-studied sponges. By shotgun sequencing DNA from 13 siliceous sponges collected near Puerto Rico, this study found that host sponge phylogeny is linked to microbial community composition and structure. Ammonia-oxidizing archaea dominated the microbial communities associated with marine sponges, likely playing key roles in utilizing metabolic byproducts and supporting host health. Other microbes also contributed to nutrient cycling and contained the potential to fix carbon, suggesting metabolic flexibility, which may benefit sponge hosts in low-resource environments. These findings emphasize the ecological importance of siliceous sponge-microbe symbioses and contribute to our understanding of the drivers shaping their structure and function.
authors: Lane KR, Meyer-Kaiser KS, Collens AB, Leal CV, Collins AG, Herrera S, Hansel CM.

title: Bovine myxovirus resistance protein (Mx)1, but not Mx2, mediates antiviral activity against human and avian influenza A viruses, including H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b.
abstract: Highly pathogenic avian influenza (HPAI) H5N1 clade 2.3.4.4b viruses have recently infected dairy cows in the United States, raising concerns about human spillover. The antiviral roles of bovine host defense factors, including myxovirus resistance proteins (bMx1 and bMx2), remain relatively understudied. We examined bMx1/bMx2 induction in differentiated bovine cells following HPAI H5N1 infection and assessed their antiviral activity using overexpression, knockdown, and mutagenesis approaches. Both bMx1 and bMx2 were more strongly induced in mammary cells than in tracheal cells. Overexpression of bMx1, but not bMx2, significantly inhibited seasonal influenza A viruses (IAVs), low-pathogenic, and highly pathogenic avian influenza viruses, including H5N1 2.3.4.4b, but not influenza B viruses. Conversely, knockdown of bMx1 resulted in enhanced IAV growth. Further, bMx1 inhibited early stages of viral replication, acting to reduce viral transcription and subsequent steps in the viral replication cycle. Known mutations that reduce human MxA (hMxA) activity also impaired bMx1 function, and mutations in the viral nucleoprotein (NP) associated with resistance to hMxA also reduced virus sensitivity to bMx1. Furthermore, phylogenetic analysis showed that a small minority (>0.03%) of avian H5N1 2.3.4.4b viruses already carry some of these NP mutations. These findings suggest that while current H5N1 viruses largely remain susceptible to bMx1, viral evolution or opportunistic reassortment could drive Mx resistance and increase pandemic risk.IMPORTANCEHighly pathogenic avian influenza viruses have spilled over into dairy cows and have been circulating on dairy farms in the United States since 2024. The innate antiviral immune responses of cows to influenza viruses have not been extensively studied. In this study, we focused on Mx proteins, a key part of the innate immune defense system toward viruses. We specifically looked at bovine Mx proteins and demonstrated antiviral activity toward different influenza viruses, including the highly pathogenic strains. We also showed that the mechanism of antiviral activity of bovine Mx1 was very similar to that of the human equivalent MxA protein. Further, we found that a small minority of these avian viruses have mutations associated with resistance to both bovine Mx1 and human MxA proteins. Overall, this work highlights the elevated pandemic risk for highly pathogenic influenza viruses through continual circulation in cows, a mammalian species in close proximity to humans.
authors: Farrukee R, Xia Y, Morris R, Barnes JB, Dapat C, Hussain S, Deng Y-M, Meliopoulos V, Schultz-Cherry S, Londrigan SL, Gilbertson BP, Reading PC.

title: Functional analysis of non-muscle myosin heavy chain IIA (amino acids 1831-1882) in facilitating pseudorabies virus entry via interaction with glycoproteins gH and gL.
abstract: Pseudorabies virus (PRV) is the etiological agent responsible for porcine pseudorabies, causing substantial financial losses in the global swine industry.
