The primary endpoint was the PROMIS-29 Physical Health Summary Score (PHSS) at 90 days; secondary and exploratory endpoints included patient-reported and objective measures of physical and neurocognitive function as well as blood-, imaging-, and tissue-based biomarkers. While AER002 was safe and well tolerated, no significant differences in physical health, quality of life, objective measures of physical function or cognition, or blood-based biomarkers were demonstrated between the treatment and control arms. In a post-hoc analysis, participants with a lower baseline SARS-CoV-2 antibody level and higher drug exposure were more likely to perceive treatment benefit based on the Patient Global Impression of Change scale (p < 0.05 for anti-S, S1, and RBD). Although AER002 was not efficacious in this proof-of-concept study, our findings could inform future trials using monoclonal antibodies to target viral persistence in Long COVID.
authors: Peluso MJ, Ryder D, Dalhuisen T, Chu DHT, Williams MC, Rodriguez AE, LaFranchi BH, Vinden J, Fehrman EA, Huang B, Hoh R, Asare KA, Bellon Pizarro K, Rahman MS, de Narvaez E, Painter MM, Wherry EJ, Swank ZN, Hansen LL, Walt DR, Fukazawa Y, Sekar A, Bellan SE, Tieu H, Asiago J, Bhuyan P, Venkayya R, Flavell RR, VanBrocklin H, Kelly JD, Hsue PY, Durstenfeld MS, Hunt PW, Calabrese L, Somsouk M, Martin JN, Glidden DV, Deitchman AN, Henrich TJ, Deeks SG.

title: Deep-learning single-cell profiling uncovers interbacterial and drug-driven reshaping of pathogen virulence.
abstract: Bacterial invasion and genotoxicity are key contributors to infectious disease progression and carcinogenesis. Yet current methods do not quantify these processes systematically and at single-cell resolution, limiting our ability to explore how interplay of virulence factors and drug effects shape pathogenicity. Here, we present MALVINA, a high-throughput deep-learning workflow integrating host-pathogen co-culture and high-content imaging to jointly measure bacterial invasion and host DNA damage. Applied to Escherichia coli isolates and human colorectal epithelial cells, we demonstrate MALVINA's versatility by deciphering (1) strains with elevated invasive or genotoxic potential, (2) interbacterial modulation of virulence, (3) pro-virulent drug effects, (4) virulence-targeting drugs, and (5) bacterial potentiation of drug toxicity. MALVINA revealed strain-specific virulence profiles and colibactin-dependent suppression of competitors' invasion coupled with enhanced genotoxicity. It also enabled identification of drug-induced modulation of bacterial invasion and genotoxicity, offering a new perspective for virulence-aware drug profiling. Overall, MALVINA offers an adaptable framework for dissecting pathogen-host-drug interactions.
authors: Bognár B, Kovács T, Muresan R, Migh E, Balogh T, Kovács NM, Somogyi Á, Molnár Á, Csörgő B, Pál C, Horváth P, Juhász S, Lázár V.

title: A role for selective ER autophagy in gametogenic rejuvenation revealed by high-throughput lifespan profiling.
abstract: During mitotic growth, Saccharomyces cerevisiae cells age by dividing asymmetrically, producing young daughter cells while retaining age-associated damage in the mother cell, which will eventually become senescent. Gametogenesis naturally and fully resets precursor cell lifespan, even for replicatively aged cells. However, the mechanisms responsible for gametogenic rejuvenation have remained mysterious. This is partly due to the existing methods to quantify lifespan resetting in this context, which are limited to low-throughput and labor-intensive approaches. Here, we introduce a high-throughput assay that allows systematic characterization of factors required for gametogenic rejuvenation. With this approach, we show that we can sensitively measure a wide range of gamete replicative lifespans that are consistent with established mutants. Excitingly, we also discover that Atg39 and Atg40, receptors involved in selective autophagy of the ER, are molecular determinants of gametogenic rejuvenation. This technique will enable systematic identification of the molecular factors that drive gametogenic rejuvenation.
authors: Spiri S, Sing TL, Phung N, Goodman JS, Ünal E, Brar GA.

title: Structural basis of stepwise G protein activation by the viral chemokine receptor US28.
abstract: G protein-coupled receptors (GPCRs) govern diverse cellular responses and are crucial drug targets. However, the sequence of structural events from G protein recognition to GDP release has remained elusive. Here, we leveraged the viral chemokine GPCR US28 to capture multiple activation states of the US28-Gq complex. Using cryo-electron microscopy and an engineered chemokine superagonist, we determined three distinct complex structures, capturing a GDP-bound Encounter state, the nucleotide-free Canonical state, and a putative intermediate bridging the two states, the Transition-to-Canonical state. These structures, along with simulations and functional data, provide high-resolution snapshots of a plausible G protein activation trajectory and support a stepwise conformational model for G protein activation. This activation cascade closely parallels mechanisms proposed for human GPCRs, suggesting a conserved GPCR signaling mechanism.
authors: Jude KM, Suomivuori CM, Waghray D, Maeda S, Fujiyoshi Y, Inoue A, Garcia KC, Tsutsumi N.

title: Membrane damage induces TagQ/TagR complex-mediated H1-T6SS assembly in Pseudomonas aeruginosa.
abstract: The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a large macromolecular complex crucial for inter-bacterial competition. Its expression and localization are tightly regulated, with the anti-bacterial H1-T6SS in Pseudomonas aeruginosa assembling in response to membrane damage. While several proteins are known to regulate this response, the mechanism remains unknown. Here, we use biochemical approaches to show formation of a complex between the membrane lipoprotein TagQ and the periplasmic protein TagR. Furthermore, Co-IP and in silico modeling indicates TagQ/R complex interactions with PpkA, likely dimerizing the kinase to initiate a phosphorylation cascade leading to H1-T6SS assembly. Mass spectrometry analysis of phosphorylated proteins in P. aeruginosa shows that PpkA does not have any targets outside of the previously reported Fha1, suggesting the sensor module acts exclusively to regulate T6SS assembly. Our work reveals the functional basis of the TagQR-PpkA signaling pathway and links membrane damage to localized H1-T6SS assembly, which is critical for efficient retaliation during inter-bacterial interactions.
authors: Kolesnikov M, Berneiser K, Prakash P, Basler M.

title: Alteromonas macleodii breaches the diatom frustule triggering protoplast emergence and programmed necrosis-like death in Thalassiosira rotula.
abstract: Diatom-bacteria interactions drive biogeochemical fluxes at the base of the marine food-web. Although bacteria are increasingly recognised as important drivers of algal mortality, the diversity of algicidal strategies remains understudied. Here we show that Alteromonas macleodii, a recurrent member of Thalassiosira rotula's microbiome, breaches the diatom's silica frustule, inducing >95% of cells to emerge from their shells within 72 h, exposing protoplasts to lysis and exploitation. Whilst protoplast formation was induced by diverse bacteria, A. macleodii uniquely caused population-wide collapse, used here to characterise this diatom stress response. Dual transcriptomics indicated the presence of a programmed necrosis-like cell death pathway in diatoms underpinning T. rotula's terminal morphological change, alongside upregulation of bacterial motility, chemotaxis and opportunistic metabolism. These findings reveal a potent algicidal strategy, recasting A. macleodii as an antagonist that exploits diatom mortality for its own benefit, removes the ballast provided by their frustules and thus reshapes oceanic carbon cycling.
authors: Short I, Martínez-Pérez C, Miravet-Verde S, Sunagawa S, Stocker R, Alcolombri U.

title: Cryo-EM structures of autoinhibited and RNA-activated ZNFX1 helicase.
abstract: ZNFX1 is an RNA helicase that plays a critical role in host defense against viral infections. Recent studies further revealed that ZNFX1 harbors an unexpected RNA-ubiquitinating E3 ligase activity, raising fundamental questions about how RNA-binding activates this multifunctional enzyme. Here, we combine cryo-electron microscopy with biochemical analyses to define the structural basis of ZNFX1 regulation. In the absence of RNA, ZNFX1 adopts an autoinhibited conformation in which a blocking helix occludes the RNA-binding groove. It exists predominantly as autoinhibited monomers, and, at higher concentrations, assembles into short helical filaments composed of repeating tetramers. Binding of single-stranded RNA (ssRNA) remodels these higher-order assemblies into RNA-bound ZNFX1 monomers and dimers. The cryo-EM structure of the ssRNA-bound ZNFX1 dimer reveals that RNA binding displaces the blocking helix and induces large-scale conformational rearrangements that remodel the helicase core into an active configuration. Biochemical analyses validate the proposed RNA-binding interfaces and demonstrate ATP-dependent RNA unwinding by ZNFX1. Together, these findings support a regulatory mechanism in which autoinhibited ZNFX1 exists as monomers or concentration-dependent higher-order oligomers, whereas RNA binding promotes structural remodeling and helicase activation.
authors: He Q, Wang F, Rassool FV, Baylin SB, Li H.

title: A global mitochondrial genomic atlas illuminates freshwater microeukaryote diversity.
abstract: Environmental genomics has transformed our view of the microbial world, yet progress remains largely prokaryote-centric. Among microbial eukaryotes, inconsistent marker choice and limited species-level resolution blunt diversity estimates and hinder cross-study synthesis. Consequently, regional‑to‑global gradients in richness, turnover, and phylogenetic structure remain poorly resolved. Here we establish a global mitogenome-based framework that converts shotgun metagenomes into species‑resolved, phylogeny‑anchored inventories. From 3,400 metagenomes spanning 362 lakes on seven continents, we reconstruct ~20,000 mitochondrial metagenome-assembled genomes (mitoMAGs), densely populating previously sparse branches of the eukaryotic tree-notably SAR (Stramenopiles-Alveolata-Rhizaria), Cryptophyceae, and Haptista. An empirically calibrated 98.1% mitoMAG‑identity threshold delineates species and tethers community profiles to an evolutionary backbone. On this backbone, coverage‑standardized inventories recover canonical ecological patterns: mesotrophic richness peaks, surface-layer expansion of phylogenetic breadth, and spring maxima with the strongest surface-deep coupling at vernal mixing; supporting the framework. Treating mitoMAGs as primer‑free barcodes yields a single, species‑level, phylogeny‑aware currency that renders richness, evenness, and phylogenetic breadth directly comparable across datasets, depths, seasons, and regions. By placing microbial eukaryotes on an analytical footing comparable to prokaryotes, the resulting atlas brings their diversity into reach and lays the groundwork for future high-throughput, species-aware monitoring and ecological forecasting.
authors: Serra Moncadas L, Ruscheweyh HJ, Woodhouse J, Salcher MM, Okazaki Y, Ngugi DK, Pester M, Posch T, Ghai R, Grossart HP, Sunagawa S, Pernthaler J, Andrei AS.

title: The biogeography of giant viruses and interactions with Eukaryotes across European lakes.
abstract: Advances in genomics have revealed a diversity of nucleocytoplasmic large DNA viruses (phylum Nucleocytoviricota) that infect eukaryotes, but their ecology beyond the oceans remains poorly understood. We recover 208 Nucleocytoviricota genomes, including 205 putative new species and 33 novel virus-host linkages by sampling 87 lakes spanning 30° of latitude from southern Italy to northern Norway. The relative abundance of Nucleocytoviricota nearly triples, on average, from northern to southern Europe, with functional genes related to autotrophic energy acquisition, stress responses, and cell death predominant at lower latitudes. These shifts are attributable to differences in light and resources, with Nucleocytoviricota hotspots in deep lakes with aromatic organic matter and diverse eukaryote communities. Increasing Nucleocytoviricota abundance and richness are associated with several-fold reductions in gross primary production. Our results highlight that Nucleocytoviricota are ecologically relevant in lakes and that understanding their roles will be essential for predicting aquatic food webs under environmental change.
authors: Kolmakova OV, Schulz F, Vasquez YM, Fonvielle JA, Braga LPP, Roux S, Woyke T, Tanentzap AJ.

title: Risk stratification for MDR/RR-TB: a comprehensive integrated patient-level analysis from TB programs and contemporary clinical trials.
abstract: Tuberculosis is the deadliest infectious disease, and treatments for multidrug-resistant tuberculosis are lengthy and toxic. By analyzing a large international database (N = 7,750), we identified patient risk phenotypes linked to unfavorable outcomes. Factors like HIV infection, age, low BMI, smoking, acid-fast bacillus smear positivity, extrapulmonary involvement, and cavitary disease were associated (p < 0.001) with worse clinical outcomes (ROC AUC 0.728; 95% CI 0.726-0.731) and were used to derive a patient risk score. Low-risk patients had a lower probability of unfavorable outcome over time since treatment initiation compared to high-risk patients (p < 0.001). External validation with a highly effective 6-month BPaL regimen showed 97% treatment success for low-risk patients and 88% for medium-to-high-risk patients. Stratifying patients by risk phenotype enables more effective, personalized tuberculosis interventions, which are key to improving cure rates.
authors: Garcia-Cremades M, Campbell JR, Strydom N, Solans BP, Mouksassi S, Li Z, Phillips PPJ, Velásquez GE, Nahid P, Menzies D, Savic RM.

title: Five-country analysis of geographic and dietary drivers of gut microbiome composition and genomic variation.
abstract: Human diet and lifestyle vary widely across cultures, shaping global diversity in gut microbiome composition and function. However, comparable cross-population studies have been limited by methodological heterogeneity. The Human Diets and Microbiome Initiative (THDMI) integrates standardized recruitment, dietary assessment, and shotgun metagenomics across 1,976 participants from the United States, United Kingdom, Spain, Mexico, and Japan to disentangle biological from technical variation. We observed pronounced geographic differences in nutrient intake, food consumption, and microbial composition, with both shared and country-specific features linked to diet. Sparse canonical correlation and machine-learning analyses revealed that microbiome-diet associations were largely population-specific, with limited cross-country generalization. Strain-level analyses further uncovered significant genomic differentiation of gut microbes, consistent with localized dietary and ecological differences. Together, these results show that while core microbial responses to healthy eating exist, the structure and function of the human gut microbiome varies strongly with culture, geography, and long-term dietary practices.
authors: Khatib L, Oles R, Hernández AR, Myers T, Zhao J, Kumar M, Laroya A, Tolosa-Enguis V, Matsunami N, Suzuki D, Chiba N, Gilbert KE, Das P, Sanders JG, Patel L, Litwin N, Nowinski B, Birmingham A, Farmer S, Brennan C, Bryant M, Tribelhorn C, Sanders-Bodai K, Cowart C, Nizet O, Diaz EA, Veiga P, Shetty SA, Knol J, Lay C, Koutnikova H, Chaumont S, Tap J, Cotillard A, Derrien M, Laiola M, González A, Tovar AR, Torres N, Sanz Y, Yamada T, McDonald D, Song SJ, Bartko A, Knight R.

title: Cryo-EM structure of ex vivo Sup35 yeast prion and the factors defining prion phenotype.
abstract: Human prions and amyloids exhibit structural diversity that correlates with different pathological manifestations. Yeast prions represent a convenient model for studying fundamental properties of prions and their strain diversity. The Sup35 yeast prion has multiple structural variants, divided into "strong" and "weak" groups differing in frequency of fibril fragmentation and resulting nonsense-suppression. The molecular origin of these distinctions remains unclear. Here, we show that the different frequency of prion fragmentation is determined by their stability, rather than the efficiency of chaperone binding. The fully protease-resistant part (residues 2-32) of the Sup35 prion core is a key for the prion phenotype and maintenance, whereas partially resistant part (33-72) is less important. We established the cryo-EM structure of a strong Sup35 prion variant purified from yeast, comprising residues 2-64, with 2.7 Å resolution. Comparison of this structure with that of Sup35 amyloid formed in vitro at 4˚C revealed their significant difference.
authors: Dergalev AA, Chesnokov YM, Burtseva AD, Mitkevich OV, Baymukhametov TN, Popov VO, Boyko KM, Kushnirov VV.

title: Evaluation of the Sysmex UF-5000 automated urine flow cytometer for detection of urethral inflammation and clinical urethritis in men.
abstract: Objective evidence of urethral inflammation is required to diagnose urethritis in men. Clinically, this is established by confirming urethral discharge on examination in symptomatic patients. Alternatively, laboratory approaches rely on identifying polymorphonuclear neutrophils (PMNs) from a urethral swab specimen or leukocyte esterase (LE) activity in urine. However, physical examination-based diagnosis may be subjective, collection of a urethral swab is invasive, and often painful, and LE has poor sensitivity. To address these limitations, we evaluated the white blood cell (WBC) parameter of the Sysmex UF-5000 automated urinary flow cytometer for the detection of urethral inflammation and clinician-diagnosed urethritis. Using 1,000 remnant male urine specimens from a sexual health clinic, we measured urinary WBC counts (WBC/μL) using the UF-5000, LE by urinalysis, and abstracted corresponding clinical data and urethral Gram stain results from the electronic medical record. Urinary WBC counts measured by the UF-5000 were significantly higher in men with urethral symptoms, LE ≥1+ status, a clinical diagnosis of urethritis, and strongly correlated with elevated and increasing urethral Gram stain PMN density. The UF-5000 demonstrated excellent diagnostic discrimination, yielding areas under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC) of 0.86 for Gram stain-defined urethral inflammation, and 0.90 for clinician-defined urethritis. Optimized thresholds provided >95% sensitivity for ruling out infection and >95% specificity for ruling it in, outperforming standard LE testing. In conclusion, the UF-5000 automated urine flow cytometer offers a robust, non-invasive alternative for male urethritis diagnosis. This approach could expand diagnostic reach-particularly for men who decline urethral swab collection-and warrants prospective clinical validation.ImportanceMale urethritis diagnostics are limited by the poor sensitivity of leukocyte esterase (LE) testing or the invasive nature of urethral swab collection for Gram stain microscopy. These limitations may create barriers to patient care and delay urethritis diagnosis. Automated urinary flow cytometry may overcome these limitations, but few studies exist. We analyzed 1,000 remnant male urine specimens to evaluate the Sysmex UF-5000 white blood cell (WBC) parameter for detecting urethral inflammation. Elevated urinary WBC counts strongly correlated with elevated WBCs on urethral Gram stain smear microscopy and positive LE. The UF-5000 outperformed LE for ruling in and ruling out urethral inflammation and clinical urethritis. Automated urinary flow cytometry is a powerful, non-invasive diagnostic approach that warrants prospective evaluation in point-of-care clinical studies.
authors: Toh E, Modi IK, Ardizzone CM, Zhang X, Alrebdi WM, Ren J, Nelson DE, Jordan SJ.

title: Proximity biotinylation at the host-Shigella interface reveals UFMylation as an antibacterial pathway.
abstract: Host cells contest invasion by intracellular bacterial pathogens with multiple strategies that recognise and/or damage the bacterial surface. To identify host defence factors targeted to intracellular bacteria, we developed a proximity biotinylation approach coupled to quantitative mass spectrometry that maps the host-bacterial interface during infection. Using this method, we discovered that intracellular Shigella and Salmonella become targeted by UFM1-protein ligase 1 (UFL1), an E3 ligase that catalyses the covalent attachment of Ubiquitin-fold modifier 1 (UFM1) to target substrates in a process called UFMylation. Shigella antagonises UFMylation in a dual manner: first, using its lipopolysaccharide to shield from UFL1 recruitment; second, preventing UFM1 decoration by the bacterial effector IpaH9.8. Absence of UFMylation leads to an increase of bacterial burden in human cells and zebrafish larvae. Contrary to ubiquitylation, the protective role of UFMylation is independent of autophagy. Altogether, our proximity mapping of the host-bacterial interface identifies UFMylation as an ancient antibacterial pathway and holds great promise to reveal other cell-autonomous immunity mechanisms.
authors: López-Jiménez AT, Théry F, Wright K, Painter H, Hoffmeister ST, Jarche L, Benjamin J, van der Heden van Noort GJ, Brokatzky D, Gomes MC, Miles SL, Lobato-Márquez D, Frickel EM, Rohde J, Pruneda JN, Impens F, Mostowy S.

title: RNA binding proteome profiling reveals RNA-dependent activation of oncogenic host signaling during KSHV infection.
abstract: Viruses encode RNA-binding proteins (RBPs) to manipulate host processes and promote infection. However, due to limited genomic space, many viral proteins are multifunctional and may engage RNA through non-canonical domains, making their identification difficult using traditional sequence-based approaches. Kaposi's sarcoma-associated herpesvirus (KSHV) is the etiological agent of many AIDS-associated cancers. Here, leveraging an unbiased proteomic approach we identified all RBPs in KSHV-infected primary effusion lymphoma (PEL) cells, uncovering 7 previously unrecognized KSHV-encoded RBPs. Among these is viral Interferon Regulatory Factor 1 (vIRF1), which we found is both necessary and sufficient to activate oncogenic RAS/MAPK signaling through an RNA-dependent interaction with host G3BP proteins. Importantly, a KSHV vIRF1 mutant lacking the ability to bind RNA exhibits a B cell-specific replication defect, highlighting the essential role of RNA interactions in viral gene regulation and pathogenesis. These findings reveal a novel strategy by which KSHV hijacks RNA-mediated signaling to support its lifecycle.
authors: Zhao Y, Ye X, Yuen M, Zhang R, McDonald WH, Karijolich J.

title: GSNO-functionalized hydroxyapatite nanofertilizer for prolonged delivery, detoxification, and yield improvement in maize.
abstract: The agricultural use of nitric oxide (NO) is restricted by the instability of conventional donors. Here, we develop a facile one-pot method to immobilize S-nitrosoglutathione (GSNO) onto humic acid-coated hydroxyapatite nanoparticles (GSNO-HAs-Fe-HAP NPs). Particle characterization confirms favorable properties for agricultural applications, including prolonged NO release (>6 days) and the mitigation of maize cadmium (Cd) stress. Release test verifies the corelease of humic acid and crop nutrients, while confocal microscopy demonstrates robust NP uptake in maize. Under Cd stress, GSNO-HAs-Fe-HAP outperforms commercial NPK fertilizer, improving photosynthetic efficiency and agronomic traits, reducing grain Cd accumulation by 86%, and upregulating phytochelatins, S-nitrosothiols, and metal transporters (ZmPCR, ZmABCC1, and ZmABCG40). The NP composite reduces ROS accumulation and enhances antioxidant enzyme activity, osmolytes, phenolics, flavonoids, and stress phytohormones. Furthermore, NPs significantly improve soil health parameters and the rhizosphere microbiome. Thus, GSNO-HAs-Fe-HAP is a promising nanofertilizer for prolonged NO delivery and Cd stress mitigation.
authors: Lee DS, Yoon HY, Kumar Das A, Kang JS, Mun BG, Hussain A, Lee IJ, Jeon JR, Yun BW.

title: Sero-catalytic and spatial modeling of dengue virus force of infection in Timor-Leste.
abstract: Dengue virus (DENV) infection causes significant morbidity and mortality across tropical and sub-tropical regions, including in Timor-Leste. In this study we present the results of a national, population-representative serological survey, used to determine the drivers of observed variations in DENV force-of-infection (FOI, i.e. the average annual per-capita risk of infection for a susceptible person) at high spatial resolution. Households were randomly selected from census data and occupants aged above one year were tested using the Panbio Indirect dengue IgG enzyme-linked immunosorbent assay between October 2021 and February 2023. Sero-catalytic models accounting for household effect were applied to estimate the DENV FOI in enumeration areas (EAs, roughly equivalent to neighbourhoods/villages). Spatial models were applied to the local FOI estimates to assess their associations with climate and environmental factors, and to predict the FOI across the rest of Timor-Leste. A total of 4780 individuals from 1755 households across 102 EAs participated. DENV seroprevalence and FOI estimates were highly spatially heterogeneous across Timor-Leste, ranging from 0.010 (95% Credible Interval (CrI): 0.005, 0.018) in EA 10104032 in Fatubossa, municipality Aileu, to 0.519 (0.295, 0.816) in EA 40403012 in Goulolo, municipality Bobonaro. Relative humidity was negatively associated with DENV FOI. The spatial models predicted highest DENV FOI along the Northern and Eastern coasts, with hotspots of transmission in Dili and Baucau cities. Findings will strengthen surveillance and guide the implementation of additional DENV control strategies such as Wolbachia-carrying mosquitoes (currently being deployed in some parts of Timor-Leste), or vaccination.
authors: Arkell P, de Neri Machado F, Vicco A, Cox VM, Tanesi MY, Ximenes D, Hinsley W, Bosco F, Gomes N, Oakley T, Solano V, Sheridan SL, David M, Amaral S, Freitas L, Draper AD, Sarmento N, Soares da Silva E, Alves L, Ferguson N, Donnelly CA, Yan J, Francis JR, Dorigatti I, Martins N.

title: Mobile genetic elements drive a plasmid fusion and deletion lifecycle shaping evolution and antimicrobial resistance.
abstract: Plasmids are key drivers of bacterial adaptation, yet the mechanisms that generate their diversity remain poorly understood. Here, we show that mobile genetic elements (MGEs) orchestrate a fusion-deletion life cycle that repeatedly remodels plasmids in Staphylococcus aureus. Large-scale genomic analyses reveal that multireplicon plasmids are widespread and strongly enriched in transposases. Using experimental assays, we demonstrate that rare MGE-mediated fusion events, via homologous recombination or transposition, combine distinct plasmids into single multireplicon elements, expanding gene content and transfer potential. Antibiotic pressure selectively enriches these fused plasmids, rescuing bacterial populations under stress, whereas opposing selective forces, including phage predation, favour deletion derivatives that preserve essential functions and phage transmissibility. This cyclical process generates dynamic plasmid repertoires with conserved backbones and diverse accessory modules. We propose that MGE-driven fusion-deletion cycles represent a general principle of plasmid evolution, explaining the rapid emergence and persistence of multidrug-resistant plasmids across bacterial pathogens.
authors: Ipoutcha T, Wang Y, Rocha EPC, Penadés JR.

title: Antagonistic roles of histone H3 lysine methyltransferases dictate tumor immune surveillance.
abstract: SETD2 is a critical tumor suppressor in lung cancer that catalyzes histone H3 lysine 36 (H3K36) trimethylation. Oncogenic histone H3 alleles, including H3K36M, causally drive cancer formation by dominantly inhibiting SETD2 and other H3K36 methyltransferases. Here we show that expression of the H3K36M oncogene paradoxically suppresses tumor growth in KRAS-driven lung cancer by promoting transcription of repetitive elements and accumulation of cytoplasmic dsRNA, activating antiviral-like immune clearance. Unexpectedly, all attendant effects of H3K36M expression require SETD2 activity despite widespread loss of H3K36 trimethylation. Reducing H3K36 dimethylation through genetic or pharmacologic attenuation of NSD2 phenocopies H3K36M expression, revealing NSD2 as the relevant target through which H3K36M triggers immune activation. Mechanistically, H3K36M expression or NSD2 attenuation reveals a SETD2-dependent mechanism that limits EZH2-mediated repression of repetitive elements, enabling dsRNA accumulation and immune activation. These findings establish opposing roles for NSD2- and SETD2-dependent H3K36 methylation in lung tumor immunity and reveal an NSD2-SETD2-EZH2 axis that can be targeted to modulate viral mimicry and immune surveillance in cancer.
authors: Gladstein AC, Charles Solomon AM, Poltorack CD, Venkatesh S, Adler KM, Robertson MR, Stransky S, Irizarry-Negron VM, Ruiz DA, Tao D, Freeburg NF, Sidoli S, Asangani IA, Shaffer SM, Feldser DM.

title: Comparative evaluation of commercial gradient diffusion and disk diffusion tests for aztreonam-avibactam susceptibility testing.
abstract: Aztreonam-avibactam (AZA) is a recently approved agent active against metallo-β-lactamase-producing Enterobacterales. However, independent evaluations of commercially available antimicrobial susceptibility testing (AST) products remain limited. We evaluated 56 carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales isolates using four newly available AZA AST products, including two gradient diffusion tests (bioMérieux Etest; Liofilchem MIC Test Strip) and two disk diffusion tests (Hardy, Liofilchem) across three Mueller-Hinton agar manufacturers at two independent clinical laboratories. A diverse isolate collection enriched for nonsusceptible and breakpoint-adjacent MICs was used to rigorously assess categorical agreement (CA). Broth microdilution (BMD) was used as the reference method. Essential agreement (EA), categorical agreement, error rates, and reproducibility were analyzed. All four commercial AST products demonstrated acceptable analytical performance compared with reference BMD. Gradient diffusion demonstrated high EA (bioMérieux 92.6%, Liofilchem 89.6%), whereas CA ranged from 81.5% to 89.3% across all four products. Minor errors accounted for all categorical discrepancies and occurred almost exclusively among breakpoint-adjacent isolates. Medium-related variability was modest, and quality control (QC) performance was generally high, with strong within-site precision and consistent performance across laboratories. This study provides the first comprehensive head-to-head comparison of commercial AZA susceptibility testing products and supports their implementation in clinical microbiology laboratories.IMPORTANCEAztreonam-avibactam is an important new treatment option for infections caused by carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales, particularly metallo-β-lactamase-producing organisms, but its clinical use requires reliable susceptibility testing. We provide the first head-to-head evaluation of four newly available commercial gradient and disk diffusion products across two independent laboratories and three Mueller-Hinton agar manufacturers. By using a diverse isolate collection enriched for MICs near clinical breakpoints, we also subjected these products to a stringent assessment of categorical agreement. Gradient diffusion demonstrated high essential agreement, and no major or very major errors remained after repeat and discrepancy testing with any product. These findings provide timely, practical evidence to guide clinical laboratories implementing aztreonam-avibactam susceptibility testing.
authors: Pfeiffer J, Subramanya SH, Kumar R, Berry GJ, Westblade LF, Green DA.

title: Performance of mCIM/eCIM in Enterobacterales strains co-encoding NDM and OXA-48-like carbapenemases from South India.
abstract: Carbapenem-resistant Enterobacterales (CRE) are an increasing public health concern, particularly as carbapenemase-producing isolates, such as NDM and OXA-48-like producers, become more prevalent. Rapid and accurate identification of carbapenemases is crucial to guide appropriate antibiotic therapy. Although recent epidemiologic data show that CRE increasingly harbor multiple carbapenemases, the performance of common phenotypic tests-the modified carbapenem inactivation method (mCIM) and EDTA-modified CIM (eCIM)-has not been well defined in these isolates. We examined the performance of mCIM and eCIM among CRE-encoding NDM, OXA-48-like, or both. We included 172 genotypically confirmed carbapenemase-encoding CRE isolates from perirectal swabs collected from patients admitted to two intensive care units at a hospital in South India. Isolates included Escherichia coli (53.5%), Klebsiella pneumoniae (41.3%), and Enterobacter species (5.3%). Overall, 112 isolates (65.1%) encoded NDM alone, 23 (13.4%) encoded OXA-48-like alone, and 37 (21.5%) encoded both NDM and OXA-48-like. mCIM positivity was 98.2% for NDM, 47.8% for OXA-48-like, and 94.6% for NDM+OXA-48-like encoders; among mCIM-positive isolates, eCIM positivity rates were 99.1%, 91%, and 97.1%, respectively. When compared to molecular carbapenemase gene detection, mCIM/eCIM was highly sensitive for classifying isolates encoding NDM as metallo-β-lactamase (MBL) producers, but significantly misclassified isolates encoding OXA-48-like as having an MBL or lacking a carbapenemase. In the largest collection of NDM and OXA-48-like co-encoding CRE isolates to date, mCIM/eCIM typically reported these as MBL producers.ImportanceCarbapenemase-encoding Enterobacterales infections are associated with substantial adverse health outcomes, making rapid and accurate carbapenemase detection essential for guiding antibiotic therapy. Although Enterobacterales carrying multiple carbapenemases are increasingly reported worldwide, the performance of common phenotypic assays, mCIM and eCIM, remains insufficiently defined for these strains. In this study of 172 genotypically confirmed carbapenemase-encoding Enterobacterales isolates from hospitalized patients in South India, mCIM/eCIM consistently classified NDM-encoding isolates as metallo-β-lactamase encoders. Additionally, mCIM/eCIM frequently misclassified OXA-48-like-encoding isolates as either metallo-β-lactamase encoders or carbapenemase-negative, highlighting the need to better understand the mechanisms underlying this variable activity. In the largest collection of NDM and OXA co-encoding Enterobacterales isolates reported to date, mCIM/eCIM generally reported co-encoding isolates as metallo-β-lactamase producers. Our results suggest that mCIM/eCIM performance may vary geographically due to variable activity, distribution, and combinations of carbapenemases.

title: Diagnosing pediatric skeletal system infections: you are as good as your lab.
abstract: Pediatric skeletal system infections are medical emergencies that may cause severe acute complications and long-term orthopedic disabilities. Because the clinical presentation of septic arthritis and osteomyelitis may mimic non-infectious conditions, early identification of the causative agent and determination of its antibiotic susceptibility profile are cornerstones of patient management. The etiology of childhood skeletal system infections has changed over time, reflecting the implementation of conjugate vaccines against Haemophilus influenzae type b and Streptococcus pneumoniae, as well as the development of sensitive molecular detection tests. These novel laboratory methods, coupled with rapid pathogen identification by MALDI-TOF technology, have reduced the fraction of "culture-negative" infections and shortened the turnaround time for pathogen identification from days to hours. However, even today, a substantial fraction of bone and joint infections remains microbiologically unconfirmed. Metagenomic next-generation sequencing holds great promise, but its high cost, the need for technical expertise, and the detection of commensal organisms of dubious significance severely limit its routine use. On the other hand, metagenomic next-generation sequencing has not expanded the list of known pediatric skeletal system pathogens, suggesting that underutilization of current diagnostic methodologies, rather than reduced sensitivity, drives suboptimal diagnosis.
authors: Yagupsky P.

title: Sensitivity and specificity of a rapid, point-of-care assay distinguishing bacterial from viral infections in acute care settings.
abstract: Differentiating between bacterial and viral infections is essential in the emergency department (ED) to guide appropriate antibiotic treatment. Recent assays, such as the Food and Drug Administration (FDA)-cleared MeMed BV assay, can help with this distinction. The MeMed BV assay measures three host immune proteins-Tumor necrosis factor (TNF)-related apoptosis-induced ligand, Interferon (IFN)-γ-induced protein 10, and C-reactive protein-in blood samples. The results are combined into a score from 0 to 100, where a higher score indicates a higher likelihood of a bacterial infection and a lower score suggests a viral infection or other non-bacterial causes. The study evaluates the feasibility of using the MeMed BV assay-generated score to help clinicians decide whether to order blood cultures in emergency departments, as well as assessing the accuracy of the MeMed BV assay in distinguishing between bacterial and viral infections in ED patients. The assay's performance was also compared with standard biomarker tests and white blood cell (WBC) counts for predicting bacterial infections. This study included 203 illness episodes, of which a total of 108 were associated with bacterial infection (25 had a positive blood culture; 107 had a non-blood sample positive for a bacterial pathogen) and 18 were associated with a viral pathogen. Combined, the MeMed BV assay's "high bacterial likelihood" and "moderate bacterial likelihood" scores yielded a sensitivity and specificity of 87% and 32%, respectively, in correctly identifying any bacterial infection; the scores had a sensitivity and specificity of 95% and 25%, respectively, in correctly identifying bacteremia. The future of differentiating between bacterial and viral infections is moving toward integrated diagnostic methods. To address antibiotic resistance, future diagnostics will leverage host immune response biomarkers, advanced molecular panels, and machine learning techniques. This will enable rapid and accurate results at the point of care.ImportanceDistinguishing between bacterial and viral infections in healthcare settings can be challenging, as patients often present with similar symptoms and clinical features. In recent years, several new biomarkers have emerged as promising targets for algorithm-based tests designed to differentiate between these types of infections. An increasing number of FDA-approved assays that utilize these biomarkers have entered the market, employing various algorithms. These tests are being used in different clinical settings, such as emergency rooms, to assist clinicians in making accurate diagnoses and prescribing antibiotics appropriately. It is essential for clinicians to correctly order and interpret the results of these assays to fully realize their potential. Our study demonstrates that when such an assay is not used within the FDA-approved context, it does not achieve its full effectiveness.
authors: Sundaram ME, Wahlig TA, Arbefeville S.

title: Comparative plaque- and liquid-based phage susceptibility testing of Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates in a cystic fibrosis randomized clinical trial.
abstract: The optimal phage susceptibility testing (PST) method is unclear. Here, two PST methods were compared using Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates recovered from patients with cystic fibrosis enrolled in a placebo-controlled clinical trial of a single intravenous dose of a four-phage cocktail (WRAIR-PAM-CF1). In total, 508 P. aeruginosa sputum isolates were evaluated, including isolates collected before or after phage or placebo treatment, isolates from the same trial participants over time, and isolates of different colony morphologies from the same participants at the same time point. Susceptibility to phages PaWRA01Φ11, PaWRA01Φ39, PaWRA02Φ83, and PaWRA02Φ87 and a cocktail of all four phages was assessed using a plaque assay (PA) and a Biolog Omnilog-based liquid assay (LA) with the same bacterial inoculum. A total of 170/508 isolates (33%) and 195/508 isolates (38%) were identified as susceptible to the cocktail by PA and LA, respectively. Among the susceptible isolates, 169/170 (99%; PA) and 187/195 (96%; LA) also tested susceptible to at least one of the four phages in the cocktail. Susceptible percent agreement between the PA and LA ranged from 76% to 100% and non-susceptible percent agreement ranged from 89% to 100% for all phages studied and the cocktail. Phage PaWRA02Φ83 demonstrated the greatest individual activity, with 164/508 (32%) and 188/508 (37%) isolates testing susceptible by PA and LA, respectively. The four-phage cocktail provided numerically broader coverage of P. aeruginosa (i.e., had the highest susceptibility rate) than did any single phage. There was high concordance between PST results by PA and LA.IMPORTANCEStandardization of phage susceptibility testing (PST) methods is essential to support phage therapy trials and any future clinical implementation. There are no standardized PST methods or interpretive criteria for PST. In this study, PST was performed by a plaque assay and a Biolog Omnilog-based liquid assay on Pseudomonas aeruginosa isolates recovered from cystic fibrosis patients enrolled in a clinical trial. Susceptibility of 508 isolates to four phages and a cocktail of all four was evaluated. There was high concordance between susceptibility assessed by plaque and liquid assays and numerically broader coverage of P. aeruginosa by the cocktail compared to any single phage. This manuscript should be of interest to those performing PST.
authors: Koscianski CA, Shao W, Komarow L, Parmar K, Greenwood-Quaintance KE, Souli M, Nikolich MP, Filippov AA, Schooley RT, Evans SR, Pride D, Van Tyne D, Chambers HF, Fowler VG, Tamma PD, Patel R, Antibacterial Resistance Leadership Group.

title: An update on novel and included taxa and revised taxonomic status of bacteria isolated from domestic companion and agricultural animals.
abstract: The recognition of novel bacteria continues to expand with the decreased cost and rapid adoption of whole genome sequencing for bacteria. A review of newly identified bacterial species and revisions to bacterial nomenclature from 2025 was performed. New members of families Staphylococcaceae, Streptococcaceae, Actinomycetaceae, Pseudomonadaceae, and Pasteurellaceae were recognized in 2025. While most novel organisms identified in 2025 were isolated from normal microbiota of the skin or gastrointestinal tract of healthy animals, there were some notable new taxa, including Macrococcus psychrotolerans sp. nov., which carries a mecB determinant from Staphylococcus aureus. In addition, Buchananella felis sp. nov., isolated from cases of feline pyothorax, becomes the second member of the genus Buchananella, alongside Buchananella hordeovulneris. Within the gram-negative organisms, a new Pseudomonas species and a novel member of Pasteurellaceae, namely, Rodentibacter abscessus sp. nov. isolated from abscesses in pet hamsters, was recognized. Additions to spiral or curved bacteria included Campylobacter canis sp. nov. and Helicobacter gastrocanis sp. nov. Proposed revisions to seven bacterial taxa are briefly described.
authors: Lawhon SD, Burbick CR, Krueger T, Munson E.

title: Sleeper agents: asymptomatic Acinetobacter colonization and underlying mechanisms.
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii and other Acinetobacter species are a growing public health concern because they commonly cause healthcare-associated infections. Acinetobacter spp. are often multi-drug resistant, leading to significant morbidity and mortality. Therefore, understanding the reservoirs for Acinetobacter spp. in healthcare settings is particularly important to infection control. Acinetobacter spp. are known to asymptomatically colonize the human gut, skin, and respiratory flora, and recent work has found the prevalence of Acinetobacter colonization is high in patients in healthcare environments, such as hospitals and long-term care facilities. Patients colonized by A. baumannii are at increased risk of developing clinical infections, including by the same strains. Additionally, multiple studies report transmission of A. baumannii strains to other patients in the same healthcare setting. Recent mechanistic studies on A. baumannii gut colonization have found that the microbiota, host immunity, and diet contribute to colonization resistance in animal models. Here, we review the epidemiologic evidence for asymptomatic colonization as a clinically important reservoir for A. baumannii and examine the nascent study of the molecular mechanisms of Acinetobacter colonization. We discuss future prospects for understanding Acinetobacter colonization that may help develop strategies to support colonization resistance and prevent infections.
authors: Clark RM, Palmer LD.

title: Valid and included novel bacterial taxa isolated from aquatic host species described in 2024-2025.
abstract: The description of new taxa and nomenclature updates to currently known taxa from aquatic animal species continues at a rapid pace. After a review of the literature from 2024 to 2025, bacteria in major morphologic categories were compiled. As previously noted, bacteria characterized as oxidase-positive Gram-negative bacilli predominated. Additions included new taxa in common families associated with aquatic environments like Aeromonadaceae, Flavobacteriaceae, and Pseudomonadaceae, as well as more uncommon families, such as Pasteurellaceae. A number of Gram-positive organisms are noted, including Planococcus notacanthi sp. nov., the sole coccus described, and multiple bacilli, including new taxa in the Streptomyces and Paenibacillus genera. Two anaerobic species are highlighted, as well as a spirochete and a new member of family Chlamydiaceae. Revised taxa are briefly mentioned. As in previous reviews, most new and revised taxa are isolated from healthy aquatic animals, and the role of these new bacteria in health and disease has yet to be elucidated. Bacteria with potential clinical significance for aquatic animals or potential production of bioactive or antimicrobial substances are highlighted.
authors: de Ruyter TE, Burbick CR, Lawhon SD, Krueger T, Javier L, Munson E.

title: Multicenter evaluation of the multiplex polymerase chain reaction QIAstat-Dx Meningitis/Encephalitis Panel for the detection of central nervous system pathogens directly in the cerebrospinal fluid.
abstract: Rapid and accurate detection of pathogens causing meningitis/encephalitis (MEN/EN) is critical to improving clinical outcomes. Multiplex polymerase chain reaction (PCR) enables simultaneous detection of multiple pathogens from the cerebrospinal fluid (CSF), offering advantages over traditional methods. This multicenter study evaluated the performance of the QIAstat-Dx Meningitis/Encephalitis (ME) Panel versus conventional methods, including the BioFire FilmArray ME (BFME) Panel. The CSF samples from patients with suspected MEN/EN along with contrived samples were tested across 13 sites in Europe/USA. Positive percent agreement (PPA) and negative percent agreement (NPA) between the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel and comparator methods were determined. A total of 1,667 clinical samples (1,527 prospective, 140 archived) were tested. Pathogens were detected by the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel in 115 (7.5%) prospective samples, including Streptococcus pneumoniae (1.1%), Haemophilus influenzae (0.5%), Listeria monocytogenes (0.3%), S. agalactiae (0.2%), Escherichia coli K1 (0.1%), Neisseria meningitidis (0.1%), S. pyogenes (0.1%), enterovirus (1.5%), human herpesvirus-6 (1.0%), herpes simplex virus-2 (0.9%) and -1 (0.3%), varicella zoster virus (0.7%), cytomegalovirus (0.3%), human parechovirus (0.3%), and Cryptococcus gattii/neoformans (0.4%). Overall PPA versus BFME (n = 1,664) was 85.4%, increasing to 95.3% after discordance resolution. PPA was 100% for N. meningitidis, S. pneumoniae, and S. agalactiae. Overall NPA was 99.9%. Among 1,154 contrived positive samples, only 27 (2.3%) incorrect results were observed. The QIAstat-Dx ME Panel demonstrated high concordance with BFME, supporting its use as a reliable, fully automated multiplex PCR platform for rapid diagnosis of community-acquired MEN/EN.IMPORTANCEThis multicenter study demonstrated that the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel delivers clinical performance comparable to that of the BioFire FilmArray ME (BFME) Panel, supporting its validity as a reliable syndromic molecular diagnostic tool for MEN/EN. With its broad pathogen coverage, rapid turnaround time (TAT), and the ability to provide amplification curves and Ct values, the QIAstat-Dx ME Panel offers a valuable option for broad and timely detection of bacterial, viral, and fungal CNS pathogens. When used alongside the SoC diagnostic methods, this panel has the potential to improve early diagnosis, guide targeted therapy, and support effective clinical management of patients with suspected MEN/EN.
authors: Farnsworth C, Ren P, González-López JJ, Bialas J, Humphries R, Davis T, Simner PJ, Ledeboer NA, Dunn J, Dhiman N, Caspar Y, Wolk DM, Rey M, Fern S, English A, Johnson S, Pancholi P.

title: DNA methyltransferase HP1208 antagonizes Fur-mediated repression of GlmU to modulate β-lactam susceptibility in Helicobacter pylori.
abstract: DNA methyltransferases in Helicobacter pylori regulate processes beyond genome defense, but whether they directly modulate β-lactam susceptibility has remained unclear. Here, we identify the conserved CATG methyltransferase M.HpyAI (HP1208) as a key determinant of cell wall homeostasis and antibiotic response. Deletion of hp1208 in strain 26695 caused a marked increase in β-lactam susceptibility and impaired growth under osmotic stress, consistent with defective peptidoglycan biogenesis. Transcriptomic profiling revealed coordinated repression of cell wall biosynthetic genes, with glmU emerging as the dominant functional target. Ectopic glmU expression restored peptidoglycan content and β-lactam MICs to wild-type values, establishing GlmU as the principal downstream effector of HP1208. Mechanistically, HP1208 methylates a CATG motif in the glmU promoter that resides within a Fur-responsive regulatory segment adjacent to the -10 element. This methyl mark reduces Fur occupancy at the glmU promoter, thereby relieving Fur-mediated repression and sustaining basal glmU transcription. When methylation is lost, Fur occupancy increases, glmU expression declines, and cell wall integrity is impaired. Thus, HP1208 modulates β-lactam susceptibility not simply by broadly remodeling the methylome, but by antagonizing a metal-responsive repressor at a critical peptidoglycan node. We further show that β-lactam exposure lowers intracellular iron availability, promotes the conversion of holo-Fur to apo-Fur, and partially derepresses glmU under methylation-deficient conditions. These findings uncover a coupled epigenetic-iron homeostasis circuit in which HP1208 and Fur coordinate cell-wall precursor production, intrinsic β-lactam susceptibility, and adaptive recovery from antibiotic stress.
authors: Deng T, Wang Y, He Y, Yan H, Liu M, She F, Wen Y.

title: Droplet digital PCR for diagnosing invasive aspergillosis in hematological malignancies: a prospective cohort study.
abstract: Our objective was to evaluate the diagnostic accuracy of Aspergillus droplet digital PCR (ddPCR) in exhaled breath condensate (EBC) and bronchoalveolar lavage fluid (BALF) for diagnosing invasive aspergillosis (IA), and to compare its performance with quantitative real-time PCR (qPCR) in patients with hematologic malignancies. We conducted a prospective single-center study, including adults admitted to leukemia and allogeneic hematopoietic stem cell transplant units who underwent bronchoscopy for pulmonary infiltrates between October 2021 and December 2024. EBC and BALF were collected concurrently. ddPCR was performed on EBC and BALF (supernatant and cell pellet); qPCR was performed on BALF samples. IA was classified according to EORTC/MSGERC criteria without incorporating PCR into the reference standard. Diagnostic performance characteristics, including area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUC-ROC), were calculated. Among 203 participants, 26 (12.8%) were diagnosed with probable or proven IA. EBC ddPCR showed poor performance (AUC-ROC 0.55, 95% CI 0.43-0.67). BALF supernatant ddPCR demonstrated the best performance (AUC-ROC 0.88, 95% CI 0.80-0.96), with sensitivity of 0.65 (95% CI 0.43-0.84) and specificity of 0.96 (95% CI 0.92-0.99). BALF supernatant outperformed BALF cell pellet testing for both ddPCR and qPCR. Compared with qPCR, ddPCR showed higher sensitivity and similarly high specificity. Among participants without prior mold-active antifungal therapy, BALF supernatant ddPCR showed improved performance (AUC-ROC 0.95, 95% CI 0.89-1.00). In this large prospective study, EBC ddPCR demonstrated limited utility for the diagnosis of IA. BALF supernatant was the optimal specimen type, and ddPCR outperformed qPCR. Diagnostic performance improved substantially without prior mold-active antifungal exposure.IMPORTANCEInvasive aspergillosis is difficult to diagnose in patients with hematologic malignancies, and non-invasive diagnostic approaches are needed. In this prospective study of 203 patients, Aspergillus droplet digital PCR performed poorly in exhaled breath condensate (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.55; 95% CI 0.43-0.67) but showed good diagnostic performance in bronchoalveolar lavage supernatant fluid (area under the receiver operating characteristic curve 0.88; 95% CI 0.80-0.96). Droplet digital PCR demonstrated higher sensitivity than quantitative PCR with similarly high specificity, and bronchoalveolar lavage supernatant fluid consistently outperformed cell pellet testing. Among patients without prior mold-active antifungal therapy, the area under the receiver operating characteristic curve was 0.95 (95% CI 0.89-1.00). These findings support bronchoalveolar lavage supernatant fluid as the preferred specimen for Aspergillus droplet digital PCR and warrant further evaluation of this approach for diagnosing invasive aspergillosis.
authors: Bitterman R, Ng CF, Arora S, Casciato M, Magyar U, Salazar S, Usman N, Pervez Z, Rehan F, Walti LN, Mattsson J, Gupta V, Mazzulli T, Husain S.

title: Clinical significance of different Histoplasma genotypes in human histoplasmosis: insights from a multicenter study from Québec comparing North American (NAm2) with Latin American (LAmA) isolates.
abstract: Histoplasmosis is recognized as endemic in Québec; however, no molecular epidemiological studies have been conducted to date. The clinical significance of identifying Histoplasma capsulatum genotypes remains unclear. We performed a retrospective multicenter study of 67 culture-confirmed histoplasmosis cases from four major academic hospitals in Québec between 1988 and 2014. Multi-locus sequence typing (MLST) was performed on isolates, and clinical data were analyzed for genotype-specific associations with demographics, clinical presentations, and outcomes. Most isolates belonged to either the North American clade 2 (48.1%) or Latin American clade A (39.2%), highlighting both endemic and imported disease patterns in Québec. A novel NAm2 sequence type (ST81) was identified, which was unique to Québec and accounted for 61% of the NAm2 isolates, but was not associated with significantly different clinical outcomes compared with other NAm2 strains. In multivariate analysis, disseminated disease was independently associated with immunosuppression (OR 14.18, P = 0.001), male sex (OR 6.01, P = 0.035), and LAmA genotype (OR 5.02, P = 0.031). Severe outcomes (intensive care unit admission, intubation, death, or amphotericin B use) were associated with immunosuppression (OR 4.48, P = 0.023), with a non-significant trend with LAmA infections (OR 3.06, P = 0.069). This first molecular characterization of histoplasmosis infections in Québec suggests a dual epidemiology, with locally acquired NAm2 and LAmA infections more often associated with travel or origin from endemic regions outside Québec. Host factors were associated with disease severity, while the potential contribution of fungal genotype requires further study. These findings highlight the value of molecular characterization for understanding the epidemiology of histoplasmosis in endemic settings.ImportanceHistoplasmosis is an important dimorphic fungal infection in North America. Although Québec is a recognized endemic region, its molecular epidemiology has not been previously characterized, and the clinical relevance of different Histoplasma genotypes remains uncertain. In this multicenter study, we performed multi-locus sequence typing with detailed clinical data from 67 culture-confirmed cases diagnosed between 1988 and 2014. This represents the first molecular characterization of clinical Histoplasma isolates from Québec and the largest Canadian cohort examining the association between molecular genotypes, clinical presentation, and outcomes. We identified both North American NAm2 (Histoplasma ohiense) and imported Latin American LAmA (Histoplasma suramericanum) lineages, suggestive of a combination of locally acquired and travel-associated infections. We also identified a novel NAm2 sequence type (ST81) that appears unique to Québec, suggesting possible regional circulation. The LAmA genotype was associated with disseminated histoplasmosis, whereas immunosuppression was the principal predictor of severe outcomes. Overall, host factors were associated with disease severity, while the potential contribution of fungal genotype warrants further study. These findings highlight the value of molecular characterization for understanding the epidemiology of histoplasmosis in endemic settings.
authors: Mah JK, Talbot J-D, Baldassarre L, Moonjely SS, Vinh DC, Pelletier R, Lavallée C, Tremblay C, Fournier E, Dufresne PJ, Dufresne SF.

title: Powerhouses of lethality: mitochondria in macrophage antimicrobial activity.
abstract: Macrophages employ multiple strategies to dispatch phagocytosed microbes, including bombardment with toxic compounds and radicals, or the deprivation of key nutrients. The lethality of macrophages depends on their ability to regulate levels of microbicidal effectors and proper targeting of these effectors to the phagosome, where many intracellular pathogens are detained. Mitochondria play important roles in establishing an antimicrobial phagosomal environment in macrophages, playing roles in both the production and targeting of these effectors. In response to infection, the mitochondrial network undergoes dramatic structural and functional perturbations that modulate macrophage microbicidal potential. As central coordinators of cellular metabolism, mitochondria control the abundance of metabolites that can either be toxic to ingested microbes or necessary for their growth. Mitochondria are also prolific producers of reactive oxygen species (ROS), which play direct roles in killing microbes and serve as signaling molecules to coordinate antimicrobial responses. While mitochondria are also known to play extensive roles in regulating cytokine production and proinflammatory responses, this review will focus on highlighting mechanisms by which mitochondria manipulate the macrophage microbicidal milieu.
authors: McFadden MJ, O'Meara TR, O'Riordan MX.

title: An open-label, Phase 1 study to evaluate the drug-drug interaction between ulonivirine and the combined oral contraceptive levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol in female participants without HIV with a validated liquid chromatograph.
abstract: Ulonivirine is a non-nucleoside reverse transcriptase inhibitor in development as an oral, once-weekly treatment for HIV-1 in combination with investigational islatravir. The effect of ulonivirine on the pharmacokinetics of an oral contraceptive, levonorgestrel (LNG)/ethinyl estradiol (EE) was evaluated in females without HIV. In this Phase 1 study (MK-8507-009), postmenopausal or oophorectomized females received a single dose of LNG/EE (0.1 mg/0.02 mg), followed by a 5-day washout period. Participants then received ulonivirine 400 mg once-weekly for 3 weeks, and LNG/EE was co-administered with the third dose. Blood samples were collected for pharmacokinetics analysis. Safety and tolerability were monitored by clinical and laboratory assessments. Twenty adults (90% White; 100% Hispanic or Latina) were enrolled (median age, 56 years; range, 47-66 years). Two participants discontinued for reasons considered unrelated to ulonivirine. The geometric mean ratios ([LNG/EE + ulonivirine]/[LNG/EE]; 90% CI) for plasma AUC0-inf of LNG and EE were 0.88 (0.84-0.93) and 0.85 (0.82-0.89). Maximum plasma concentration of LNG and EE decreased (26% and 20%, respectively) with LNG/EE + ulonivirine versus LNG/EE alone. Ulonivirine pharmacokinetics were similar for LNG/EE + ulonivirine and LNG/EE alone. Four participants (20%) experienced ≥1 adverse event: 2 (10%) after administration of LNG/EE alone and 2 (10.5%) after co-administration of LNG/EE + ulonivirine. All adverse events were mild and considered unrelated to study intervention. Co-administration of ulonivirine 400 mg once-weekly with a single dose of LNG/EE had no clinically meaningful effect on the pharmacokinetics of LNG or EE in females without HIV and was generally well tolerated.
authors: Robinson M, Gillespie G, Kandala B, Ankrom W, Iwamoto M, Pajkovic N, Liu Y, Garrett GC, Hernandez-Illas M, Nussbaum JC.

title: The Aspergillus fumigatus septation components Bud4 and Rho4 are essential for virulence.
abstract: Aspergillus fumigatus is the primary etiologic agent of pulmonary mold infections, the most severe of which is invasive pulmonary aspergillosis (IPA). As the currently approved antifungal drugs are threatened by growing resistance rates and host toxicity, novel therapeutic options are urgently needed. Our recent work suggests that septation inhibition may be one such strategy, as aseptate strains of A. fumigatus are hypersusceptible to the echinocandin antifungal drugs and display significantly reduced virulence in animal models of IPA. In the current study, we expand upon our understanding of the anillin-like protein, Bud4, and Rho GTPase, Rho4, which regulate septation in Aspergillus nidulans and A. fumigatus, respectively. Whereas AnBud4 is not essential for septation in A. nidulans, deletion of the A. fumigatus ortholog (∆bud4) resulted in complete loss of septation. A similar phenotype was also observed in ∆rho4, consistent with previous studies. Supporting a critical role for hyphal septation in the establishment of invasive aspergillosis, we find that ∆bud4 and ∆rho4 display avirulence in a mouse model of IPA characterized by a loss of tissue-invasive growth. Furthermore, both deletion mutations were able to convert anti-Aspergillus echinocandin activity from static to cidal. Through titratable bud4 expression using a doxycycline-repressible promoter system, we also find that even partial repression of septation significantly increases echinocandin susceptibility. Taken together, these studies support a therapeutic strategy which could incorporate a septation inhibitor in combination with echinocandins to reduce tissue-invasive growth and improve antifungal susceptibility.
authors: Guruceaga X, Thorn HI, Perez-Cuesta U, Martin-Vicente A, Xie J, Bale DNJ, Nywening AV, Nandi A, Fortwendel JR.

title: Neutrophil remodeling during chlamydial infection: recognition, survival, inflammatory signaling, and tissue injury.
abstract: Chlamydia species are obligate intracellular bacteria with a biphasic developmental cycle. They cause trachoma, urogenital tract infection, community-acquired pneumonia, and zoonotic respiratory disease. A common feature of these conditions is not simply infection but the combination of persistence, recurrent inflammation, and tissue injury. Neutrophils arrive early at infected tissues and can initiate phagocytosis, degranulation, reactive oxygen species production, and neutrophil extracellular trap formation through pattern-recognition receptors, complement receptors, and Fc receptors. That response is not uniformly beneficial. When recruitment is excessive or poorly resolved, neutrophils can amplify inflammation, weaken epithelial barriers, and contribute to fibrosis and chronic immunopathology. Here, we review Chlamydia-neutrophil interactions as a staged biological process: recognition, recruitment, effector activation, apoptosis delay, inflammatory amplification, negative feedback, and tissue injury. Particular attention is given to TLRs, NF-κB, MAPK, PI3K/Akt, the NLRP3 inflammasome, mitochondrial reactive oxygen species, and IL-10/JAK-STAT-related feedback. We distinguish evidence obtained directly from neutrophils from evidence inferred from epithelial cells, macrophages, PBMCs, animal tissues, or other pathogen systems. This distinction is essential because mechanisms supported in one cell type or one chlamydial species cannot be transferred automatically to another. A more precise view of this network may refine current models of chlamydia-host interaction and pathogen persistence and help frame future studies on stage-specific immunomodulation.
authors: Liu X, Xiao J, Tang C, Chen Q, Wang C.

title: Global diversification and regional spread of Candidozyma (Candida) auris clades: a comparative genomic epidemiology review of the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, and the Asia-Pacific.
abstract: Candidozyma auris (formerly Candida auris), first described in 2009, has spread to 82 countries across 6 continents, with more than 84,000 cumulative colonization and infection cases reported through December 2025. Whole-genome sequencing has resolved the species into six deeply divergent clades (I-VI) that differ geographically and in antifungal susceptibility. This minireview synthesizes peer-reviewed literature and public health surveillance data on whole-genome-sequencing-confirmed clade distribution and susceptibility across the United States, the European Union/European Economic Area, the United Kingdom, Latin America and the Caribbean, Saudi Arabia and the wider Gulf region, Canada, Singapore, Australia, and New Zealand. Clades I and III are now the most geographically widespread outbreak-associated lineages, documented across nearly every region reviewed. The United States has diversified from early clade I dominance to a four-clade landscape by 2013-2022 (clade I, 56.0%; clade III, 29.4%; clade IV, 14.1%; and clade II, 0.5%). Latin America remains the principal reservoir of clade IV; Saudi Arabia and the Gulf region are dominated by clade I, and the discovery of clade VI in Singapore and Bangladesh illustrates continuing genomic diversification. Clade I carries the highest burden of multidrug and pan-resistance; clade III shows high fluconazole resistance but lower echinocandin resistance; and clade IV, historically associated with lower resistance, is now rising. Because regional antifungal resistance largely reflects clade composition rather than independent regional drift, clade-aware surveillance should directly inform local stewardship, diagnostic inclusivity, and regulatory bridging across markets.
authors: Kamau E.

title: AI/ML-enabled sepsis prediction systems: laboratory considerations from development to deployment.
abstract: Sepsis prediction algorithms based on machine learning are increasingly embedded in electronic health record systems, and clinical laboratories have been largely absent from their development, validation, and governance. This is a consequential gap. Laboratory variables are central inputs to most deployed sepsis artificial intelligence (AI) tools, and routine analytical events such as platform transitions, reagent reformulations, and reference interval updates can shift the distributions of these inputs. Such distribution shifts are a recognized cause of degraded model performance; however, the effects of laboratory-specific changes remain insufficiently characterized for sepsis tools in clinical use. Neither clinical teams nor laboratories are currently well positioned to detect these effects. This review is written for clinical laboratorians who encounter these tools in practice or are asked to evaluate them for implementation. We describe the data sources used as model inputs and how analytical context, preanalytical variability, and ordering patterns influence model behavior. Five deployed algorithms with real-world implementation evidence are profiled alongside the broader preclinical landscape, including early warning systems, mortality and complication prediction models, and sepsis subtyping research. Development and implementation pitfalls are reviewed with attention to laboratory-specific considerations, and the regulatory and governance landscape is addressed with emphasis on where laboratorian involvement is most needed. Controlled outcomes data supporting currently deployed tools remain limited, and reported performance frequently does not replicate at external sites. Laboratorians bring expertise in analytical quality, data provenance, and change management that is not replicated elsewhere on implementation teams. As the field moves toward sepsis subtyping, continuous monitoring, and local model calibration, laboratorian expertise in analytical quality and monitoring will become increasingly central to how these tools are built, deployed, and maintained.
authors: Durant T, Aldewereld Z, Peaper DR, Wheeler SE.

title: Update to the CDC influenza A(H3) subtyping assay for improved detection of influenza A(H3N2) viruses, including subclade K viruses.
abstract: Influenza A(H3N2) viruses circulate globally and cause respiratory illness. The FDA-cleared CDC Human Influenza Virus Real-Time RT-PCR Influenza A (H3/H1pdm09) Subtyping assay is used to subtype seasonal influenza A viruses. However, emerging mutations in the H3 reverse primer region raised concerns about reduced assay sensitivity for contemporary circulating viruses. We updated the H3 assay by redesigning the reverse primer to target a more conserved region of the hemagglutinin gene, and incorporating minor adjustments into the forward primer and probe. Analytical sensitivity, inclusivity, and exclusivity evaluations were performed using cultured influenza viruses, synthetic RNA, and panels of non-influenza respiratory pathogens. Clinical performance was evaluated using seasonal A(H3N2) residual respiratory specimens. The updated assay (H3_v2) demonstrated analytical sensitivity comparable to or improved over the initial H3 assay, with a limit of detection of approximately 101.7-102.1 EID50/mL and five copies of RNA per reaction. Improved performance was observed for viruses containing A21G with T23G, T23C, or T23A double mismatches in the reverse primer, with a measurable Ct value shift between the initial H3 and H3_v2 assay. The assay showed 100% agreement with expected results in 139 clinical specimens, and no cross-reactivity with other influenza subtypes or other respiratory pathogens. These findings indicate the updated H3_v2 assay improves sensitivity for contemporary and emerging seasonal A(H3N2) viruses while maintaining high specificity. This update ensures continued reliable detection of seasonal A(H3N2), including genetically drifted A(H3N2) viruses, such as the recently emerged A(H3N2) subclade K viruses, and supports global influenza surveillance and diagnostic preparedness.ImportanceAccurate detection and subtyping of influenza A(H3N2) viruses are essential for clinical diagnostics, outbreak response, and global influenza surveillance. The emergence and fixation of mutations leading to primer mismatches in the FDA-cleared CDC A(H3) real-time RT-PCR assay raised concerns about reduced sensitivity for contemporary circulating A(H3N2) viruses. To address this, we redesigned the reverse primer and optimized additional assay components to improve detection of currently circulating seasonal A(H3N2) viruses. The updated H3_v2 assay restores and enhances sensitivity, including for viruses harboring key reverse primer mismatches, while maintaining high specificity and complete agreement with clinical specimens. This update ensures reliable detection of seasonal influenza A(H3N2) and A(H3N2) variant viruses, including recently emerged A(H3N2) subclade K viruses, and strengthens diagnostic preparedness and surveillance capacity nationally and internationally.
authors: Shu B, Liddell J, Wong P, Duron ES, Liu J, Hassell N, DaSilva J, Wu K-H, Foust A, Kondor RJ, Davis CT, Kirby MK.

title: An update on novel and included taxa and revised taxonomic status of bacteria isolated from non-domestic animals described in 2025.
abstract: Maintaining an updated list of and analyzing new and revised microbial taxa originating from non-domestic animal species are considered important annual endeavors. As researchers continue to investigate complex microbiota in animal and environmental samples, it is critical that findings are accessible to all with an interest in wildlife animal species. Herein, data concerning novel bacterial taxa and taxonomic revisions of bacteria derived from non-domestic wildlife specimens that were published in peer-reviewed literature and/or accepted during 2025 are summarized and analyzed. While few of the newly identified or accepted bacteria are associated with clinical disease in the host of origin, some are closely related to bacteria that have been implicated in disease or opportunistic infections. Others may contribute valuable information toward future research involving probiotics, antimicrobial resistance, metabolic health, detoxification, and the degradation of toxic materials. Notable bacteria include Helicobacter cappadocius sp. nov., the first species of psychrotrophic Helicobacter, and Limosilactobacillus allomucosae sp. nov., which has potential for use as a probiotic in domestic pigs.
authors: Masterson H, Burbick CR, Lawhon SD, Carapia L, Munson E.

title: Pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic evaluation of multidose oritavancin for prolonged durations of therapy.
abstract: Managing multidrug-resistant gram-positive infections is challenging, especially when prolonged therapy is needed for conditions like bacteremia, endocarditis, osteomyelitis, or other deep-seated infections. Oritavancin, a long-acting lipoglycopeptide, is increasingly used in these scenarios and offers an alternative to central catheter placement. However, despite its growing use for extended treatment, optimal dosing strategies and pharmacokinetic targets remain unclear. An in silico pharmacokinetic/pharmacodynamic simulation was performed to assess the predicted oritavancin concentration resulting from weekly and every 2-week dosing regimens. The simulations utilized a previously published model, which utilized pharmacokinetic sampling data from two single-dose, phase 3 clinical trials. A 100% free time above the MIC was utilized as the pharmacodynamic target. The Clinical and Laboratory Standards Institute breakpoint (0.12 µg/mL) and MIC90 (0.06 µg/mL) values for both Staphylococcus aureus and Enterococcus faecalis were utilized as benchmarks. Eighty-five percent protein binding was assumed. A six-dose regimen of 1,200 mg weekly is expected to maintain free plasma concentrations above the breakpoint for a median of 10.4 weeks (lower 5th percentile 9.6) and above the MIC90 for about 1.5 weeks longer, exceeding what is usually required for acute treatment of most infections. Alternatively, using a three-dose regimen of 1,200 mg every 2 weeks is expected to maintain free plasma concentrations above the breakpoint for a median of 8.4 weeks (lower 5th percentile 7.9), with trough values remaining therapeutic between doses. Every 2-week dosing strategies are expected to maintain therapeutic concentrations between doses. This strategy may be employed to reduce the cost of treatment and improve patient convenience.
authors: Volk CF, Blumenthal M, Thomas N, Kufel WD, Rose WE, Lim SY.

title: A machine learning framework for precision dosing of daptomycin across diverse disease states.
abstract: The large pharmacokinetic variability of daptomycin across disease states poses a challenge for individualized dosing. Conventional population pharmacokinetic (PopPK) models are often limited to specific conditions, lacking generalizability. This study used a machine learning (ML) framework to predict daptomycin exposure and guide dose optimization across heterogeneous populations. Nine published PopPK models were used to generate 90,000 simulated profiles across patients with infections and/or patients treated with renal transplantation and/or renal replacement therapy. Seven ML algorithms were trained to predict the 24 h area under the concentration-time curve (AUC0-24). Model performance was evaluated using statistical metrics and clinical scenario assessments, and comparison with PopPK models. External validation was conducted with real-world data. CatBoost demonstrated the highest predictive accuracy, identifying dose, creatinine clearance, disease state, and weight as key predictors. The validation cohort comprised 20 patients with infections (501 concentration measurements) and 19 patients receiving renal replacement therapy (513 concentration measurements). In infected patients, the prediction error of AUC0-24 was reduced by 60.1% compared with existing PopPK models (root mean square error [RMSE], 141 vs 353 mg·h/L; mean absolute prediction error, 23.5% vs 58.1%). The ML model correctly classified 75.0% of patients into the appropriate clinical AUC categories (939 mg·h/L), outperforming PopPK models (average overall accuracy: 30.0%). In patients undergoing renal replacement therapy, ML also improved performance (RMSE, 197 vs 218 mg·h/L; overall accuracy, 52.6% vs 31.6%). The ML model demonstrated accurate prediction of steady-state daptomycin AUC in heterogeneous clinical populations and was successfully validated using real-world data. By enabling accurate pre-treatment exposure prediction, it provides a flexible and clinically useful pathway toward precision dosing of daptomycin.
authors: Zhang X-F, Sun J, Hao G-X, Chen X-M, Zhou Y, Wang X-J, van den Anker J, Zhao W, Sun D-Q, Tang B-H.

title: Population pharmacokinetics of piperacillin based on multicenter data to support model-informed precision dosing in critically ill women.
