This Tn insertion generates a truncated version of the ArgA protein (ArgA188-432) that retains NAGS activity but, unlike the wild-type protein, is unrestrained by arginine feedback inhibition. However, the Tn::argA mutant readily re-acquired a prototrophic phenotype through the acquisition of spontaneous secondary mutations outside of the argA locus. Whole-genome sequencing and complementation analyses of one such 'bypass mutant' allowed us to trace this epistatic effect to an Ala128→Val substitution in AmbA, a LysE-type transmembrane transporter. Using a variety of genetic approaches, we show that the ambA Ala128Val mutation gives rise to a change/expansion of function in the encoded gene product and that this mutation is directly or indirectly responsible for bypassing the auxotrophy associated with the original Tn::argA mutation. Further analysis of the Tn::argA ambA Ala128Val mutant revealed that, compared with the 'wild-type' progenitor, the mutant exhibited large-scale changes in its proteome and metabolome consistent with elevated intracellular arginine and enhanced polyamine degradation. We conclude that the ambA Ala128Val mutation overcomes the phenotypic impact of the dysregulated ArgA188-432 enzyme, possibly by enabling efflux of toxic polyamines (which we also show can competitively inhibit NAGS).
authors: Mohan V, Labrini E, Aksoy CS, Behrends V, Evangelista LC, Spring DR, Welch M.

title: Proteomics insight into phosphate limitation response in Burkholderia phytopathogens.
abstract: Inorganic phosphate (Pi) limitation is a pervasive environmental constraint that shapes microbial behaviour in soil and plant-associated niches. To determine how Pi scarcity influences the pathogenic potential of rice-infecting Burkholderia species, we performed comparative proteomic and lipidomic analyses of Burkholderia glumae and Burkholderia plantarii grown under Pi-replete and Pi-deplete conditions. Pi starvation triggered strong activation of the Pho regulon in both organisms, including induction of alkaline phosphatases, phosphonate transporters and the high-affinity PstSABC uptake system. Beyond classical phosphate-stress responses, Pi limitation markedly enriched proteins associated with virulence, secretion systems, toxins, chemotaxis and cell envelope modification. Both species also activated PlcP/Agt-mediated lipid remodelling pathways and synthesized phosphorus-free glycolipids exclusively during Pi depletion, indicating substantial membrane lipid restructuring. These results demonstrate that Pi limitation acts as a major environmental cue coordinating nutrient acquisition with multiple virulence-related functions. Our findings provide new insight into how phosphate scarcity shapes the environmental fitness and pathogenic capacity of Burkholderia phytopathogens and highlight nutrient limitation as an important driver of plant disease emergence.
authors: Xu L, Kaur M, Ham JH, Wang M, Jackson RW, Chen Y.

title: Microbial Primer: Mirror bacteria.
abstract: Mirror bacteria are hypothetical synthetic organisms built from molecules of opposite chirality to those used throughout nature. This primer discusses their potential dangers: because of their chiral mismatch to the natural environment, mirror bacteria could plausibly evade predation, immunity and other ecological control mechanisms to a degree never seen before. This property could simultaneously make them unprecedented invasive species and dangerous pathogens.
authors: Cooper VS, Sweere JM.

title: In vitro and in vivo functional roles of three region 1 promoters in Escherichia coli K1 capsule gene cluster.
abstract: Capsular polysaccharides are key virulence determinants in extraintestinal pathogenic Escherichia coli, protecting bacteria from host immune defences while modulating interactions with host tissues. In group 2 capsule gene clusters, transcription of region 1 genes required for capsule export is controlled by a complex regulatory region (PR1) containing three tandem promoters (PR1-1, PR1-2 and PR1-3).In this study, targeted mutations were introduced into the -10 elements of each PR1 promoter in the uropathogenic strain UTI89. Transcriptional output from the PR1 region was assessed using a chromosomal PR1-lacZ fusion, and capsule expression was evaluated by K1 bacteriophage sensitivity assays, flow cytometry and immunofluorescence microscopy. Growth in Lysogeny Broth medium demonstrated that all three promoters contributed to capsule expression in vitro, with expression from both PR1-2 and PR1-3 being dependent on a functional upstream PR1-1.In contrast, infection of PD07i bladder epithelial cells revealed a distinct regulatory pattern in which, following invasion, intracellular capsule expression was restored in the absence of PR1-1 and PR1-2, indicating that PR1-3 was sufficient for capsule induction within bladder cells. The presence of a predicted binding site for the oxygen-responsive regulator fumarate and nitrate reduction regulatory protein near PR1-3 suggests a possible mechanism for intracellular activation of PR1-3 under microaerobic host conditions in the absence of a functional PR1-1 promoter.Together, these findings reveal a niche-dependent, multi-promoter regulatory architecture that enables adaptive control of capsule expression during infection.
authors: Aldawood E, Roberts IS.

title: A novel promoter driving the expression of the quorum-sensing PqsE protein shows substantial differences in Pseudomonas aeruginosa and Pseudomonas paraeruginosa.
abstract: Pseudomonas aeruginosa is an important bacterial pathogen due to its production of different virulence factors, several of which, like rhamnolipids elastase and pyocyanin (PYO), are regulated by the quorum-sensing (QS) response, which is composed of three transcriptional regulators/autoinducer systems. At the top of the regulatory cascade is LasR/3-oxo-dodecanoyl homoserine lactone, which activates the expression of the RhlR/butanoyl homoserine lactone system and of PqsR. The latter, when coupled with its autoinducer 2-heptyl-3,4-dihydroxyquinoline (PQS), activates the transcription of the pqsABCDE operon, which encodes the enzymes responsible for the synthesis of 4-hydroxy-2-heptylquinoline which is the precursor of PQS. The Pqs system plays a key role in the production of PYO, mainly by regulating the expression of PqsE. The PqsE protein forms a protein complex with RhlR required to activate the transcription of the phz operons for PYO production. This hierarchical QS regulatory network is conserved in the recently described Pseudomonas paraeruginosa species, which produces the same virulence factors as P. aeruginosa. In this work, we characterize a promoter that is located directly upstream of pqsE in P. aeruginosa PAO1 and show that transcription from this promoter is repressed by the global regulator Vfr. By contrast, in P. paraeruginosa strains, whereas the -10 and -35 promoter sequences are conserved, the Vfr-binding site is not present, enabling the constitutive expression of the pqsE ORF independent of PqsR/PQS regulation. The implications for PYO production as a virulence-related trait in P. paraeruginosa are discussed.
authors: Montelongo-Martínez LF, Quiroz-Morales SE, Cocotl-Yañez M, Soberón-Chávez G.

title: Microbe Profile: Acinetobacter baumannii: persist and resist.
abstract: Acinetobacter baumannii is a Gram-negative opportunistic pathogen associated with a wide variety of healthcare-associated infections, including ventilator-associated pneumonia, urinary tract infections, bacteraemia and wound infections. It adopts a 'persist and resist' pathogenic strategy to establish infection in the host. It can form robust biofilms and survive in a desiccated state for months at a time, driving its persistence in the hospital-built environment. It also has a remarkable capacity to rapidly develop antimicrobial resistance, with >90% of contemporary clinical isolates being multidrug-resistant. This combination of pathogenic traits has caused A. baumannii to emerge as a major clinical challenge.
authors: de Dios R, McCarthy RR.

title: Evaluating packaged ice safety using culture-based and metagenomic methods.
abstract: Ice can serve as a vector for microbial contamination, presenting potential risks to public health. This study aimed to evaluate the microbial quality and safety of commercially available ice in Manitoba as well as to characterize the microbiome of ice cubes and assess the presence of antimicrobial resistance (AMR) genes. Samples from five different brands, four non-International Packaged Ice Association (IPIA)-accredited and one IPIA-accredited brand, were collected from retail stores between May and August 2024. Ice samples were tested using membrane filtration for total plate count, Escherichia coli, coliforms, Pseudomonas, yeasts, moulds and Enterococcus and screened for Listeria monocytogenes and Salmonella. Separate filtration samples were collected for metagenomic analysis. Membrane filtration results showed that 12.8% of samples from non-IPIA-accredited brands failed to meet IPIA standards for total coliforms, whereas 100% of samples from the IPIA-accredited brand complied. All samples tested negative for foodborne pathogens when conventional culture-based methods were used. However, metagenomic sequencing revealed the presence of pathogen-associated DNA. A diverse resistome was identified across all brands, including the IPIA-accredited sample, with genes conferring resistance to β-lactams, aminoglycosides and biocides. Recovered Pseudomonas isolates were identified as Pseudomonas lactis, a psychrotrophic species capable of growth at refrigeration temperatures. Biofilm assays demonstrated that recovered P. lactis formed biofilms at both 4 and 10 °C, with significantly greater biofilm formation observed at 4 °C. Our findings demonstrate consistent compliance among the IPIA-accredited brand, while variability and failures occurred among non-accredited producers. The detection of cold-adapted, biofilm-forming bacteria such as Pseudomonas spp., which can reduce sanitizer efficacy and protect co-existing micro-organisms, including potential pathogens harbouring AMR genes, highlights the need for targeted environmental monitoring using key indicator organisms such as Pseudomonas spp. Broader adoption of IPIA standards could strengthen microbial control practices and enhance consumer protection within the Canadian packaged ice industry.
authors: Cromb S, Mayboca-Padilla D, Bedi R, Narvaez-Bravo C.

title: Comparison of Streptococcus mutans growth-phase-dependent transcriptome changes in two different simulated microgravity models.
abstract: Streptococcus mutans is a cariogenic member of human dental plaque biofilm. Our previous study of S. mutans early stationary-phase rotary cell culture system (RCCS) cultures revealed significant transcriptome changes under low-shear modelled microgravity (LSMMG) compared to normal gravity (NG), as well as an altered cell clumping phenotype. In this current study, S. mutans mid-exponential phase and late-exponential phase cultures were compared using the RCCS (LSMMG and NG orientations) as well as simulated microgravity ('0 g') using a random positioning machine (0 g RPM). The previously described stationary-phase LSMMG-altered cell clumping phenotype was also observed at earlier growth phases in LSMMG and 0 g RPM. Significant fold-change differences in gene expression (late-exponential/mid-exponential phase) were observed in LSMMG, NG and 0 g RPM, with 24 genes shared between LSMMG and 0 g RPM cultures (including upregulated pyrimidine biosynthesis genes and decreased genes involved in purine biosynthesis, iron transport and malolactic fermentation). Additional significant functional enrichments included TCA cycle (LSMMG and NG), starch and sucrose metabolism (LSMMG and 0 g RPM) and folate biosynthesis (LSMMG, 0 g RPM and NG). Overall, these data provide insight into S. mutans physiology in response to simulated microgravity. Further investigation of transcriptome changes shared between LSMMG and 0 g RPM may allow us to better predict how this bacterium responds to spaceflight conditions.
authors: Davis KAT, Rice KC.

title: Type VI secretion drives reciprocal growth inhibition among symbiotic Vibrio fischeri strains.
abstract: Bacterial cells are often in direct contact with one another and compete for nutrients and space. The type VI secretion system (T6SS) is a contact-dependent mechanism that enables bacteria to deliver toxic effectors into neighbouring cells. Vibrio fischeri is a bacterial symbiont of the Hawaiian bobtail squid Euprymna scolopes and encodes a T6SS on its second chromosome (T6SS2) that promotes interference competition among strains within the squid light organ. Effector diversity among T6SS2+ strains is poorly understood, which impedes predicting compatibility among strains within the light organ. Here, we report our investigation of strain ANM004 and how T6SS2 facilitates its interactions with other strains including the model T6SS2+ strain FQ-A001. We show that both strains exhibit reciprocal T6SS2-dependent antagonism. Comparative genomics reveals each strain encodes unique effectors within T6SS2 gene loci. Heterologous expression of an ANM004-encoded AHH nuclease effector in FQ-A001 inhibits kin growth in a T6SS2-dependent manner. This effect on FQ-A001 kin is abrogated by expression of the cognate immunity factor encoded downstream of the effector gene. Together, these results establish an experimental framework for investigating intercellular interactions between two T6SS2+ symbiotic strains.
authors: McNeil AE, Teeter LB, Burkhart JI, Flores NJ, Shabana YA, Giacobe EJ, Moore PJ, Jensen JP, Donnelly AR, Murtha AN, Aslan H, Cecere AG, Guckes KR, Miyashiro TI.

title: In vitro characterization of Bacillus sp. LS100 for detoxifying deoxynivalenol.
abstract: The mycotoxin deoxynivalenol (DON) contamination in animal feed has been reported to reduce the growth performance of animals and compromise their immune system, especially pigs. Bacterial detoxification is considered a promising strategy to mitigate its harmful effects. We previously identified a bacterial isolate (Bacillus sp. LS100) from the chicken gut with the ability to detoxify DON. To explore its potential application in swine production, the current study was focused on in vitro characterization of Bacillus sp. LS100 with regard to its capacity to detoxify DON. The bacterium was stable in keeping its activity to fully detoxify DON when subcultured for 12 passages under anaerobic conditions. The bacterial culture was successfully scaled up and stored for at least 1 month without losing any activity to detoxify DON. In addition, it was able to fully detoxify DON in mouldy corn with a diluted medium in an anaerobic atmosphere. While the bacterium exhibited a certain degree of tolerance to oxygen, it was sensitive to low pH and bile salts, including pig gastric fluid. In the presence of digesta from the pig jejunum or ileum, the bacteria retained near-full or full detoxification activity of DON after 24 or 48 h incubation under anaerobic conditions. To protect Bacillus sp. LS100 from the detrimental effects of gastric acid and bile salt, the bacterium was encapsulated anaerobically. The encapsulated bacteria stored in wet beads at 22 °C exhibited greater stability and retained detoxification activity longer than those stored in dry beads. After exposure to simulated gastric fluid for 2 h, the bacterium in the wet beads retained the DON detoxification activity. The current study suggests that, when adequately protected, Bacillus sp. LS100 holds promise as a viable strategy for DON removal in the pig gut.
authors: Yu C, Yu H, Guo T, Zhu H, Mats L, Yang C, Wang Q, Gong J.

title: How cystic fibrosis modulator therapy could transform Pseudomonas aeruginosa epidemiology.
abstract: The advent of cystic fibrosis transmembrane conductance regulator modulators has revolutionized cystic fibrosis (CF) care by restoring epithelial ion transport and improving airway physiology in people with CF. These therapies reduce infection burden, especially from Pseudomonas aeruginosa, through enhanced mucociliary clearance and immune responses. Yet, P. aeruginosa often persists, raising concerns about microbial adaptation. Emerging evidence suggests that modulator-altered airways impose novel selective pressures, favouring mutations in genes linked to biofilm formation, iron metabolism and immune evasion. This may drive the emergence of strains adapted to a 'hybrid' airway; neither fully CF-like nor fully healthy. Such adaptations could potentially increase transmissibility or virulence, with implications beyond the CF population. Understanding how pathogens evolve under modulator pressure is essential in this new treatment era. Continued surveillance of microbial dynamics will be key to anticipating shifts in infection risk and informing future clinical and public health strategies.
authors: Gurney J, Letizia M, Azimi S, Diggle SP.

title: Decoupling metabolic defense: Mutational and recombinational chaos in Sod1-deficient cells.
abstract: Superoxide dismutase 1 (Sod1) is long recognized as a frontline antioxidant, yet its broader role in safeguarding the eukaryotic genome remains under-explored. Here, using a yeast model, we reveal that Sod1 is an indispensable guardian of genomic integrity. Its absence unleashes a genomic storm: whole-genome sequencing uncovered a dramatic surge in single nucleotide variations (13-fold), loss of heterozygosity (12-fold), chromosomal rearrangements (4-fold), and a staggering 48-fold increase in aneuploidy. Remarkably, this genomic instability was completely abolished under anaerobic conditions, identifying reactive oxygen species as the sole executioner. We demonstrate that Sod1 deficiency sculpts a unique mutational landscape dominated by C:G to A:T transversions-a molecular fingerprint of 8-oxoguanine overproduction. Mechanistically, these lesions are exacerbated by error-prone DNA polymerase ζ but mitigated by the concerted actions of Ogg1-mediated excision and DNA polymerase η. Critically, we show that Amyotrophic Lateral Sclerosis-associated variants are not created equal: the H48Q mutation shatters genome stability, whereas others (A4V, G36R, and G93A) remain benign in this context. Unlike yeast Sod1, human Sod1 is highly resistant to amino acid substitutions outside copper-binding sites, thus preventing the loss of enzyme function. Overall, our findings provide a mechanistically framework for understanding how Sod1 dysfunction drives genome instability in eukaryotic cells.
authors: Sui Y, Zheng DQ, Wang Y, Zhao SS, Li KJ, Ye C, Zhang K.

title: Molecular basis of quorum-sensing signal transduction by CqsS and its inhibition by CqsA, the autoinducer synthase.
abstract: Vibrio bacteria possess multiple quorum-sensing systems, each of which conveys information into the cell concerning the cell density and species composition of the vicinal community. Germane to the present work is the CqsA-CqsS quorum-sensing pathway that vibrios use for intragenus communication. CqsA is the synthase for the autoinducer (S)-3-hydroxytridecan-4-one (CAI-1), and CqsS, a bifunctional two-component kinase-phosphatase, is the CAI-1 receptor. Here, we determine the cryo-EM structures of the full-length Vibrio harveyi CqsS dimer in the apo- and ATPγS-bound states. Our structures reveal the molecular basis for the initiation of the phosphorylation cascade, which we support through biochemical and genetic analyses. Autophosphorylation of CqsS occurs in cis at the conserved histidine residue (H1), whereas phospho-transfer to the conserved aspartate residue (D1) in the C-terminal receiver domain occurs in trans. By coexpressing CqsS and CqsA to capture CqsS bound to CAI-1, we unexpectedly find a tight interaction between the CqsS intracellular domain and CqsA. In the complex, the CqsS H1 residues are positioned away from the catalytic cavity, and CqsS kinase activity is inhibited. Cryo-EM analysis, focused on the transmembrane domain of CqsS in this complex, reveals the presence of two CAI-1 molecules. CAI-1 binding induces an obvious movement of transmembrane helix 6, disrupting its extension into the cytosol, providing a structural basis for how CAI-1 binding in the periplasm is coupled to signal transduction into the cytoplasm. Together, our findings advance the understanding of CqsS-CAI-1-mediated quorum-sensing signal transduction, an activity that underpins the coordination of group behaviors in vibrios.
authors: Liu M, Yang Y, Valastyan JS, Zhang Y, Beggs GA, Liu Y, Wang Z, Bassler BL, Qian H.

title: Septin binding restricts Shigella growth and triggers intracellular tolerance.
abstract: Pathogen survival relies on their ability to adapt to changing environments, yet how intracellular bacteria tolerate cell-autonomous immunity remains unclear. Septins assemble into cage-like structures around cytoplasmic Shigella targeted by autophagy, but their antibacterial activity was unknown. Using advanced microscopy and cell-free reconstitution, we show that septins polymerize into circumferentially oriented filaments that inhibit bacterial growth. RNA-sequencing reveals that septin binding to Shigella upregulates type III secretion system (T3SS) effectors and triggers a stress response. Underlying this, septin-bound Shigella possess hyperpolarized membranes, but without lethally damaged cell envelope. We show that exposure to septin binding enhances the impact of the cell envelope-targeting antibiotic polymyxin B. During infection, T3SS effector OspC1 prevents septin recruitment, while stress-response regulator cspC protects against septin-mediated changes to membrane potential. Hence, septin binding is intrinsically antibacterial and is sensed by Shigella as a danger signal to promote mechanisms of intracellular tolerance.
authors: Özbaykal Güler G, Zhang C, Brokatzky D, Das R, Wheeler R, Boneca IG, Cortes T, Manley S, Mostowy S.

title: A functional two-pore-domain K<sup>+</sup> channel from a large DNA virus.
abstract: The evolutionary history of proteins helps to understand their structure/function correlates and suggests on how functional complexity evolved from primitive precursors. In the superfamily of K+ channels, functional features of complex eukaryotic inward rectifier (Kir) channels and voltage-dependent (Kv) channels could be understood in terms of an increase in structural complexity of their prokaryotic precursors. K2P channels, which are made from tandem repeats of two pore domains, are not found in prokaryotes and their evolutionary origin is still unknown. In searching for primitive K2P channel precursors, we screened the genomes of nucleocytoplasmic large DNA viruses (NCLDVs) for genes coding for K2P channels. This was motivated by two reasons: NCLDVs are already known for coding primitive Kir type channels, and they play important roles in the evolution of eukaryotes. Here, we report that the NCLDV Pyramimonas orientalis virus codes for K2P-like K+ channels. With only 178 amino acids and no cytosolic domains, this Kpov protein is much smaller than any eukaryotic K2P channel, but still functional as K+ selective channel in lipid bilayers. Phylogenetic analysis suggests that Kpov is not the product of molecular piracy from the host but may result from fusion of primitive viral K+ channel pore domains.
authors: Rauh O, Mach S, Clarke O, Toews J, Van Etten JL, Althaus M, Moroni A, Thiel G.

title: c-FLIP loss links arrest of gene expression to TNFα-dependent antiviral guard immunity.
abstract: Cells sense infection through dedicated receptors, yet these surveillance pathways are often subverted by pathogen-encoded virulence factors. Guard immunity provides complementary defense by rapidly killing infected cells in response to infection induced stress. However, the symptoms of infection frequently resemble noninfectious stress, raising the question of how they are distinguished. Using quantitative transcriptomics, proteomics, and global translation measurements during viral infections in vitro and in vivo, we show that infection globally suppresses host gene expression and prevents direct antiviral responses. However, the resulting proteostatic stress does not activate guard immunity unless tumor necrosis factor-α (TNFα) is present. We identify the anti-apoptotic protein c-FLIP as a guard for gene expression integrity: its loss sensitizes cells to TNFα, triggering cell death and limiting viral spread. Modeling demonstrates that TNFα and c-FLIP loss function as a biological AND-gate, providing specificity and speed. These findings show how cells integrate internal stress signals with external inflammatory cues to improve the fidelity of death decisions, and how this circuitry may misfire during noninfectious inflammation.
authors: Sonnett M, Boersma S, Ward ME, Van Eyndhoven LC, Centofanti E, Brambach M, Zhou C, Knipe DM, Raj A, Oyler-Yaniv A, Oyler-Yaniv J.

title: Bridging spatial scales in respiratory viral infection.
abstract: Respiratory viruses spread within the host through a combination of local expansion and occasional long-range dissemination that seeds new infection foci. We present LEAP (Lotka-Euler Airway Pathogen model), an analytically tractable within-host model that captures this two-scale process. The model takes the form of an age-dependent branching process and yields a closed-form expression for the exponential growth rate during early infection. Using empirical data to parameterize the model, we find that productive dissemination requires only a small number of successful long-range seeding events per infected cell, with distinct values for SARS-CoV-2 and influenza A virus. LEAP further predicts that, in these well-adapted viruses, interferon-mediated restriction only weakly affects exponential growth, while remaining decisive for poorly adapted pathogens. More broadly, the model provides a flexible framework for experimentally testable predictions of early infection dynamics.
authors: Hvid U, Nielsen BF, Sneppen K.

title: A muscle-enriched mitochondrial protein regulates postnatal heart growth through mitonuclear ubiquinone-PPAR signaling.
abstract: Increased mitochondrial biogenesis and aerobic respiration in postnatal mammalian organs are essential for adaptation to extrauterine life, yet the functions of many tissue-enriched, developmentally regulated mitochondrial proteins remain poorly defined. By integrating mitochondrial proteome annotations with mouse and human transcriptomic datasets, we identified Coenzyme Q10a (Coq10a), a striated muscle-enriched mitochondrial protein, as a regulator of postnatal cardiac growth. Coq10a, the mammalian homolog of the yeast ubiquinone-binding protein Coq10p, is highly induced in the heart after birth through thyroid hormone-, Nkx2.5-, and Tbx5-dependent regulation. To define its physiological function, we generated three independent Coq10a-deficient mouse models. Both global and cardiomyocyte-specific loss of Coq10a promoted postnatal cardiac hypertrophy without impairing basal cardiac function or mitochondrial respiration. Instead, Coq10a deficiency altered intracellular ubiquinone partitioning, resulting in increased ubiquinone accumulation in a microsomal membrane fraction. Transcriptomic analyses revealed enrichment of PPAR-associated metabolic gene sets and induction of established PPAR-responsive genes in Coq10a-deficient hearts. Pharmacological inhibition of PPARα and PPARγ, but not PPARδ, attenuated the hypertrophic phenotype. Molecular dynamics simulations, docking analyses, and mutagenesis identified PPARα residues that contribute to differential responsiveness to ubiquinone. Although Coq10a-deficient hearts maintained near-normal function under basal conditions, they exhibited increased susceptibility to pressure-overload stress. Together, these findings establish Coq10a as a regulator of intracellular ubiquinone partitioning and support a model linking altered mitochondrial lipid distribution and PPAR-associated signaling to postnatal cardiac growth. More broadly, they demonstrate how tissue-enriched mitochondrial proteins can mediate organ-specific physiological functions beyond energy production.
authors: Hirose K, Chen X, Kalyanaraman C, Waddingham MT, Nakamura M, Zhang F, Chen C, Yao S, Chang S, Yu H, Wang J, Barca E, Nakano H, Hsu A, Khyeam S, Gonzalez Ortega S, Tajima K, Yoneshiro T, Zhang H, Padmanabhan A, Kajimura S, Haldar S, Nakano A, Murai M, Fujihara Y, Otsu K, Quinzii CM, Jacobson MP, Hu G, Pearson JT, Huang GN.

title: S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine triggers an adaptive response that extends lifespan through the YBT1 ABC transporter.
abstract: S-adenosyl-L-methionine (SAM) is a fundamental methyl donor; however, the physiological role of its byproduct and competitive inhibitor, S-adenosyl-L-homocysteine (SAH), remains unclear. Here, we show that transient reactive oxygen species (ROS) production triggered by SAH during the early logarithmic phase mimics partial SAH hydrolase inhibition, extending the yeast chronological lifespan (CLS) through a hormetic mechanism. This study reveals that the dual nature of ROS in aging is determined by the specific degree of SAH hydrolase activity. We identified the adenosine 5'-triphosphate-binding cassette (ABC) transporter Ybt1 as a key downstream effector of SAH. Ybt1 localizes to the vacuolar membrane and facilitates the sequestration of SAM from the cytosol into the vacuole. Notably, YBT1 overexpression extends CLS, mimicking SAH effects through an integrated pathway involving target of rapamycin complex 1 downregulation, autophagy, and adenosine 5'-monophosphate-activated protein kinase activation. Our findings establish that SAH acts as a metabolic signal coupling nutrient and energy availability to longevity via Ybt1, defining an adaptive/hormetic response for lifespan regulation in yeast.
authors: Masumura K, Kawasaki S, Tsutsumi M, Yamashita H, Kanai M, Nakajo H, Yagi W, Katsunoi S, Yoneyama K, Kawano-Kawada M, Sekito T, Ogawa T, Soga T, Mizunuma M.

title: The impact of modulator therapy on the Pseudomonas aeruginosa cystic fibrosis lung transcriptome.
abstract: Chronic lung infection with Pseudomonas aeruginosa is a major complication of cystic fibrosis (CF), contributing to lung function decline and increased morbidity and mortality. Laboratory models are used to study CF infections, but their relevance depends on how accurately they reproduce microbial physiology during human infection. We previously developed a framework that uses bacterial gene expression in human infections to quantify model accuracy. Here, we applied this framework to determine how a major therapeutic intervention impacts P. aeruginosa physiology in the lungs of people with CF (pwCF) and to develop and evaluate refined preclinical models. We focused on elexacaftor/tezacaftor/ivacaftor (ETI), a highly effective CFTR modulator therapy that has improved outcomes for pwCF. However, evidence indicates that P. aeruginosa lung infections persist despite ETI therapy. Analysis of P. aeruginosa transcriptomes from human sputum collected before and after ETI initiation revealed minimal changes in gene expression, indicating that the CF airway continues to support a similar bacterial transcriptional state despite therapy. We then evaluated how strain selection, zinc limitation, and polymicrobial coculture influence the ability of laboratory models to recapitulate P. aeruginosa gene expression in human CF sputum. Growth of CF clinical isolates in zinc-limited synthetic CF sputum medium produced the most accurate model, whereas population-based cultures and coculture with Staphylococcus aureus had limited effects. These findings show that ETI therapy has little impact on the conserved P. aeruginosa transcriptional state in human CF sputum and that refined sputum-like models remain useful for studying persistent infection in the postmodulator era.
authors: Letizia M, Whiteley LE, Diggle FL, Davis AN, Morgan SJ, Grogan B, Baugh J, McKone EF, Singh PK, Whiteley M.

title: Structural insights into the coupling mechanism of vectorial CO<sub>2</sub> uptake by DAB1.
abstract: CO2 transporters enable bacterial CO2-concentrating mechanisms by catalyzing directional hydration of CO2, yet the basis of this vectorial carbonic anhydrase (CA) activity remains an open question. We used cryoelectron microscopy to determine the structure of the DAB1 complex from Thermocrinis albus to 2.29 Å, revealing a heterotrimer in which a deeply buried β-CA active site in DabA is structurally coupled to the proton-translocating subunit DabB. Two conformational states define distinct solvent channels for substrate entry and product exit. A suppressor screen identifies mutations that disrupt coupling while retaining CA activity, underlying the importance of conserved residues that link proton translocation to active-site remodeling. These results support a model in which proton-driven conformational changes regulate substrate access to the active site, enabling vectorial CO2 hydration.
authors: Phillips NR, Oltrogge LM, Remis JP, Savage DF.

title: Nutrient legacies from elephant megacarcasses create coldspots of biodiversity and hotspots of ecosystem processes.
abstract: Terrestrial megafauna (animals >1,000 kg) have substantial impacts on ecosystems while alive; yet, we know little about the impacts of these ecosystem engineers after they die. Like whale carcasses in the ocean, terrestrial megacarcasses may leave ecological legacies via the nutrient pulses they create on the landscape. Here, we investigated the impact of elephant megacarcasses on savanna ecosystems in Kruger National Park, South Africa. To determine how elephant carcasses affect below- and aboveground biodiversity and ecosystem processes, we collected soil and plant samples from 40 carcass sites (pairing "on carcass" and "off carcass" samples) ranging from 8 d to 7.7 y postmortem. We found that elephant carcasses released enormous pools of nutrients into savanna soils, increasing ammonium by 31×, nitrate by 7×, and phosphorus by 3× on average. These extreme ammonium concentrations were negatively correlated with the biodiversity of bacteria and plants, which were both suppressed at elephant carcass sites. Despite these decreases in biodiversity, ecosystem processes were strongly elevated at elephant carcass sites, with soil microbial respiration elevated for 1 to 2 y and herbivore grazing >3× higher for 7+ y postmortem. These results demonstrate that elephant megacarcasses generate coldspots of biodiversity but hotspots of ecosystem processes, unveiling a cryptic ecological function of megaherbivores that is extreme in both magnitude and duration relative to carcasses of smaller animals. As humans drive terrestrial megafauna toward extinction, we risk losing not only their ecosystem engineering abilities while they are alive but also the ecological legacies their carcasses create after death.
authors: Reed CG, Lemoine NP, Budny ML, Clarke VC, du Toit JT, Helcoski R, Knoetze H, Lucas JM, Schimel JP, Smit IPJ, Strydom T, Tallian AG, Thompson DI, Burkepile DE.

title: Pyrrolysine supply and demand shapes the translational landscape in Methanosarcina acetivorans.
abstract: The amber stop codon (UAG) can encode for pyrrolysine (Pyl) or be read as a stop codon by methylamine-metabolizing organisms including methanogenic archaea. The fate of UAG is decided during the decoding step of translation by competition between the pyrrolysine-aminoacylated transfer RNA (Pyl-tRNAPyl) and release factor. To further understand the consequences of pyrrolysine based genetic code expansion, we integrated RNA sequencing, tRNA charging analysis, and codon-resolved mono- and disome ribosome profiling in Methanosarcina acetivorans. During conditions of high pyrrolysine demand, we observed increased expression of the pyrrolysine biosynthetic operon with a concurrent increase in acylation of tRNAPyl and ribosome occupancy at UAG codons. During low pyrrolysine demand, the population of Pyl-tRNAPyl decreases and we observe a strong ribosome pausing signal during UAG decoding. We find that the dwell time on UAG codons is shorter during high demand, but ribosome collisions increase due to greater ribosome density on UAG-containing transcripts. Together, these results show how pyrrolysine demand modulates tRNA charging and controls elongation dynamics, clarifying the cellular consequences of decoding an ambiguous stop codon.
authors: Britt GD, Utter DR, Park Y, Orphan VJ, Tollerson R.

title: Myeloid cell reprogramming drives enhanced defense against Streptococcus pneumoniae lung infection following exposure to commensal Prevotella.
abstract: Clinical data link the prevalent respiratory tract anaerobe Prevotella with reduced pneumonia mortality, but the mechanisms directing Prevotella regulation of lung immune homeostasis are unclear. Here, single-cell RNA sequencing was employed to define the transcriptional immune signatures underlying improved clearance of Streptococcus pneumoniae following lung exposure to Prevotella melaninogenica. Overall, we observed a substantial shift in myeloid cell transcriptional programming from interferon-dominant to a more antibacterial profile in S. pneumoniae-infected mice after pre-exposure to P. melaninogenica, correlating with increased macrophage and neutrophil phagocytosis of S. pneumoniae and improved pathogen clearance. In neutrophils, tumor necrosis factor (TNF) signaling through TNFR2 was essential for increased antimicrobial function. Moreover, improved defense required CCR2-dependent monocyte-derived macrophages, with selective enrichment of more a mature Cxcl3+ population which was distinct from the hallmark S. pneumoniae-associated C1qa+ population enriched in the absence of effective clearance. Together, these findings inform the myeloid cell transcriptional changes associated with natural infection resistance mediated by pulmonary microbial exposures.
authors: Stoner SN, Larson ED, Fulte S, Shaw SC, Fish ER, Janoff EN, Mack M, Clark SE.

title: Structural basis for membrane-dependent positive feedback regulation of DOCK11 by activated Cdc42.
abstract: The guanine nucleotide exchange factor DOCK11 is widely expressed across tissues and activates Cdc42, a Rho family GTPase that regulates cytoskeletal remodeling and cell polarity. Loss-of-function mutations in DOCK11 have recently been linked to inborn errors of immunity. DOCK11 has also been implicated in facilitating hepatitis B virus infection in hepatocytes and has emerged as a potential target for therapeutic interventions. A positive feedback mechanism has been proposed for DOCK11-mediated Cdc42 activation; however, the structural basis for this regulation has remained unclear. Here we report the cryoelectron microscopy structures of full-length DOCK11 as an apo dimer, a binary complex with nucleotide-free Cdc42, and a ternary complex containing both nucleotide-free and activated Cdc42. DOCK11 predominantly adopts a U-shaped dimer that binds to nucleotide-free Cdc42 via the catalytic domain, whereas activated Cdc42 engages a distal site within the armadillo-repeat domain. Biochemical and cellular analyses demonstrate that binding of activated Cdc42 is critical for enhancing the membrane-dependent nucleotide exchange activity of DOCK11, promoting its localization to the plasma membrane, and facilitating intracellular activation of Cdc42. We also determined the structure of the membrane-bound ternary complex using membrane-coated grids. Strikingly, the ternary complex adopts an extended conformation that aligns multiple membrane-contact elements, revealing how activated Cdc42 stabilizes DOCK11 membrane binding for efficient exchange activity. Collectively, these findings provide a structural framework for the coordinated mechanism underlying membrane-dependent positive feedback in Rho GTPase signaling.
authors: Hisano T, Shinoda T, Kukimoto-Niino M, Katsura K, Kondo R, Ishizuka-Katsura Y, Miyata-Yabuki Y, Hanada K, Nakagawa R, Nishikimi A, Shirouzu M.

title: Plant Identity Shapes Core Microbiomes on Green Roofs.
abstract: Extensive green roof substrates support plant-microbe interactions that may contribute to ecosystem functioning. Yet the role of plant identity in shaping substrate-associated microbiomes remains insufficiently resolved beyond Sedum-dominated systems. We examined bacterial and fungal communities associated with three plant species representing contrasting functional groups in sterilized and non-sterilized green roof substrates, integrating taxonomic differentiation with plant functional traits and predicted metabolic pathways. Plant identity was associated with distinct microbial community patterns in sterilized and non-sterilized substrates, and these associations varied with the substrate's initial microbial state. LEfSe identified 13 discriminant fungal genera in ITS data and 65 bacterial genera in V4 data; strong discriminant taxa included Mortierella, Schizothecium, and Serendipita in fungal communities, and Sphingomonas, Brevundimonas, and Tumebacillus in bacterial communities. Lotus corniculatus showed particularly distinct plant-associated microbial patterns, while differences in predicted metabolic pathways provided a complementary functional perspective on taxonomic differentiation. Integrating plant functional traits with bacterial and fungal community analyses provided an ecological framework for interpreting plant-associated microbiome differentiation in extensive green roof substrates. Integrating plant functional traits with microbial community analyses provides an ecological framework for interpreting plant-associated microbiome differentiation in extensive green roof substrates.
authors: Larysz K, Ludynia M, Trzebny A, Klencz W, Malcherczyk N, Sierka E.

title: Integrated Genotypic and Phenotypic Determinants Underpin the Environmental Persistence of Escherichia coli in Treated Sewage in Japan.
abstract: Escherichia coli poses global health risks, affecting human, animal, and environmental systems. To investigate the determinants underpinning its environmental persistence, we conducted an integrated genotypic and phenotypic analysis of 365 E. coli isolates recovered from treated sewage in Hiroshima, Japan. Isolates were confirmed by uidA-PCR and screened for virulence, antimicrobial resistance (AMR), phylogroup, and siderophore-associated genes using multiplex PCR. Phenotypic assays assessed biofilm formation on microtiter plates and motility on soft agar. Among the isolates, 13.7% carried one or more virulence genes, with astA being the most prevalent (70.0%), followed by eaeA (8.0%), bfpA (6.0%), and the aggR-astA combination (4.0%). AMR genes were detected in 50.0% of isolates, predominantly blaTEM. The major phylogroups were D (36.0%) and B1 (24.0%). All isolates carried entA-F and tonB, while fecA and chuA were the predominant accessory iron-acquisition genes (52.0%). Phenotypic analysis showed that 92.0% of isolates formed biofilms and 100.0% were motile. aggR-positive isolates exhibited the highest biofilm production, whereas astA-, bfpA-, and eaeA-positive isolates demonstrated greater motility than ipaH-positive isolates. Principal component analysis indicated that biofilm formation was associated with aggR, whereas motility showed an opposing trend. Together, these traits contribute to the environmental persistence of E. coli in treated sewage.
authors: Munfarida I, Caigoy JC, Xedzro C, Shimamoto T, Shimamoto T.

title: Artificial Intelligence for Predictive Microbiome Engineering: Integrating Community Design and Environmental Validation.
abstract: Microbial ecosystems can now be measured across genomic, transcriptomic, proteomic, metabolomic, and environmental dimensions, yet their emergent functions remain difficult to predict and control. Artificial intelligence (AI) can integrate heterogeneous data, but predictive accuracy alone does not establish causality, transferability, or controllability. This review developed a five-layer framework: observe, infer, predict, design, and learn that connects microbial measurement to prospective intervention and experimental feedback. We critically synthesise evidence from sequence and protein learning, multi-omics integration, metabolic modelling, synthetic microbial communities, environmental biotechnology, and temporal forecasting. Recent primary studies illustrate progress in forecasting community trajectories, predicting microbial competition and designing consortia for pollutant degradation; they also reveal important boundaries between model performance and demonstrated ecosystem control. We examine risks arising from compositional data, information leakage, dependent observations, batch effects, uncertain calibration, sparse perturbation data, ecological instability, and evolutionary change. We propose operational criteria for ecosystem programmability and a staged validation pathway from controlled systems to field-relevant environments. Progress will depend on standardised context-rich data, hybrid AI-mechanistic models, prospective benchmarks, independent replication, and safety-constrained design.
authors: Bhuiyan MNI, Hossain SJ.

title: Beyond Mycorrhizae: A Multi-Kingdom Community in Epiphytic Orchid Roots Reveals Cyanobacteria Intracellular and a Velamen Microbial Refuge.
abstract: Orchid biology has long been dominated by the paradigm of mycorrhizal dependency; however, the nutrient acquisition strategies of epiphytic orchids in canopy niches remain poorly understood. Using an integrated approach of multilocus metabarcoding (16S, ITS, 18S) and advanced microscopy (SEM, TEM, CLSM), we characterised the root microbial community of the threatened epiphytic orchid Cattleya purpurata. We report the discovery of intracellular Nostoc-like cyanobacteria within cortical cells, coexisting with the mycorrhizal fungus Tulasnella at a root colonisation rate of 18%. Furthermore, we identified: (1) a diverse velamen-associated microbiome hosting plant growth-promoting bacteria (e.g., the Burkholderia-Caballeronia-Paraburkholderia complex), nematodes and microalgae; and (2) a vast unknown fungal diversity, with over 39 genera and numerous ASVs unmatched in databases. We demonstrate that C. purpurata roots sustain a complex multi-kingdom community. We propose that the root velamen acts as a multi-kingdom microbial refuge, expanding the concept of symbiosis in orchids beyond fungi. Based on the intracellular presence of Nostoc-like cyanobacteria and their known diazotrophic capacity in other plant symbioses, we hypothesise a previously little-known nitrogen pathway mediated by cyanobacteria in a canopy environment, to be functionally tested in future studies.
authors: de Medeiros Oliveira E, Meyer E, Lovato PE, Guerra MP, Gris T, de Almeida AFN, Mayer JLS.

title: Quinone-trapping filaments enhance respiratory capacity.
abstract: Cells expand respiratory capacity by adding internal membranes or forming cristae. A new study by Kropp and colleagues shows that the Gram-positive bacterium Bacillus subtilis instead builds hollow protein filaments that sequester and transport quinones, extending the cell's respiratory capacity without adding membranes. This strategy, widespread across Bacillota, reveals an alternative route to bioenergetic expansion.
authors: Kumar A, Schuller JM.

title: Integrated Microbial Profiling Identifies Bacterial and Fungal Communities in Pseudomyxoma Peritonei Mucin.
abstract: Pseudomyxoma peritonei (PMP) is a rare mucinous malignancy in which tumour-associated microbial communities remain poorly characterised, particularly, their fungal component and spatial organisation. We applied an integrated workflow combining 16S and 18S rRNA gene sequencing, microbial culture, histochemical staining, chromogenic RNAscope in situ hybridisation and a patient-derived xenograft model to investigate bacterial and fungal communities in control tissues and low- and high-grade PMP mucin. Bacterial and fungal DNA was detected in PMP-associated mucin, with grade-associated differences in bacterial composition and predicted functional potential. Viable bacteria were recovered from human PMP samples and xenograft-derived mucin. Fungal structures were independently supported by periodic acid-Schiff and Calcofluor White staining, while RNAscope localised bacterial 16S and fungal 18S rRNA signals within epithelial and mucin-rich tumour regions. Comparable microbial signals were observed in the xenograft model. Together, these complementary approaches identify PMP mucin as a multi-kingdom microbial niche and provide the first characterisation of its associated mycobiome. This integrated analytical framework may facilitate the investigation of microorganisms in other low-biomass, mucin-rich tumour environments and provides a basis for future mechanistic studies of microbe-host interactions in PMP.
authors: Pezzopane R, Barbudo-Lunar M, Bura FI, Granados-Rodríguez M, Martínez-López A, Rodríguez-Ortiz L, Rufián-Andújar B, López-Jiménez J, Luna-Guerrero V, Alhama J, Michán C, Vázquez-Borrego MC, Arjona-Sánchez Á, Romero-Ruiz A.

title: The Arms Race Between Bacteria and Their Viruses: Update on Phage Countermeasures Against Bacterial Defence Systems.
abstract: In this editorial, I summarize recent progress on phage-encoded anti-defence against bacterial anti-phage systems (APS). Computational approaches based on structural predictions of co-folding bacterial and phage proteins identified many new PAD sponge proteins. New anti-CRISPR-Cas systems were characterized that destroy cas12a mRNA, inactivate Cas12a by acetylation, engage the seed region of the crRNA, or prevent Cas3 from cleaving DNA. The phage defence protein Gad1 forms an octamer web that wraps around the complex of the Gabija APS. Tad1 and 2 are phage sponge proteins that sequester signalling nucleotides of the Thoeris APS. Tad3 to 7 interact directly with the ThsB sensor and Tad8 with the ThsA effector of the Thoeris APS. Phage sponge proteins were also described inactivating the CBASS and Pycsar APS. Still other phages use phosphodiesterases that cleave cyclic nucleotide signals to inactivate APS. Many bacterial APS effectors are NADase, destroying the essential metabolite NAD+. Phages evolved enzymes that resynthesize NAD+ from its cleavage products or proteins directly inactivating the NADase. Many phages degrade the bacterial genome which creates signals activating the Metis or the Kongming APS. Phages counteracted these APS by suppressing pathways leading to the creation of particular mononucleotides degradation products detected by these APS. Several APS cleave specific tRNA, phages responded by mutating cleavage sites in tRNA (anti-PARIS) or increasing tRNA expression to compensate for their destruction (anti-Septu). Phages counteract toxin-antitoxin APS by evolving their own antitoxin or by blocking the toxin protein. Researchers described cases where phages escaped detection by mutating phage proteins detected by bacterial sensors. Against the stringent response phages responded by destroying alarmones or inactivating enzymes producing these stress signals. The arms race between bacteria and phages can involve complicated layers of defence and anti-defences and both bacteria and phages encode multiple defence systems.
authors: Brüssow H.

title: Systematic Evaluation of Cyanidioschyzon merolae Across Photobioreactor Systems: Linking Reactor Design to Biomass Production and Biochemical Composition.
abstract: Extremophilic red microalgae are promising platforms for sustainable biotechnology, combining robust growth under selective thermoacidophilic conditions with production of thermostable phycobiliproteins and carbon-rich biomass. However, reactor-dependent effects on growth, product formation, and biomass composition remain insufficiently resolved. Here, we systematically evaluated the extremophilic red microalga Cyanidioschyzon merolae across cultivation scales and reactor formats and benchmarked its performance against the well-established Galdieria javensis and Limnospira platensis. In small-scale multi-cultivator photobioreactors and microfluidic growth chambers, C. merolae showed superior growth, reaching a maximum growth rate of 0.034 ± 0.001 h-1 and 8.3 ± 0.3 g L-1 cell dry weight. Microfluidic cultivation enabled growth analysis at single-cell resolution and matched growth rates obtained in photobioreactors. To identify scalable production strategies, C. merolae was further cultivated in a flat-panel photobioreactor (FPR) and a custom-designed internally illuminated photobioreactor (IIPBR). The custom-designed photobioreactor delivered the highest biomass concentration and productivity, yielding 11.5 ± 0.6 g L-1 cell dry weight and 1.07 ± 0.06 g L-1 d-1, and comparable yields with regard to R-phycocyanin and R-allophycocyanin (R-APC). Biomass analysis revealed substantial carbon and nitrogen contents, starch accumulation up to > 20% of cell dry weight, and fatty acids dominated by palmitic, linoleic, and oleic acids. Despite its reduced cell wall fraction, C. merolae contained structurally diverse, cultivation-dependent polysaccharides. These results establish C. merolae as a versatile chassis for thermostable pigment production and renewable feedstock generation, highlighting photobioreactor design as a key determinant of productivity and biomass quality.
authors: Ernst P, Vanselow J, Denter M, Li W, Witting L, Gätgens J, Pauly M, Kohlheyer D, Urlacher VB, Feldbrügge M, Frunzke J.

title: Unravelling the Chemolithoautotrophic Metabolism of the Carboxydotrophic Knallgas Bacterium Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava.
abstract: The sustainable production of chemicals is critical to reducing greenhouse gas emissions and environmental pollution. Gaseous feedstocks from industrial waste streams and waste gasification, including CO, CO2 and H2, represent abundant and underutilized resources for biotechnology. Syngas fermentation has been predominantly studied under anaerobic conditions, whereas aerobic processes may offer advantages for the biosynthesis of energy-intensive products. One promising organism is the aerobic carboxydotroph Hydrogenophaga pseudoflava DSM 1084, whose chemolithoautotrophic metabolism remains poorly understood. To address this, we performed proteome analysis under different growth conditions and characterized deletion mutants of key enzymes involved in CO and H2 oxidation. Deletion mutants showed that only CO dehydrogenase I and the membrane-bound hydrogenase are essential for CO and H2 oxidation, respectively. The role of the putative second CO dehydrogenase remains to be elucidated, and the soluble hydrogenase may contribute to redox balancing under microaerobic or anaerobic conditions. In addition, the H2-sensing regulatory system appears to be nonfunctional, and the transhydrogenase PntAB supports redox homeostasis during chemolithoautotrophic growth. Electrons from CO or H2 are transferred via the reduced quinone pool to NADH through proton-motive force-driven reverse electron transfer. Nevertheless, growth on CO remains slower than on CO2/H2. In contrast to CO2/H2, an unphysiologically high CO concentration (80%) led to a major proteome rearrangement, with 1879 of 3640 reliably quantified proteins showing altered abundance compared to fructose-grown cells, including a pronounced stress response. Under such conditions, cells are likely to invest additional energy to maintain redox balance. Together with the less energy-conserving autotrophic branch of the respiratory chain and cytoplasmic CO oxidation, this results in inefficient CO conversion and reduced growth.
authors: Grieshaber S, Ebert A, Kehr P, Siebert DL, Al-Shameri A, Sieber V, Ebert BE, Marcellin E, Blombach B.

title: Unilateral cross-feeding constrains adaptive evolution, even in the producer without direct fitness effects.
abstract: Cross-feeding interactions are pervasive in microbial communities and profoundly shape community structure, stability, and function. While previous studies have explored how cross-feeding affects evolvability, this work has predominantly focused on bidirectional mutualistic interactions in engineered auxotrophic systems where both partners reciprocally exchange essential metabolites. However, most metabolic interactions in natural microbial communities are unidirectional, with organisms feeding on the metabolic waste products of other species. Our study addresses this gap by examining how a unidirectional cross-feeding interaction affects the evolutionary dynamics of both the producer (Acinetobacter johnsonii) and consumer (Pseudomonas putida) over 800 generations of experimental evolution. We found that co-culture constrained adaptive evolution in both species. Co-cultures exhibited lower πN/πS ratios (0.75 for P. putida; 1.04 for A. johnsonii) than monocultures (1.44 and 2.02, respectively), indicating stronger purifying selection against nonsynonymous mutations in the community context. Lineage tracking through whole genome sequencing of populations and clones revealed greater lineage diversity and complexity in monocultures, with more mutations showing significant parallelism across replicate populations. Additionally, P. putida evolved increased dependence on its partner; co-culture-evolved P. putida grew significantly worse than its ancestor when A. johnsonii was removed. These findings indicate that ecological interactions can reshape fitness landscapes and constrain adaptive evolution even when fitness benefits are unidirectional, with implications for understanding microbial community stability and predicting evolutionary dynamics in complex communities.
authors: Al-Tameemi Z, Rosazza T, Rodríguez-Verdugo A.

title: Microbiome-dependent phytosterol sulfates production and tissue distribution in mice.
abstract: Microbial biotransformation of dietary lipids, such as cholesterol, influences host homeostasis. Despite extensive studies on animal sterols in host-microbiota interactions, the role of phytosterols in homeostasis remains unclear. In this study, we characterized phytosterol sulfates as microbiota-derived metabolites using untargeted lipidomic data mining. The levels of sitosterol sulfate (SIS), campesterol sulfate, and stigmasterol sulfate, the three major phytosterol sulfates, along with coprostanol sulfate, were reduced in the feces of germ-free mice compared with those of specific pathogen-free mice. We characterized a series of Bacteroidota species and their sterol sulfotransferases that produced phytosterol sulfates more efficiently than mammalian enzymes. Furthermore, SIS significantly accumulated in host tissues in a microbiota- and age-dependent manner, whereas unconjugated phytosterols were mostly undetectable. Our work provides insights into host-microbiome interactions via gut bacterial phytosterol metabolism.
authors: Tomita K, Nakano T, Morozumi S, Okahashi N, Arita M.

title: LPS and quorum sensing protect Pseudomonas aeruginosa bacteria from phagocytosis and destruction by Dictyostelium discoideum amoebae.
abstract: Free-living amoebae like Dictyostelium discoideum and environmental bacteria like Pseudomonas aeruginosa are engaged in complex predator-prey interactions. Amoeba can notably ingest and kill bacteria. In this study, we report that three different strains of the opportunistic pathogen Pseudomonas aeruginosa are protected from amoebal phagocytosis. Analysis of P. aeruginosa mutants revealed that OSA-type lipopolysaccharides (LPS) allow these P. aeruginosa strains to escape phagocytosis by amoebae. Amoebae can also kill extracellularly un-ingested P. aeruginosa bacteria. Our results indicate that induction of the Las quorum sensing (QS) makes P. aeruginosa resistant to reactive oxygen species, to bacteriolytic factors secreted by D. discoideum, and ultimately to extracellular destruction by amoebae. Together, these observations suggest that LPS and QS probably play a key role in P. aeruginosa escape strategies against phagocytic amoebae in the environment and shed new light on the transition of infectious P. aeruginosa from the environment to the human body.
authors: Ayadi I, Pain E, Oddy J, Lamrabet O, Vijay H, Koehler T, Distler T, Persat A, Munoz-Ruiz R, Cosson P.

title: High-risk ARGs in environmental E. coli from the Taihu Lake watershed.
abstract: The global antimicrobial-resistance crisis is exacerbated by environmental bacterial reservoirs. This work investigated antibiotic-resistance genes (ARGs) carried by E. coli from 118 surface-water samples across the Taihu Lake watershed. We isolated E. coli using mTEC agar and uidA PCR and screened isolates for 92 ARGs covering 15 resistance classes. Samples from Huzhou showed higher ARG detection rates than samples from other regions, with aminoglycoside, sulfonamide, and glycopeptide resistance genes predominant. Urban sampling sites represented ARG hotspots. Co-occurrence analysis revealed associations between quinolone and aminoglycoside resistance genes, suggestive of horizontal gene transfer. Risk assessment categorized 25.3% of samples as high risk. These observations illustrate human-driven ARG pollution in local aquatic environments and support targeted surveillance and One Health-oriented mitigation strategies.
authors: Wang A, Xu X, Jiang W, Li B, Zhu W, Xiao Q, Xu L, Sun J, Chen K, Yi Y, Guo Y, Qiang X, He J, Zhou H, Lin Y, Wang X.

title: Arbitrium crosstalk enables shared signaling among phages.
abstract: The arbitrium system has transformed our understanding of phage biology by demonstrating that temperate phages communicate through extracellular peptides to coordinate lysis-lysogeny decisions. Initially considered a highly specific signaling pathway restricted to individual phage lineages, arbitrium communication has now been shown to extend beyond lineage boundaries in some phage systems. Recent studies have shown that non-cognate arbitrium peptides can interact with heterologous receptors, providing evidence of inter-phage crosstalk. Here, we synthesize current knowledge of the molecular basis of arbitrium signaling, the structural determinants of peptide-receptor specificity, and the potential ecological and evolutionary consequences of inter-phage communication. We suggest that arbitrium crosstalk may shape phage ecology by mediating competitive and potentially cooperative interactions within shared signaling environments. We also discuss its potential uses in engineered phage systems, synthetic biology, and microbiome engineering. Collectively, the available evidence broadens the concept of viral communication beyond lineage-specific signaling, while the ecological significance and practical applications of arbitrium crosstalk remain to be established.
authors: Lomeli-Ortega CO, Balcázar JL.

title: Baseline microbial ecology encodes probiotic responsiveness through distinct metabolic and network configurations.
abstract: Probiotic efficacy in inflammatory bowel disease varies widely between individuals, and the sources of that variability remain poorly understood. D-lactate is a microbiota-derived metabolite that accumulates during intestinal inflammation and is associated with epithelial barrier dysfunction, which motivated our use of a consortium selected to contribute none of it. Here we show that its benefit is not an intrinsic property of the administered strains but is determined by the pre-existing ecological state of the recipient microbiome. Across three independent mouse resources, preventive administration reduced disease severity and histopathological damage only where baseline communities carried higher diversity and more complex co-occurrence architecture; in those animals the consortium preserved community structure and metabolic output, restoring disease-disrupted metabolites, and selectively raising butyrate and propionate. Sustained exogenous D-lactate did not abolish protection, placing D-lactate as a tractable readout of ecological restoration rather than its effector. Responsiveness is encoded in the baseline microbiota and predictable before intervention, establishing probiotic efficacy as a stratifiable property of the host microbiome.
authors: Li J, Özkurt AG, Baertschi I, Wang J, Aeschlimann L, Goepfert C, Misselwitz B, Sokollik C, Yilmaz B.

title: Structural remodeling and activation of the hdeAB and proVWX operons in response to pH and salt stress.
abstract: Escherichia coli is highly sensitive to acid and osmotic stress but adapts by modulating the expression of stress-responsive genes. Nucleoid-associated proteins (NAPs) play key roles in DNA organization and sensing environmental changes. The histone-like nucleoid structuring protein H-NS is an NAP acting as a global regulator of stress genes. H-NS may alter local chromatin structure to modulate the expression of such genes in response to environmental stress. The H-NS homolog suppressor of td phenotype A (StpA) co-regulates several target genes, but its role is poorly defined. To investigate the regulatory interplay between these two proteins, we examined transcription, DNA binding, and chromatin structure at two regulated operons, hdeAB and proVWX, in E. coli following exposure to acid and salt shock. Our results show that H-NS senses pH and osmotic cues to remodel chromatin and relieve repression, while StpA-in part-compensates for H-NS loss, particularly at proVWX, highlighting a coordinated regulatory network.
authors: Ge P, Rashid FM, Gaarthuis LKF, Cajili MKM, Tan M, Pang B, Schnetz K, Dame RT.

title: E2 displacement of CIP2A from TOPBP1 activates the DNA damage response during papillomavirus life cycles.
abstract: The papillomavirus life cycle is linked to epithelial differentiation, and the virus manipulates differentiation to facilitate viral production. One such manipulation is the activation of the DNA damage response (DDR), which promotes viral replication via homologous recombination. Here, we show that the papillomavirus transcription/replication/segregation factor E2 activates the DDR. During differentiation, E2 attenuates sirtuin 1 (SIRT1) activity, enhances the acetylation of DDR factors, and displaces cancerous inhibitor of protein phosphatase 2A (CIP2A) from DNA topoisomerase II-binding protein 1 (TOPBP1), resulting in CIP2A-mediated inhibition of protein phosphatase 2A (PP2A) and ataxia-telangiectasia mutated (ATM) activation. E2 associates with TOPBP1 and ATM while reducing TOPBP1-ATR complexes and ataxia-telangiectasia and Rad3-related (ATR) activation. This ATM-high, ATR-low DDR phenotype promotes viral replication and cell proliferation. We observe this DDR activation in E2-expressing keratinocytes, human papillomavirus 16 (HPV16)-positive cells, Mus musculus papillomavirus 1 (MmuPV1)-induced lesions, HPV-positive head and neck cancer cell lines, and HPV16-positive patient-derived xenografts. ATM inhibition preferentially kills E2-expressing cells, supporting ATM signaling as a potential therapeutic target in HPV-associated disease retaining E2 expression and episomal genomes.
authors: Prabhakar AT, James CD, Nguyen AQ, Bridy PV, Wang X, Zoldork RJ, Roe JD, Witt AJ, Panidepu SS, Giri S, Bristol ML, Dalton K, Wieland A, Diab A, Faber AC, Androphy EJ, Basu D, Lambert PF, Spurgeon ME, Morgan IM.

title: Glycolipid MPIase is essential for the TAT (twin-arginine translocation) pathway.
abstract: TAT (twin-arginine translocation) is a preprotein translocation system dedicated to membrane translocation of prefolded proteins in plants and bacteria. The TAT translocon, consisting of the TatABC subunits, drives translocation using proton motive force. However, there have been no reports on the successful reconstitution of the TAT system. In this report, we show that MPIase, a glycolipid that has been known to catalyze membrane protein integration, is essential for the TAT system. Our findings in recombinant Escherichia coli demonstrate that overproducing TatABC increases MPIase levels, and that depleting MPIase results in TAT precursor accumulation in the cytosol. Furthermore, co-reconstitution of MPIase with TatABC revealed the translocation activities of TAT substrates in a proton motive force-dependent manner. This is the first successful reconstitution of the TAT system and will be advantageous for understanding its mechanisms.
authors: Nishikawa H, Yamamoto N, Kunezaki H, Shirogane Y, Kanno K, Sawasato K, Yamada M, Nishiyama KI.

title: Quantifying microbial fitness in high-throughput experiments.
abstract: Few concepts are as central to evolution as is fitness, and yet the quantification of fitness is often ambiguous. In particular, high-throughput experiments to measure mutant fitness in microbes are increasingly common, but vary widely in their definitions of fitness, which makes their results difficult to compare. What are the consequences of these different fitness statistics, and is there a best way to quantify fitness in a given context? Here, we systematize the set of possible fitness statistics according to the following three choices: (1) the encoding of relative abundance (e.g., transforming by a log or logit function), (2) the time scale over which to measure the change in relative abundance, and (3) the choice of a reference subpopulation for calculating relative fitness in bulk competition experiments, such as those using DNA-barcoded mutants. We show that these different choices can lead to significantly different interpretations of mutant fitness in Saccharomyces cerevisiae and Escherichia coli, affecting the magnitude of fitness effects, the apparent presence of epistasis, and even the fitness ranking across mutants. This can confound predictions for evolutionary dynamics and gene functions. Altogether, our results demonstrate the importance of consistent fitness definitions for reproducible results across experiments.
authors: Fink JW, Manhart M.

title: Lateral opening site of human oligopeptide transporter 2 plays a key role in the interaction with polymyxins.
abstract: Multidrug-resistant (MDR) Gram-negative bacteria pose a critical global health threat, while polymyxins remain a last-line therapy. However, their clinical use is limited by nephrotoxicity. Human oligopeptide transporter 2 (hPepT2) is a membrane transporter mediating the reabsorption of polymyxins in renal cells and contributes to their nephrotoxicity, but the molecular basis of their interaction remains unclear. Here, we investigated the structure-interaction relationship (SIR) of polymyxins with hPepT2 by integrating computational, chemical, and cell biology approaches. Bioinformatic modeling predicted an outward-facing hPepT2 structure and a potential transport pathway, with polymyxins interacting at the lateral opening, particularly E214, D215, D317, D342, and E622. Transporter mutagenesis and molecular analyses confirmed that D215 is critical for polymyxin binding, while other residues influence transporter turnover and/or expression. We subsequently synthesized polymyxin analogs with modifications at Dab1, Dab3, Dab5, and Dab9 of polymyxins, which reduced interactions with hPepT2. Notably, alanine substitution at Dab3 reduced nephrotoxicity in mice while retaining antibacterial activity. Overall, this proof-of-concept study demonstrates that the hPepT2-polymyxin SIR model provides a viable strategy for developing novel, safer lipopeptide antibiotics.
authors: Jiang X, Luo Y, Azad MAK, Xu L, Xiao M, Velkov T, Roberts KD, Thamlikitkul V, Zhou QT, Zhou F, Li J.

title: Structural insights into peptidoglycan hydrolysis by the FtsEX system in Escherichia coli during cell division.
abstract: Bacterial cell division relies on precise peptidoglycan (PG) remodeling, a process orchestrated by the FtsEX complex. Comprised of FtsE and FtsX, this complex collaborates with EnvC, a periplasmic lytic enzyme activator, to regulate septal PG hydrolysis by amidases like AmiB. While recent structural investigations, particularly of Pseudomonas aeruginosa FtsEX (PaeFtsEX), have shed light on complex interactions and proposed activation mechanisms, the structural intricacies governing PG degradation by the FtsEX complex and EnvC in Escherichia coli cytokinesis remain unexplored. In this study, we present a comprehensive biochemical and structural analysis of E. coli FtsEX complexes, unveiling a key role for ATP in complex stabilization that extends across bacterial species. Upon EnvC binding, ATPase activity markedly increases. High-resolution structures of EcoFtsEX, both in the presence and absence of EnvC, reveal a symmetrical conformation of EcoFtsEX capable of accommodating the inherent asymmetry of EnvC, mediated by flexible loops within the periplasmic domain. Our negative-staining imaging showcases an elongated EcoFtsEX/EnvC/AmiB complex reminiscent of the PaeFtsEX system. These findings collectively provide intricate insights into the regulation of PG cleavage by FtsEX in E. coli-a pivotal model system used in pilot genetic studies, suggesting a conserved mechanism for precise hydrolase activation in bacteria.
authors: Li J, He Y, Xu X, Alcorlo M, Shi J, Naskar S, Briggs NS, Roper DI, Hermoso JA, Sham LT, Luo M.

title: Out-of-balance growth enables cost-free synthesis of the flagellum and other proteins in a single bacterium.
abstract: The cost of expressing unnecessary genes on growth has been explained at the population level through balanced growth assumptions. However, due to the high degree of stochasticity in growth and gene regulation, it remains unclear how classical growth laws derived from bulk measurements manifest at the level of individual cells. For example, flagellar gene expression, one of the most energy-intensive processes in Escherichia coli, is typically associated with reduced growth rates in bulk measurements. By contrast, we find at the single-cell level that a strikingly opposite behavior coexists: flagellar gene activity is associated with an increase in growth rate. We show that this apparent contradiction, reminiscent of Simpson's paradox, results from examining in each cell instantaneous growth and gene expression without indiscriminately aggregating the single-cell data like in bulk measurements. We attribute this unrecognized behavior to out-of-balance growth boosts that temporarily offset the burden of flagellum production, likely driven by a surplus of growth factors inherited across cell division. Furthermore, we show that this non-intuitive relationship between growth and gene expression at the single-cell level is general, as we observe similar effects with synthetic systems driving the expression of fluorescent proteins downstream of constitutive promoters. Finally, we use a computational model to show that the inheritance of parental growth factors can explain the apparent contradiction and constitutes a general mechanism for mitigating the short-term cost of nonessential and biosynthetically demanding genes in the single cell.
authors: Garcia Alcala MP, Kratz JC, Cluzel P.

title: Tracking West Nile virus dynamics using viral loads from trapped mosquitoes.
abstract: Mosquito-borne virus transmission is increasing globally. Due to a lack of effective vaccines or targeted treatments, mitigation relies on reducing human exposure to infectious mosquitoes. Entomological surveillance provides estimates of human risk by quantifying the prevalence of arboviruses in mosquito populations. Testing of pooled mosquitoes via RT-qPCR is often used to infer infection prevalence; however, these data are often binarised and ignore semi-quantitative cycle threshold (Ct values) that may provide valuable information on virus kinetics, mosquito infectiousness, and ultimately human risk. West Nile virus (WNV) is a globally distributed arbovirus and endemic to the United States. In this study, we analysed pooled Ct values from retrospective mosquito surveillance and found substantial variation that could not be explained by laboratory factors alone. To understand how underlying viral load and epidemiological dynamics might explain this variation, we developed a multi-scale model linking pooled Ct values to heterogeneous within-host viral kinetics in mosquitoes and birds and seasonal transmission dynamics. Our modelling suggests that Ct values from positive pools might reflect a mixture of potentially infectious and non-infectious mosquitoes, indicating that a substantial proportion of PCR-positive mosquitoes might not contribute to transmission. We then developed a method to estimate mosquito infection prevalence using only pooled Ct values that distinguishes infectious from non-infectious prevalence. Estimates of overall prevalence were comparable to standard methods using binarised data and remained accurate at higher prevalences where standard approaches fail. Overall, these findings demonstrate that entomological viral load data reflect biologically meaningful variation in mosquito infection status that is lost through binarisation. Accounting for heterogeneous mosquito viral kinetics can improve interpretation of surveillance data and estimates of transmission risk, with implications for arbovirus surveillance beyond WNV.
authors: Alahakoon P, Marchinton I, Koch R, Fauver JR, Hay JA.

title: Correction: Inhibitors of the small membrane (M) protein viroporin prevent Zika virus infection.
authors: Brown E, Swinscoe G, Lefteri DA, Singh R, Moran A, Thompson RF, Maskell D, Beaumont H, Bentham MJ, Donald C, Kohl A, Macdonald A, Ranson NA, Foster R, McKimmie CS, Kalli AC, Griffin S.

title: Novel but stable endosymbionts have contrasting effects on aphid dispersal and plant feeding damage in the cereal pest Diuraphis noxia.
abstract: Endosymbiotic bacteria can affect many ecological attributes of their insect hosts, including (in herbivorous insects) how they interact with plants where they feed. This raises the issue of whether deliberate endosymbiont introductions could be used to decrease crop damage caused by insect pests. Here, we investigate how transinfecting Rickettsiella viridis and Regiella insecticola endosymbionts into a novel pest aphid host, the Russian wheat aphid (Diuraphis noxia), influences population growth, alate production, dispersal ability, and crop damage. Both the Rickettsiella (originating from pea aphids) and Regiella (from green peach aphids) were stably maintained in their new host where they had contrasting effects. Rickettsiella increased the severity of aphid feeding damage on wheat and barley, resulting in greater leaf loss, chlorotic streaking, and higher aphid populations, whereas Regiella reduced aphid population growth and the severity of feeding damage by aphids. Their effects on dispersal morphology also differed: Regiella had no detectable impact on alate incidence, while Rickettsiella consistently suppressed wing formation in small cages, and in larger mesocosms with multiple wheat plants this endosymbiont suppressed dispersal. Endosymbiont-mediated changes in feeding damage did not involve the main plant immune response pathways: transinfected and wild type aphids induced similar levels of jasmonic acid, jasmonic acid-isoleucine, and salicylic acid in plant tissues, even though these plant defenses were strongly activated during aphid feeding. Novel endosymbionts can therefore modulate the severity of plant feeding damage by aphids as well as influencing aphid dispersal. Potential applications in controlling pest D. noxia populations are discussed.
